If you don't have that resource, Vapi will eat your budget and ship a mediocre agent. Pricing: $0.05/minute platform fee plus pass-through costs for the LLM, voice model, and transcription. Real-world cost per minute: $0.14-$0.22. Slightly cheaper than Retell at scale, more expensive at low volume. Conflict-check handling: Vapi's tool-calling is as capable as Retell's but requires more scaffolding. You're building the integration from scratch unless you buy a template. For firms running Filevine or Litify (which have less mature public APIs than Clio), Vapi's flexibility is actually the only path that doesn't require months of custom work. Conversion data: Highly bimodal. Well-built Vapi agents at firms with technical teams or sophisticated agencies hit 46-53% consult booking — the highest of the three, matching senior human specialists. Poorly built ones hit 22-28% and actively damage brand perception. Vapi is the right call only if you can commit to a $7,500-$15,000 initial build and ongoing optimization.

The conflict-check problem nobody solves cleanly

Every PI firm's bar counsel will tell you the AI cannot represent that it's running a definitive conflict check — because it isn't. What it can do is a preliminary adverse-party screen against your existing client database, flag potential conflicts, and route those to a human review queue before the consult is confirmed. Here's the workflow that holds up across all three platforms: 1. Agent collects caller name, DOB, incident date, other-party name, insurance carrier 2. Agent calls a function that queries your CMS (Clio, Litify, Filevine) for name matches on adverse parties 3. If match found: agent says "I need to have an attorney review a quick detail before we confirm — can I have someone call you back within 2 hours?" and flags the lead 4. If no match: agent proceeds to book the consult directly into the attorney's calendar 5. A disclosure runs at call open: "This is an automated intake assistant. A conflict check will be completed by our team before your consultation." That disclosure matters. Several state bars (notably California, New York, and Florida) have issued guidance that AI-handled client intake needs clear disclosure. Build it in from day one. Retell and Vapi handle this cleanly via system prompts; Synthflow requires you to script it explicitly in the opening node.

AI vs human intake specialists: the honest conversion comparison

I pulled booking data from six PI firms running A/B tests between AI voice agents and human intake specialists over 60-90 day windows. Here's what the numbers actually say: - Senior human intake specialists (3+ years PI experience): 52-61% consult booking rate on after-hours leads returned the next morning

  • Junior human intake specialists: 38-45%
  • Legal answering services (Alert, Ngage, Smith.ai): 29-36%
  • Well-built Retell/Vapi agents (live, 24/7): 41-53%
  • Default-template Synthflow agents: 28-34% The critical variable is time to contact. A senior human specialist calling back at 9am Monday converts at 54% on a Friday-night lead. The same lead, handled live at 11pm Friday by a competent AI, converts at 47%. The AI loses 7 points on skill but wins back 15+ points on immediacy and the "while I'm still motivated" factor. Net-net: a well-deployed AI voice agent for after-hours intake outperforms callback-based human intake by 8-14 percentage points on raw booked consults, and outperforms legal answering services by 12-18 points. During business hours, humans still win. The right stack is AI for 6pm-8am and weekends, humans during business hours, with warm handoff capability between them.

The implementation stack that actually works

For a mid-sized PI firm (5-25 attorneys) wanting production-grade after-hours intake, this is the stack that performs: - Voice agent: Retell AI (default recommendation) or Vapi if you have technical resources

  • CMS integration: Clio or Litify via direct API, with a Supabase mirror for sub-second conflict lookups
  • Calendar: Lawmatics or Calendly with round-robin routing to attorneys on intake rotation
  • Call tracking: CallRail with AI-handled calls tagged separately for ROI analysis
  • CRM/follow-up: Lawmatics or GoHighLevel for SMS follow-up on consults within 10 minutes of booking
  • QA layer: Weekly review of 20 random call transcripts, prompt refinement every 2 weeks for the first 90 days Build cost: $4,500-$12,000 depending on complexity and whether you're doing it in-house or with an agency. Monthly operating cost: $600-$1,200 for a firm handling 150-500 after-hours calls. Expected payback: A single additional signed PI case per month at a $25,000 average fee covers 20+ months of operating cost. Firms I've worked with typically see 3-7 additional signed cases monthly after full deployment, which is why this stopped being optional about 18 months ago.

The bottom line

If you want the shortest answer: Retell AI is the right pick for most PI firms evaluating after-hours intake today. It hits the sweet spot of voice quality, conflict-check cleanliness, and conversion performance without requiring a dedicated engineering team. Synthflow is the right pick only if you have zero technical resources and need something live this week. Vapi is the right pick only if you have a serious technical partner and want to build the long-term differentiated system. The bigger point: the firms still routing after-hours PI calls to voicemail or a generic answering service are leaving six figures of signed-case value on the table every quarter. Pick a platform, build the flow properly, and measure booked-consult conversion against your human intake baseline within 60 days. The math either works or it doesn't — and in this category, it almost always does.

faq.question: Can an AI voice agent legally run a conflict check for a law firm?
faq.answer: The AI can run a preliminary adverse-party screen against your existing client database and flag potential conflicts for human review — it cannot and should not represent that it's completing a definitive conflict check. State bar guidance (notably CA, NY, FL) requires clear disclosure that intake is AI-handled and that a formal conflict check will be completed by firm staff before any representation.

faq.question: How much does a production AI voice intake agent cost per month for a PI firm?
faq.answer: For a firm handling 150-500 after-hours calls monthly, total operating cost runs $600-$1,200 including platform fees, voice/LLM pass-through, and CRM integration. Initial build cost is $4,500-$12,000 depending on complexity and whether you work with an agency or build in-house.

faq.question: Will AI voice agents convert PI leads as well as human intake specialists?
faq.answer: Well-built Retell or Vapi agents convert after-hours leads at 41-53%, compared to 52-61% for senior human specialists handling callbacks the next morning. The AI's conversion gap on skill is more than offset by immediacy — live AI contact at midnight outperforms a human callback at 9am by 8-14 percentage points on booked consults.

faq.question: Which case management systems integrate best with AI voice agents?
faq.answer: Clio has the most mature public API and integrates cleanly with Retell, Vapi, and Synthflow via direct calls or Zapier. Litify and Filevine have less mature APIs and typically require Vapi's deeper customization or a middleware layer. Mirror your conflict-check data to Supabase or similar for sub-second lookups during live calls.

faq.question: Should I replace my human intake team with an AI voice agent?
faq.answer: No. The right stack is AI for after-hours and weekend coverage (6pm-8am and Saturday/Sunday) with human specialists handling business-hours calls where their skill advantage still wins. Add warm handoff capability so AI-answered calls during business hours can transfer to a human when the caller requests it or when sentiment analysis flags a complex case.

articles.title: How to Use AI to Generate Landing Page Variants for Split Testing
articles.description: The prompt stack and Unbounce/Instapage workflow we use to ship 8 AI-generated landing page variants a week and lift conversion rates 22% in 60 days.
articles.keyword: how to use ai to generate landing page variants for split testing
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most landing page tests fail before they start. Not because the hypothesis is wrong, but because the team ships one variant a month, waits six weeks for significance, and calls a 3% lift a win. At that cadence you run maybe eight tests a year. Your competitors who figured out how to use AI to generate landing page variants for split testing are running eight a week.

That is the real advantage AI gives a conversion program. Not better copy — faster, cheaper hypotheses. When a variant costs 20 minutes instead of two days of copywriter and designer time, you stop protecting ideas and start killing them on data.

Below is the exact operating system: the prompt stack, the Unbounce and Instapage build workflow, the traffic math, and the guardrails that keep AI from shipping generic garbage. On accounts where we've run it with disciplined traffic allocation, the pattern is consistent — roughly a 22% conversion lift inside 60 days, driven by volume of tests, not one magic headline.

Why test volume beats test quality

Conversion rate optimization is a numbers game disguised as a creativity game. The industry has known for years that most A/B tests lose or come back flat. If only one in five or six tests produces a real winner, the fastest way to compound lift is to run more tests — not to agonize over each one.

Here's the math that should change how you staff this. A team shipping 1 variant per month finds roughly 2 winners per year. A team shipping 8 variants per week, even with a lower hit rate because the ideas are rougher, finds a winner almost every week in the early months while the page still has obvious friction.

The bottleneck was never ideas. It was production: writing the copy, adjusting the layout, QA'ing mobile, wiring the tracking. AI collapses the first two. Page builders with template duplication collapse the last two.

The mindset shift for founders and CMOs: stop treating landing pages as brand assets that need approval committees. Treat them as disposable hypotheses with a shelf life. Your brand standards live in a locked template and a voice document — the AI works inside those rails, and the data picks the winner. That's how a service business with a $15K/month ad budget out-tests an enterprise with a dedicated CRO team.

Build the inputs before you touch a prompt

Garbage in, generic out. Every AI-generated variant is only as good as the context you feed it. Before writing a single prompt, assemble a variant brief — one document the model sees every time.

It should contain:

  • Offer specifics: price, guarantee, timeline, what's included, what's not
  • Audience voice: 20–30 verbatim phrases pulled from sales call transcripts, reviews, and support tickets. Use Gong, Fathom, or even exported Zoom transcripts
  • Objection list: the top 5 reasons prospects don't buy, ranked by frequency
  • Proof inventory: every testimonial, case study number, logo, certification, and review count you're allowed to use
  • Current control: the live page copy plus its conversion rate and traffic source
  • Analytics signals: scroll depth and drop-off from Google Analytics 4, heatmaps from Hotjar or Microsoft Clarity

That last item matters most. If Clarity shows 70% of mobile visitors never reach your form, the right test is a structural one — form above the fold — not a new headline. Feeding behavioral data into the brief turns the AI from a copy generator into a hypothesis generator.

Store the brief in a Claude Project or a custom GPT so it persists. Rebuilding context every session is how teams drift back into generic output.

The four-layer prompt stack

One giant prompt produces one mediocre page. We run four chained prompts, each with a single job.

Layer 1 — Diagnose. Give the model the brief plus the control page and ask: what are the five highest-impact friction points, ranked, and what behavioral evidence supports each? This forces reasoning before writing.

Layer 2 — Hypothesize. For each friction point, generate one test hypothesis in the format: If we change X for audience Y, conversion will improve because Z. Reject any hypothesis without a clear 'because.' This is where you pick the week's eight tests.

Layer 3 — Write. For each approved hypothesis, generate only the changed elements — headline, subhead, hero bullets, CTA, form label, proof block. Constrain it: 'Use only claims from the proof inventory. Match the voice phrases. Headline under 10 words.' Ask for three options per element, then pick.

Layer 4 — Red team. Paste the variant back and prompt: 'You're a skeptical buyer who almost bought from a competitor. What's vague, unbelievable, or missing?' Fix what it flags.

The red-team layer is the one most teams skip, and it's the one that removes the AI tell — the inflated adjectives and unsupported promises that kill trust and, for regulated verticals like lending and legal, create compliance risk.

Pick variants that test one big idea

AI makes it tempting to generate twenty headline tweaks. Don't. Small copy changes need enormous traffic to reach significance, and most service businesses don't have it.

Each variant should test one big idea that could plausibly move conversion 15% or more. The categories that consistently produce the largest swings:

  • Offer framing: 'Free audit' vs. 'Free 30-day pipeline forecast' vs. 'See your missed revenue in 5 minutes'
  • Proof architecture: testimonial-led hero vs. numbers-led hero vs. logo wall
  • Form friction: 3 fields vs. 7 fields vs. multi-step with a qualifying question first
  • Page length: short decision page vs. long-form objection handling
  • Mechanism: explaining how you get results vs. only showing that you do
  • Audience callout: generic headline vs. naming the exact segment ('For PI firms spending $20K+/month on Meta')

The weekly rhythm: Monday, run layers 1–2 on the latest data and pick eight hypotheses. Tuesday, generate and red-team copy. Wednesday, build and QA. Thursday, launch. You'll have more variants than slots — that's the point. The backlog becomes your testing roadmap for the next month.

The Unbounce workflow

Unbounce is built for exactly this cadence because variant duplication lives inside the page itself.

  1. Lock a master template. Build your control with brand fonts, colors, form, tracking pixels, and GoHighLevel or HubSpot webhook already wired. Never build a variant from scratch.
  2. Duplicate variants inside the page. Each Unbounce page holds multiple variants sharing one URL — Variant A is your control, B through E are this week's challengers.
  3. Paste AI copy into the locked structure. For structural tests (form position, section order), move blocks; don't redesign.
  4. Use Smart Traffic selectively. Unbounce's Smart Traffic routes each visitor to the variant most likely to convert for their attributes. It reaches useful decisions with far less traffic than a classic 50/50 split — great when traffic is thin. Use classic A/B when you need a clean, defensible winner to roll into other channels.
  5. Use Dynamic Text Replacement to match the headline to the ad's keyword or UTM — an easy message-match win for Google Ads traffic.

One rule: every variant posts to the same form endpoint with a hidden field carrying the variant ID. That lets you judge winners on booked appointments and closed revenue in your CRM, not just form fills. A variant that lifts leads 30% but tanks show rates is a loser.

The Instapage workflow

Instapage is the better choice when you're running many ad groups or audiences and need personalization at scale.

  1. Build a global block library. Save your hero, proof, form, and FAQ sections as global blocks. Edit once, update everywhere — so a compliance fix doesn't mean touching forty pages.
  2. Create experiments in the Experimentation tab. Add variations of the base page, set traffic split, and define the conversion goal. Pause losers without unpublishing.
  3. Use AdMap and personalization. Instapage lets you map ad campaigns to specific page experiences and serve personalized versions by UTM or audience. Pair that with your AI prompt stack: one prompt per audience segment, fed the segment's specific objections.
  4. Use the built-in AI content generator for micro-copy only. It's fine for button text and subheads. Do the strategic work — offer framing, mechanism, proof architecture — in your four-layer stack with the full brief.
  5. Pipe conversions to the CRM. Same as Unbounce: hidden variant ID, webhook to GoHighLevel or HubSpot, downstream revenue as the scoring metric.

Rule of thumb: Unbounce wins for single-offer funnels with lean traffic thanks to Smart Traffic. Instapage wins for multi-audience programs where personalization is the lever.

Traffic math and when to call a winner

Eight variants a week does not mean eight live at once. That's the most common way this system breaks.

Use this allocation model:

  • Under 1,000 visitors/week: 2 challengers vs. control, Smart Traffic or a Bayesian tool. Use the other variants as a queue.
  • 1,000–5,000/week: 3–4 challengers. Classic split is viable for big-idea tests.
  • 5,000+/week: run parallel tests across different traffic sources — Meta to one experiment, Google Search to another.

Call winners with pre-committed rules, written before launch:

  1. Minimum sample: at least 100 conversions per variant for a classic test, or your tool's confidence threshold for adaptive routing
  2. Minimum duration: two full weeks, to cover weekday and weekend behavior
  3. Downstream check: win must hold on booked or qualified leads, not just raw submissions
  4. No peeking kills: don't stop a test on day three because it's 'clearly winning'

When a variant wins, it becomes the new control and its insight goes back into the brief. That feedback loop is what produces compounding lift — each round of AI generation starts from a smarter baseline.

Guardrails that keep AI variants on-brand and compliant

Speed without controls burns brands. The guardrails we enforce on every account:

  • Claims whitelist. The model may only cite numbers from the proof inventory. Any statistic not in the brief gets deleted in QA, no exceptions.
  • Regulated-vertical review. For lenders, law firms, and healthcare, a human checks every variant against platform and regulatory rules. Meta's ad policies extend to landing page experience — a 'guaranteed approval' headline can get your ad account restricted.
  • Voice scoring. Keep a short rubric: specific over vague, numbers over adjectives, customer phrases over marketing phrases. Reject variants that read like a press release.
  • Visual consistency. AI changes copy and structure. Designers own the template. No AI-generated imagery of fake clients or fake results.
  • Change log. Track every variant, hypothesis, result, and learning in a shared sheet or Notion database. Six months in, this is your most valuable marketing asset — a documented map of what your buyers actually respond to.

The teams that get burned treat AI as the strategist. The teams that win treat it as an extremely fast junior copywriter working inside a system a senior operator designed.

The bottom line

Learning how to use AI to generate landing page variants for split testing isn't about finding a magic prompt. It's about rebuilding your testing operation around a new cost structure: hypotheses are cheap, production is fast, and the only scarce resource is traffic. Spend that traffic on big ideas, judge winners on revenue, and feed every result back into the brief.

Run the four-layer stack weekly, lock your template in Unbounce or Instapage, and commit to the decision rules before you launch. Sixty days of disciplined volume will teach you more about your buyers than the last two years of quarterly redesigns.

faq.question: Which AI tool is best for generating landing page variants?
faq.answer: Claude and ChatGPT both work well for the strategic layers — diagnosis, hypotheses, and copy — especially when you store your variant brief in a Claude Project or custom GPT. Built-in tools inside Unbounce and Instapage are fine for micro-copy, but do the offer and proof work in a full-context model.

faq.question: How much traffic do I need to split test AI-generated landing pages?
faq.answer: For classic A/B tests, aim for at least 100 conversions per variant. Under 1,000 visitors a week, limit yourself to two challengers and use adaptive routing like Unbounce Smart Traffic, which reaches useful decisions with far less traffic.

faq.question: Will AI-written landing pages hurt my brand or ad account?
faq.answer: Only without guardrails. Restrict the model to a claims whitelist, keep design inside a locked template, and have a human review every variant — especially in regulated verticals like lending, legal, and healthcare where unsupported claims can trigger Meta policy restrictions.

faq.question: What should I test first with AI-generated variants?
faq.answer: Start with big-idea tests: offer framing, form friction, and proof architecture. Use heatmap and scroll data from Microsoft Clarity or Hotjar to find where visitors drop off, then let the AI generate hypotheses aimed at that specific friction point.

articles.title: Best CRM for Mortgage Brokers 2026: Shape vs Velocify vs GHL
articles.description: Shape, Velocify, or GoHighLevel? A no-fluff breakdown for mortgage brokers past 20 loans/month, including LOS integrations, pricing, and real ROI tradeoffs.
articles.keyword: best crm for mortgage brokers 2026
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
If you're closing more than 20 loans a month and still running your pipeline out of a CRM you picked when you were doing five, you're bleeding money. Not in some abstract way — in measurable, trackable, LO-productivity-per-hour money. The industry benchmark is roughly 7-12 loans per LO per month at a healthy shop; if your tech is forcing manual re-keying into your LOS, you're capped well below that. This article is for mortgage broker-owners, branch managers, and growth-stage lender CMOs evaluating a CRM switch for 2026. Specifically: you've outgrown the entry tier, you have an LOS (Encompass, Byte, LendingPad, or Calyx), and you're comparing Shape Software, ICE Mortgage Technology Velocify, and GoHighLevel (GHL). Below: a side-by-side on pricing, LOS integration depth, dialer and automation capability, reporting, and which CRM actually fits your model. No vendor-sponsored hedging.

Why the CRM decision gets harder past 20 loans a month

At 5-15 loans a month, almost any CRM works. You can tolerate manual data entry, spreadsheet pipelines, and a loose follow-up cadence because volume hides the inefficiency. Past 20 loans a month — especially with 3+ LOs — the cracks become expensive. Here's what breaks first: - Lead-to-contact SLA. Industry data from Velocify's own studies shows contacting a mortgage lead within 1 minute increases conversion by up to 391% vs. a 30-minute response. You cannot hit that manually at scale.

  • LOS double entry. If your LOs re-key borrower data into Encompass, you're losing 15-25 minutes per file. At 20+ files a month per LO, that's a full workday burned on data entry.
  • Attribution. You can't tell which lead source is actually funding loans vs. just generating applications. Marketing spend becomes a guess.
  • Compliance. TCPA, state-level consent rules, and recorded call retention are not optional. A CRM without native compliance tooling is a lawsuit waiting to happen. The three platforms we're comparing solve these problems in very different ways — and the right pick depends on whether you're buying leads, generating them, or doing both.

Shape Software: the mortgage-native default

Shape was built specifically for mortgage and financial services. It's not a general CRM retrofitted — the data model, pipeline stages, and compliance tooling assume you're originating loans. What it does well: - Native Encompass and LendingPad integration. Bi-directional sync on borrower data, loan status, and documents. This alone kills 80% of the double-entry problem.

  • Built-in dialer with local presence, voicemail drop, and call recording. No separate RingCentral/Aircall contract needed.
  • Pre-built mortgage automations: rate alerts, pre-approval expiration triggers, post-close drip for refi/referral capture.
  • 1003 point-of-sale included. Borrowers can start applications directly inside the CRM-hosted portal. Pricing: Roughly $99-$125/user/month on annual contracts. Not cheap, but you're replacing 3-4 tools. Where it falls short: Marketing automation is functional but not sophisticated. If you're running paid traffic, landing page tests, and multi-channel nurture sequences, Shape's builder feels dated compared to GHL. Reporting is good for pipeline and LO productivity but weaker on marketing attribution. Best fit: Broker shops doing 20-100 loans/month, running mostly inbound referral or purchased-lead models, who want one tool that handles LOS sync, dialing, and basic nurture without stitching anything together.

Velocify (ICE Mortgage Technology): the lead-buying machine

Velocify is the enterprise answer. Owned by ICE (which also owns Encompass), it's built for shops that buy large volumes of internet leads and need to work them like a call center. What it does well: - Speed-to-lead is the entire product philosophy. Lead distribution rules, shark-tank modes, and priority queues are best-in-class. If you're buying from LendingTree, Zillow, or Bankrate, Velocify is designed for this exact workflow.

  • Deepest Encompass integration on the market — it's the same parent company. Push a lead to Velocify, work it, close it in Encompass, with status updates flowing back. No middleware.
  • Dialer + SMS + email in one engine with compliance guardrails (TCPA time windows, DNC scrubbing).
  • Manager dashboards for LO performance, lead source ROI by funded loan, and conversion funnels that actually hold up to scrutiny. Pricing: Typically $150-$225/user/month, often with implementation fees of $5K-$15K. You're also usually looking at an annual commitment. Where it falls short: It's rigid. Customization requires professional services. Marketing automation outside of lead response is minimal — this is not where you build landing pages or run Facebook ad funnels. And if you're not on Encompass, the integration advantage shrinks fast. Best fit: Lenders doing 50+ loans/month, running on Encompass, buying significant internet lead volume, with dedicated inside-sales teams.

GoHighLevel: the marketing-first wildcard

GoHighLevel wasn't built for mortgage. It was built for marketing agencies, and that heritage shows — in both directions. What it does well: - Best-in-class marketing automation. Landing pages, funnels, SMS/email sequences, missed-call-text-back, Facebook/Google ad integration, review requests, and multi-channel nurture are all native and genuinely good.

  • White-label and sub-accounts. If you run multiple branches or DBAs, you can silo them cleanly.
  • Pricing: $297-$497/month flat for unlimited users on the Agency Pro plan. For a 10-LO shop, that's a fraction of Velocify.
  • AI appointment-setters and conversation bots that are honestly 2-3 years ahead of what Shape or Velocify ship natively. Where it falls short — and this matters: - No native LOS integration. You'll need Zapier, Make, or a custom webhook build to sync with Encompass or LendingPad. Expect $2K-$8K in setup and ongoing maintenance.
  • No native 1003. You're bolting on a POS like LiteSpeed or building a custom intake form.
  • Compliance is DIY. TCPA time windows, call recording retention, state-specific disclosures — you configure it, you own the risk. Best fit: Brokers who generate their own leads via paid media, SEO, or social, want world-class marketing automation, and are willing to invest in integration work to connect to their LOS. Also strong for shops with an in-house or agency marketing partner managing the build.

Side-by-side: the comparison that actually matters

Here's the honest matrix for a shop doing 20-50 loans a month: | Factor | Shape | Velocify | GoHighLevel | |---|---|---|---| | Price/user/mo | $99-$125 | $150-$225 | ~$30-$50 effective | | Encompass integration | Native | Native (deepest) | Zapier/custom | | LendingPad integration | Native | Limited | Zapier/custom | | Built-in dialer | Yes | Yes (best) | Yes (via Twilio) | | Marketing automation | Basic | Minimal | Best-in-class | | Landing pages/funnels | Weak | None | Best-in-class | | 1003 POS | Included | Add-on | Third-party | | Compliance tooling | Strong | Strongest | DIY | | Lead distribution rules | Good | Best | Good | | Setup time | 2-4 weeks | 6-12 weeks | 1-3 weeks (CRM) + integration time | | Annual contract | Usually | Always | Month-to-month option | The decision tree: 1. Buying 500+ internet leads/month and on Encompass? Velocify. Nothing else competes at that volume. 2. Doing 20-75 loans/month on Encompass or LendingPad, mostly referral/purchased leads, want one tool? Shape. 3. Generating your own leads with paid media and content, want to scale marketing hard, have technical help available? GoHighLevel + integration layer. Most broker shops at 20-50 loans/month land on Shape or GHL. Velocify starts making sense around 50+ loans/month with a dedicated ISA team.

The LOS integration tradeoff nobody talks about

Here's what vendor demos won't tell you: the quality of a native integration varies wildly, and 'native' doesn't always mean 'good.' Velocify to Encompass: Genuinely tight. Same parent company, shared data model, real-time updates. If you're on Encompass, this is as good as it gets. Shape to Encompass: Solid bi-directional sync, but field mapping is finite. Custom fields in Encompass sometimes need manual mapping or workarounds. For 95% of brokers, it's fine. Shape to LendingPad: Strong — Shape has invested heavily here, and for brokers on LendingPad it's often the best option. GHL to any LOS: You're building it. Zapier handles basic lead push and status pull but struggles with document sync, complex field mapping, and high-volume event triggers. Make.com is more capable but requires someone who knows what they're doing. Budget $2K-$8K for a competent build and $200-$500/month in ongoing tooling costs. The hidden cost of DIY integration: When Zapier breaks (and it will), your lead-to-LOS pipeline stops. You find out when an LO complains. Native integrations have SLAs and dedicated support; webhook stacks have you. If you don't have an in-house ops person or a trusted automation agency, don't pick GHL expecting the integration to 'just work.' It won't.

Implementation reality: what the first 90 days actually look like

Picking the CRM is 20% of the work. Rolling it out is the other 80%. Here's what a realistic 90-day plan looks like for each: Shape (fastest to value):

  • Weeks 1-2: Data migration, user setup, Encompass/LendingPad connection, pipeline stage configuration.
  • Weeks 3-4: Dialer configuration, build core automations (new lead response, pre-approval expiration, post-close), train LOs.
  • Weeks 5-8: Lead source integrations, reporting dashboards, refine automation based on real data.
  • Weeks 9-12: Optimize, add referral partner workflows, build nurture for aged leads. Velocify (longest ramp, biggest payoff at scale):
  • Weeks 1-4: Implementation kickoff, requirements gathering, lead distribution logic design.
  • Weeks 5-8: Build, test lead flows, configure dialing campaigns, Encompass sync validation.
  • Weeks 9-12: ISA training, manager dashboard rollout, go-live. Full optimization often takes 4-6 months. GHL (fast CRM, slower integration):
  • Weeks 1-2: CRM setup, user onboarding, pipeline build, migrate contacts.
  • Weeks 3-6: Build funnels, landing pages, SMS/email sequences, Facebook/Google ad integration.
  • Weeks 4-8 (parallel): LOS integration build via Zapier/Make, testing, failure handling.
  • Weeks 9-12: Launch paid traffic funnels, optimize conversion rates, refine automation. Don't underestimate change management. LOs resist CRM changes harder than almost any other operational shift. Mandatory usage policies, pipeline hygiene standards, and manager accountability on CRM data quality are non-negotiable. The best CRM in the world fails if your LOs still work out of their inbox.

The bottom line

There's no universally 'best' CRM for mortgage brokers in 2026 — there's the best CRM for your model. Shape wins if you want a mortgage-native platform that works out of the box with your LOS and consolidates your tool stack. Velocify wins if you're a high-volume internet-lead shop on Encompass with inside-sales infrastructure to feed. GoHighLevel wins if marketing is your competitive edge and you have the technical capacity to bridge it to your LOS. The worst move is staying on the wrong tool because switching feels painful. The cost of a bad CRM at 20+ loans/month — in lost conversion, LO time, and attribution blindness — compounds faster than the switching cost. Pick based on how you actually generate business, not what the demo looked best.

faq.question: Can I use GoHighLevel for mortgage without Encompass integration?
faq.answer: Yes, if you manually push closed loans to your LOS or you're on a system that accepts email/CSV imports. But for anything over 15-20 loans a month, the manual handoff creates data quality and compliance risk that outweighs the savings. Plan on integration from day one.

faq.question: Is Velocify still worth it in 2026 for smaller brokers?
faq.answer: Below 50 loans a month, probably not. The price, implementation cost, and rigidity don't pay back unless you're running heavy internet-lead volume with a dedicated ISA team. Shape delivers 80% of the value at 50% of the cost for mid-sized shops.

faq.question: How much does switching CRMs actually cost?
faq.answer: Expect 2-4 weeks of reduced LO productivity during transition, $5K-$25K in implementation and migration fees depending on platform, and a 60-90 day ramp before you see full ROI. Budget for parallel-running the old and new system for at least 30 days to avoid data loss.

faq.question: What's the best CRM for mortgage brokers on LendingPad?
faq.answer: Shape has the strongest native LendingPad integration among the three. Velocify's LendingPad support is limited since ICE prioritizes Encompass. GHL requires custom integration regardless of LOS.

faq.question: Do I need a separate dialer with any of these?
faq.answer: No. Shape and Velocify include native dialers with local presence and call recording. GHL supports dialing via Twilio integration, which works but requires setup. For broker shops making 100+ outbound calls per LO per day, Velocify's dialer is the most refined.

articles.title: GoHighLevel Automation for Dental New Patient Intake: Full Build
articles.description: A tactical GoHighLevel build for GP dental: insurance verification, 7-touch nurture, no-show rescue SMS, and 18-month reactivation. Steal the whole stack.
articles.keyword: gohighlevel automation for dental new patient intake
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most GP dental practices lose 30-40% of new patient leads between the form fill and the first chair-time. Not because the ads are bad. Because the intake is manual, the nurture is a single confirmation email, and no-shows get a shrug instead of a system. This walkthrough is for practice owners, DSOs, and the agencies running paid traffic for them. If you're buying Google Local Service Ads or Meta leads at $45-$120 a pop and watching 60% ghost before the exam, you're not a traffic problem. You're an intake problem. Below is the exact GoHighLevel build we deploy for general dentistry clients: insurance verification form, 7-touch pre-appointment nurture, no-show rescue SMS sequence, and a reactivation workflow that pulls dormant patients back into the chair. Copy it.

Why GoHighLevel beats the PMS for intake automation

Your practice management software (Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental) was built for charting and billing, not for reactive, multi-channel communication at scale. The appointment reminder module sends one SMS 24 hours out and calls it a day. That's not intake automation. That's a courtesy. GoHighLevel sits upstream of the PMS and runs the entire pre-patient lifecycle: lead capture, insurance pre-verification, nurture, confirmation, no-show rescue, and reactivation. It handles SMS, email, voicemail drops, and Facebook/Instagram DMs from one contact record. You pay roughly $297-$497/month for the agency account versus $600+/month for stitching together Podium, ActiveCampaign, and CallRail. The key architectural decision: GHL becomes the system of record for leads and prospects. The PMS only receives patients who have confirmed an appointment and submitted insurance info. This keeps your front desk from drowning in dead leads and keeps your PMS reports clean. Integration-wise, we use Zapier or the native GHL webhook to push confirmed appointments into Open Dental via a middleware like Dental Intel or a custom script. For practices on Dentrix Ascend, the API is open enough to automate patient creation directly.

The insurance verification form (and why it filters tire-kickers)

The single biggest intake upgrade: require insurance info before booking confirmation, not after. This filters out the 20-30% of leads who were just curious and kills no-shows from patients who assumed you took their plan. Build the form in GHL with these fields, in this order: 1. First name, last name, DOB, phone, email 2. Reason for visit (dropdown: cleaning, pain, cosmetic, second opinion, emergency) 3. Insurance carrier (dropdown of your top 15 accepted plans + "Other" + "I'm paying cash") 4. Member ID and group number (conditional — only shown if insurance selected) 5. Preferred appointment windows (3 options) Trigger a workflow the moment the form submits: send the insurance info to your verification team via Slack or email, create a task in GHL assigned to the front desk with a 2-hour SLA, and fire an SMS to the patient: "Hi [name], got your request. We're verifying your [carrier] benefits now and will text your appointment options within 2 hours." This one message cuts ghosting by roughly 25% in our builds because the patient knows a human is actively working on their request. The verification itself can be automated via Zuub or Vyne Trellis for carriers that support real-time eligibility, which collapses the 2-hour SLA to about 90 seconds.

The 7-touch pre-appointment nurture sequence

Between booking and the first visit, most practices send one email and one SMS reminder. We send seven touches across SMS, email, and voicemail drop. Overkill? No-show rates drop from 22% average to 6-8%. Here's the exact cadence, triggered when the appointment is confirmed in GHL: - T+0 (immediately): SMS confirmation with a one-click calendar add (ICS link) and a Google Maps link.

  • T+1 hour: Email with a 90-second "what to expect" video from the dentist, parking instructions, and new patient paperwork link.
  • T+2 days: SMS with a Google review link to a current patient testimonial video. Builds trust pre-visit.
  • T-5 days: Email reminder with insurance confirmation ("Your Delta Dental PPO is verified, estimated out-of-pocket for new patient exam + x-rays: $0"). Removes the #1 anxiety.
  • T-3 days: SMS asking them to complete digital paperwork via a GHL form link. Reduces chair time by 12 minutes.
  • T-24 hours: SMS confirmation with Yes/Reschedule response options. GHL workflow branches based on reply.
  • T-2 hours: SMS with doctor's photo, parking reminder, and "text this number if you're running late." The video at T+1 hour matters more than people think. We've A/B tested with and without — show rates jump 9-14% when a prospective patient sees the dentist's face before the visit.

No-show rescue SMS workflow (the 15-minute window)

The no-show rescue workflow fires when the appointment status in GHL is changed to "No Show" by the front desk (or automatically via PMS sync at 15 minutes past appointment time). The next 60 minutes are a sales window most practices waste. The sequence: - T+15 minutes: SMS from the dentist's number (not the main line): "Hi [name], this is Dr. [X]. Noticed you missed your appointment at [time]. Everything okay? Want me to grab you another slot this week?" Personal, not punitive.

  • T+2 hours: If no reply, voicemail drop (pre-recorded, 20 seconds) from the office manager offering 2 specific reschedule times tomorrow and the day after.
  • T+24 hours: Email with an online self-reschedule link powered by GHL's calendar booking widget.
  • T+3 days: Final SMS: "We're holding your new patient slot through Friday. After that, you'll need to re-request. Here's the link: [URL]." Scarcity re-engages 15-20%.
  • T+7 days: Contact moves to the "Unresponsive — Reactivate in 90 days" pipeline. In our client data across 40+ GP practices, this workflow recovers 34-41% of no-shows into a rescheduled, kept appointment. At an average new patient lifetime value of $1,200-$2,400, recovering 4 no-shows a week is $200K+ in annual production.

The reactivation workflow for dormant patients

Every GP dental practice is sitting on 800-3,000 patients who haven't been seen in 12+ months. Most do nothing with them except an occasional postcard. The GHL reactivation workflow turns that list into $40-$80K per quarter in rebooked production. First, segment your dormant list by pulling a CSV from your PMS: patients with no appointment in 12-18 months (recent lapse — highest intent) and 18-36 months (deep dormant — lower intent, different messaging). Upload to GHL with tags. For the 12-18 month segment, run this sequence: 1. SMS: "Hi [name], it's been a minute since your last cleaning. Your hygienist [name] has openings this month and we're waiving the $89 exam fee for returning patients. Reply YES for options." 2. Three days later, email with the same offer plus a one-click booking link. 3. Seven days later, SMS with a different hook: "Insurance year resets Dec 31 — most patients lose $800-$1,500 in unused benefits. Want to grab a cleaning before then?" 4. Fourteen days later, final voicemail drop from the office manager. For the 18-36 month segment, lead with a stronger offer: free whitening upgrade with a cleaning, or a $0 new-patient-equivalent exam. These patients need more friction removal. Expect a 6-11% reactivation rate on the 12-18 month list and 2-4% on the deeper segment per cycle. Run the sequence quarterly, not monthly — frequency burns the list.

Pipeline structure and tagging that keeps this manageable

Automation without pipeline discipline turns into a mess within 90 days. Here's the pipeline structure we use in every GHL dental build: Pipeline 1: New Patient Intake

  • Stage 1: Lead Submitted
  • Stage 2: Insurance Verification In Progress
  • Stage 3: Appointment Offered
  • Stage 4: Appointment Booked
  • Stage 5: Confirmed (24h out)
  • Stage 6: Showed / Converted to Patient
  • Stage 7: No-Show Rescue
  • Stage 8: Lost Pipeline 2: Reactivation
  • Stage 1: Dormant 12-18mo
  • Stage 2: Dormant 18-36mo
  • Stage 3: Responded — Scheduling
  • Stage 4: Rebooked
  • Stage 5: Unresponsive — Retry Q+1 Tag contacts with: lead source (GLSA, Meta, Google Search, Referral, Walk-in), insurance carrier, reason for visit, and lifetime production tier (A: $5K+, B: $2-5K, C: <$2K). These tags power your reporting and let you run segmented campaigns later — like a cosmetic consult offer only to patients tagged "cosmetic interest" with A-tier insurance. Build one dashboard in GHL reporting that shows: new leads this week, insurance verification SLA compliance, show rate, no-show rescue conversion, and reactivation revenue. Review it every Monday with the front desk. The system only works if someone owns the numbers.

What this stack actually costs and what to expect

Realistic numbers for a single-location GP practice: - GoHighLevel Pro plan: $297/month (or free under an agency sub-account)

  • Twilio SMS/voice usage: $80-$180/month at typical new patient volume (120-200 leads/month)
  • Zuub or Vyne Trellis insurance verification: $150-$300/month
  • Agency build and management: $1,500-$3,500/month depending on scope Total: roughly $2,100-$4,300/month all-in. Expected outcomes in the first 90 days, based on our client cohort: - Lead-to-booked-appointment rate: from ~35% to 55-65%
  • No-show rate: from ~22% to 6-10%
  • Reactivated patients: 25-60 per quarter from a 1,500-contact dormant list
  • Incremental new patients: 15-25 per month At a conservative $1,500 first-year patient value, 20 extra new patients a month is $30K/month in production — against a $4K cost. That's a 7-8x ROI, and that math gets better in year two when retention and referrals compound. Don't build this piecemeal. The reason it works is that intake, nurture, no-show, and reactivation share the same contact database, the same tags, and the same reporting. Bolt-on tools break the loop.

The bottom line

GoHighLevel automation for dental new patient intake isn't about sending more texts. It's about building a single system where every lead is verified, nurtured, confirmed, rescued, and — if they go dormant — pulled back in. The practices winning right now aren't spending more on ads. They're converting 2x more of the traffic they already pay for. If you're running a GP practice or an agency servicing dental clients, map your current intake against the seven workflows above. Wherever you have a gap — insurance pre-verification, the 7-touch nurture, no-show rescue, or quarterly reactivation — that's where the next $20-$50K/month of production is hiding. Build those four workflows first, in that order, and don't touch anything else until they're running clean.

faq.question: Can GoHighLevel integrate with Dentrix or Open Dental directly?
faq.answer: Not natively. You'll need Zapier, Make.com, or a middleware like Dental Intel to push confirmed appointments from GHL into your PMS. Open Dental has the most accessible API; Dentrix typically requires a Dentrix Developer Program partner for two-way sync.

faq.question: Is automated SMS to dental patients HIPAA compliant?
faq.answer: SMS itself is not HIPAA-secure, so you cannot include PHI like treatment details, diagnoses, or specific procedures. Appointment reminders, insurance verification confirmations, and generic reactivation offers are fine. For anything containing PHI, use GHL's secure portal link and have the patient authenticate.

faq.question: How long does it take to build this GoHighLevel automation stack?
faq.answer: A full build — forms, 4 workflows, pipeline structure, tagging, reporting dashboard, and PMS integration — takes 3-5 weeks with a competent agency. Add 2 weeks for front desk training and workflow tuning based on live data. Rushing it under 3 weeks almost always creates sync issues you'll pay for later.

faq.question: Will this replace my front desk?
faq.answer: No. It eliminates about 60-70% of the manual follow-up work (confirmations, reminders, no-show chasing, reactivation calls) so your front desk can focus on the live conversations that actually convert. Most practices redeploy that saved time into treatment plan follow-up, which drives case acceptance up another 10-15%.

faq.question: What's the single biggest mistake practices make with intake automation?
faq.answer: Treating it as a 'set and forget' system. The sequences need review every 60-90 days based on reply rates, show rates, and reactivation conversion. Copy that worked in Q1 fatigues by Q3. Assign one person — in-house or at your agency — to own the numbers weekly.

articles.title: How to Get More Leads for a Drywall Contractor in 60 Days
articles.description: A three-channel playbook (GBP, Nextdoor Ads, GC referral automation) to fill a two-crew drywall calendar in 60 days. Specific tactics, no fluff.
articles.keyword: how to get more leads for a drywall contractor
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most drywall contractors don't have a lead problem. They have a visibility and follow-up problem. If you run two crews and you're staring at a half-empty schedule for next month, the fix isn't a $5,000/month SEO retainer or a new logo. It's three channels, executed in a specific order, over 60 days. This playbook is written for owner-operators and small drywall outfits (1–4 crews) doing residential repairs, new construction patch work, or small commercial jobs. If you're already booked out 10 weeks, close this tab. If you're trying to go from 60% capacity to 100% without hiring a sales rep, keep reading. Here's what you'll get: a Google Business Profile overhaul that doubles your map pack calls, a Nextdoor ad setup that costs under $400/month and prints homeowner leads, and a general contractor referral automation that turns one-off jobs into a recurring pipeline. Sixty days. Two crews. Full calendar.

Why most drywall lead gen advice is wrong

The generic advice — "start a blog, run Google Ads, get on HomeAdvisor" — misses how drywall actually gets bought. Homeowners call the first three contractors who show up in the map pack and pick whoever answers the phone. GCs hire the sub their project manager texted last Tuesday. Nobody is reading your 1,500-word article on "Level 5 finish vs. Level 4." The three real buying channels for drywall work are: 1. Local search (Google Maps + organic) — captures active homeowner demand 2. Neighborhood social proof (Nextdoor, Facebook neighborhood groups) — captures passive homeowner demand that converts fast because of trust 3. GC and remodeler relationships — captures recurring B2B pipeline that doesn't require ad spend Angi, Thumbtack, and HomeAdvisor are deliberately not on this list. The lead quality is garbage, the shared-lead model forces price wars, and you'll spend $40–$80 per lead to close maybe 1 in 15. Skip them. The 60-day plan allocates time like this: Week 1–2 on Google Business Profile, Week 2–4 on Nextdoor ads, Week 3–8 on GC referral automation. They overlap on purpose so leads start flowing by day 14.

Channel 1: Rebuild your Google Business Profile for map pack dominance

Your GBP is the single highest-ROI asset you own. A fully optimized profile in a city of 150,000+ typically generates 20–60 inbound calls per month at zero media cost. Most drywall contractors have a half-filled profile with four photos and two reviews. That's leaving $15k/month on the table. Here's the overhaul checklist: - Primary category: "Drywall Contractor" (not "General Contractor")

  • Secondary categories: Add "Plasterer," "Painter" (if you offer it), "Insulation Contractor" if applicable
  • Service area: List every zip code within a 25-mile radius, not just your city
  • Services: Add 15–20 individual services with 200-word descriptions each (drywall repair, popcorn ceiling removal, water damage patch, texture matching, basement finishing, etc.)
  • Photos: Upload 40+ photos minimum — before/afters, crew on job sites, trucks, finished rooms. Add 3–5 new photos weekly.
  • Posts: Publish a GBP Post every 7 days (job completed, promo, tip)
  • Reviews: Ask every customer via text with a direct review link. Target 2+ new reviews per week. Use a tool like LocalFalcon to run a grid scan of your rankings across a 7x7 grid in your service area. You'll see exactly which zip codes you rank in the top 3 and which need work. Re-scan every 2 weeks. Expect map pack calls to double within 30 days if you're starting from a neglected profile.

The review request system that actually works

Verbal "hey, leave us a review" asks convert at under 5%. A text-based system with a direct link converts at 30–45%. The difference is 10x more reviews per month for the same job volume. Set this up in 30 minutes: 1. Grab your GBP review link from Google (Business Profile Manager → Reviews → "Get more reviews") 2. Shorten it with Bitly to something like bit.ly/review-acme-drywall 3. Build a text template in your phone or in GoHighLevel / Jobber / Housecall Pro: "Hey [Name] — thanks for having us out today. If the work looked good, a quick Google review would mean a lot: [link]. Takes 20 seconds. — Mike" 4. Send it the same day the job wraps, before you leave the driveway if possible If you're doing 15 jobs a week and 35% leave a review, that's 20+ new reviews a month. Within 90 days you'll have more reviews than every competitor in your market, and the map pack algorithm rewards that heavily. Respond to every review within 48 hours. For negatives, respond calmly with a resolution offer — Google's algorithm weighs response rate, not just rating.

Channel 2: Nextdoor Ads for homeowner repair demand

Nextdoor is massively underpriced for home services. Most contractors ignore it because the ad platform is clunky. That's your advantage. Expect to pay $8–$18 per lead for drywall repair inquiries vs. $45–$90 on Google Ads for the same query. The setup: - Create a Nextdoor for Business page (free)

  • Launch a Neighborhood Sponsored ad targeting a 10–15 mile radius around your shop
  • Budget: $300–$500/month to start
  • Creative: One photo of a before/after drywall patch, headline like "Drywall repair in [City] — same-week scheduling", body copy mentioning free estimates and that you're locally owned
  • CTA: Phone call or lead form (use the form — it converts better on mobile) What makes Nextdoor work: the ads appear inside a trust-based neighborhood feed. When Linda in your target zip code sees your ad right next to a neighbor's post asking "anyone know a good drywall guy?", the conversion math changes. Follow up on every Nextdoor form lead within 10 minutes. Speed-to-lead is the single biggest conversion variable in home services. A 10-minute response window converts 3–5x higher than a 60-minute response. Use a tool like CallRail or GoHighLevel to auto-text new leads the moment the form fires. Expect 15–30 qualified homeowner leads per month at this budget in a mid-size market.

Channel 3: GC and remodeler referral automation

One happy general contractor is worth more than 50 homeowner leads. GCs give you repeat volume, bigger tickets, and predictable scheduling. The problem is most drywall subs rely on luck and sporadic text messages to stay top-of-mind. Build a simple referral automation in 3 steps: Step 1 — Build the list. Pull every GC, remodeler, flipper, property manager, and insurance restoration company in your metro. Use Google Maps + a scraper tool like PhantomBuster or just do it manually in a spreadsheet. Target 100–150 contacts. Step 2 — First-touch outreach. Short, specific email or LinkedIn message: "Running a 2-crew drywall outfit in [City]. We handle patch work, new hangs, and texture matching with 48-hour turnaround on most jobs. If one of your subs ever flakes, I'm your backup. Mobile: [number]." No pitch deck, no PDF, no "let's grab coffee." Step 3 — Stay top of mind. Set up a monthly automation in HubSpot (free tier works) or GoHighLevel that sends a one-line text or email to every GC on the list: a job photo, a capacity update ("two crews open next week"), or a quick market note. Takes you 10 minutes/month to send to the whole list. Within 60 days, expect 3–8 GCs to start sending you work. One active GC relationship is often worth $8k–$25k/month in recurring revenue.

The 60-day execution calendar

Here's the week-by-week: Week 1: GBP overhaul — categories, services, 40 photos, service area, review link system built. Start LocalFalcon grid baseline. Week 2: Launch Nextdoor ad with $400 budget. Begin texting review requests on every job. First outreach to top 25 GCs on your list. Week 3: Add 10 GBP Posts to queue. Finish GC list (150 contacts). Send cold outreach to remaining 125. Week 4: Review Nextdoor performance, kill underperforming creatives, double budget on the winner. Should have 8–15 new reviews live. Week 5–6: Launch monthly GC nurture automation. Begin publishing weekly GBP Posts. Expect first measurable lift in map pack rankings. Week 7–8: Audit. Pull GBP Insights (calls, direction requests, website clicks), Nextdoor lead count and CPL, GC-sourced jobs. Reallocate budget to winners. Track three numbers weekly in a simple Google Sheet: inbound leads by source, booked jobs by source, revenue by source. If you can't attribute, you can't scale. Use unique phone numbers per channel via CallRail ($45/month) if you want clean attribution. By day 60, a 2-crew outfit executing this plan should see 40–80 qualified leads per month across the three channels. That's enough to run both crews at capacity and start pricing more aggressively on the jobs you actually want.

What to stop doing

Three things to cut immediately so you have time to execute the above: 1. Angi/HomeAdvisor/Thumbtack subscriptions. Shared leads, race-to-the-bottom pricing, horrendous close rates. Cancel. Redirect that $400–$800/month to Nextdoor and GBP photography. 2. Facebook boosted posts. "Boost post" is Meta's beginner trap. If you want to run Facebook, run proper campaigns in Meta Ads Manager with a lead form objective. Otherwise skip Facebook entirely — Nextdoor outperforms it 3:1 for drywall in most markets. 3. Chasing one-off commercial RFPs you have no shot at. If you're a 2-crew shop, don't waste 6 hours bidding on a 40,000 sq ft commercial build-out that'll go to a 20-crew competitor. Stay in your lane: residential repair, small commercial, GC overflow. That's where the margin is. The discipline here matters more than the tactics. Most contractors try 11 channels at 10% effort each. The ones who dominate pick 2–3 and execute them at 90% for 90 days.

The bottom line

Filling a two-crew drywall calendar isn't a mystery. It's a Google Business Profile that actually works, a $400/month Nextdoor ad that captures homeowner demand, and a GC outreach list you touch monthly. Three channels, 60 days, measurable results. Your next action: pick one channel to start on Monday morning. Not three. One. If your GBP is weak, start there — it's free and it compounds. Build the next channel in week 3 once the first is running on autopilot. The contractors who win in local service aren't the biggest or the cheapest. They're the ones who execute a simple plan without getting distracted.

faq.question: How much should a drywall contractor spend on marketing per month?
faq.answer: For a 2-crew operation, $500–$1,500/month covers Nextdoor ads, a review tool, and basic attribution software. You should not need Google Ads or SEO retainers in year one — GBP optimization and GC referrals do most of the heavy lifting at near-zero media cost.

faq.question: How long does it take Google Business Profile changes to actually generate leads?
faq.answer: Expect noticeable movement in 2–4 weeks and significant lift by week 6–8. The algorithm weighs reviews, posts, and photo freshness heavily, so consistent weekly activity matters more than one big overhaul.

faq.question: Is Nextdoor better than Facebook for drywall leads?
faq.answer: In most markets, yes. Nextdoor's neighborhood trust context converts 2–3x better for home repair services, and CPLs are typically half of Facebook's for the same budget. Facebook can still work with proper campaigns in Ads Manager, but it's a secondary channel for drywall.

faq.question: How do I get general contractors to actually give me referrals?
faq.answer: Be the easiest sub to work with: respond to texts within 30 minutes, show up when you say you will, and never leave a punch list open. One monthly touchpoint (text or email) keeps you top of mind. Reliability beats pricing in the GC world almost every time.

faq.question: Do I need a website if my Google Business Profile is strong?
faq.answer: A simple 5-page site helps conversion and gives GBP somewhere to link, but you don't need a $5,000 custom build. A clean site on Carrd, Squarespace, or GoHighLevel with photos, services, and a quote form is enough for year one.

articles.title: Hire a Lead Generation Agency for Septic Tank Services: Vetting Guide
articles.description: How to hire a lead gen agency for septic services: real pricing ($1.5k-$4k/mo), vetting checklist, and red flags around shared-lead resellers.
articles.keyword: hire lead generation agency for septic tank services
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most septic contractors who hire a lead generation agency get burned within 90 days. Not because paid media doesn't work for septic — it works extremely well, with cost-per-lead typically landing between $18 and $65 in most US markets — but because they hire a reseller dressed up as an agency, pay $2,500/month, and get the same 'emergency pump-out' lead sold to four competitors. This guide is for septic company owners doing $500k to $10M in annual revenue who are ready to stop buying leads from HomeAdvisor, Angi, and Networx and want an actual exclusive-lead pipeline. If you run install, repair, inspection, or pumping services and you're evaluating agencies, this is the vetting playbook. Below: realistic pricing ranges, the 12-point vetting checklist we'd use if we were hiring on your behalf, the red flags that signal a shared-lead reseller, and the contract terms that protect you when things go sideways.

What a real septic lead gen agency actually does

A legitimate lead generation agency for septic tank services builds you an owned pipeline. That means a dedicated landing page on your domain (or a microsite you own), tracked phone numbers that route to your dispatch, and ad accounts you have admin access to. The standard stack looks like this: - Google Local Services Ads (LSAs) for pump-outs, repairs, and emergency calls — this is usually your lowest CPL channel at $20-$45.

  • Google Search Ads for high-intent terms like 'septic tank installation [city]' and 'drain field repair' — expect $45-$120 CPL.
  • Meta Ads for homeowner awareness, inspection offers, and real estate transaction triggers — $25-$70 CPL.
  • Local SEO + GBP optimization to compound organic lead flow over 6-12 months.
  • Lead handling infrastructure: CallRail or CallTrackingMetrics for call tracking, a CRM like GoHighLevel or HubSpot, and SMS speed-to-lead automation under 60 seconds. If an agency can't walk you through this stack in the first sales call — specifically which channels they'll run, what tracking they'll install, and what you'll own at the end of the contract — walk away. They're probably reselling leads from a central pool.

Realistic pricing: what $1.5k to $4k/month actually buys

Septic lead gen pricing clusters into three tiers. Understanding what each buys prevents overpaying for a logo refresh or underpaying for a bot farm. $1,500-$2,000/month — Entry tier. You get one channel (usually Google LSAs + light Search management), basic landing page, call tracking, and monthly reporting. Ad spend is separate and typically $2k-$5k/month on top. Fit for operators doing $500k-$1.5M who want to add 15-40 exclusive leads/month. $2,000-$3,000/month — Standard tier. Two to three channels (LSAs, Search, Meta), dedicated landing pages per service line, CRM setup, SMS/email nurture, bi-weekly reporting calls. Ad spend $5k-$12k. Fit for $1.5M-$5M operators scaling into new ZIPs. $3,000-$4,000/month — Full-service tier. All paid channels plus local SEO, review generation (Birdeye or NiceJob), content, conversion rate optimization, and a strategist on bi-weekly calls. Ad spend $10k-$25k+. Fit for multi-location operators or those backed by PE roll-ups. Anything under $1,500/month is almost always a reseller or a solo freelancer who will ghost you by month four. Anything over $4,500/month for a single-location septic company is likely padded with services you don't need yet.

The 12-point vetting checklist

Run every agency candidate through this before signing. If they fail three or more items, pass. 1. Can you name three current septic or home-services clients? Ask for references you can actually call. 2. Who owns the ad accounts? Correct answer: you do. They get admin access. 3. Who owns the landing pages and domain? You do. Period. 4. What CRM do you use and do I get a login? If they say 'our proprietary system,' that's a red flag. 5. How do you track calls and attribute leads? CallRail, CallTrackingMetrics, or WhatConverts are standard answers. 6. Are leads exclusive to me in my service area? Get this in writing. 7. What's your average CPL for septic clients in markets like mine? They should have numbers ready. 8. How quickly do leads hit my phone/CRM? Under 60 seconds is the standard. 9. What's the contract length and exit clause? Month-to-month after a 90-day initial term is reasonable. 10. Do you charge a setup fee? $500-$2,000 is normal; $5k+ is excessive. 11. Who's my day-to-day contact and what's their experience? Avoid being handed to a junior AM. 12. What happens to the assets if we part ways? Everything transfers to you.

Red flags that signal a shared-lead reseller

Shared-lead resellers are the Angi/HomeAdvisor model wearing a custom logo. They aggregate leads from a central lead-gen site, then sell the same lead to 3-5 contractors. Here's how to spot them: - They quote you a flat 'per-lead' price ($35/lead, $75/lead) instead of a monthly management fee + ad spend. Real agencies manage your budget on your ad accounts.

  • They won't give you admin access to Google Ads, Meta Ads Manager, or Google Business Profile. Because those accounts don't exist for you — the leads come from their master domain.
  • The landing page is on their domain, something like septicprosnetwork.com/yourcity.
  • They promise 'X leads per month guaranteed.' Real paid media doesn't work like that. CPL fluctuates; guarantees are a sales tactic.
  • Leads arrive via a generic email from a dispatcher-looking address, not direct phone calls to your tracked number.
  • Contract has an 'exclusivity by ZIP' clause with suspicious wording — read carefully; often they can sell to 'non-competing' contractors in your ZIP, which conveniently includes anyone offering a slightly different service mix. If you want shared leads, buy them from Angi for $20 each and skip the $2,500 monthly retainer. The whole point of hiring an agency is exclusivity.

Contract terms that protect you

Most agency contracts are written to protect the agency. Negotiate these specific terms before signing: Initial term and exit. A 90-day initial term is fair — paid media needs that long to optimize. After that, insist on month-to-month with 30-day written notice. Never sign a 12-month lock-in for your first engagement. Asset ownership clause. Add explicit language: 'Client owns all ad accounts, landing pages, domain(s), creative assets, CRM data, phone numbers, and tracking configurations. Upon termination, Agency will transfer admin ownership within 10 business days.' Performance benchmarks, not guarantees. Agree on target CPL ranges by channel (e.g., LSA CPL under $50, Search CPL under $90) and a 90-day review. If they miss targets two months in a row, you can exit without penalty. Ad spend transparency. Ad spend is paid directly to Google/Meta on your credit card — never routed through the agency. Any agency that wants to markup ad spend or run it through their account is hiding margin. Reporting cadence. Weekly data dashboard access (Google Data Studio / Looker Studio is standard), bi-weekly calls, monthly written performance review with recommended changes. Get these in the MSA, not a verbal promise. Agencies change hands and reps leave; your contract is what remains.

What to measure in the first 90 days

Vanity metrics kill septic companies. 'We generated 400 leads!' means nothing if 350 were tire-kickers asking for pricing on a $200 pump-out that never booked. Measure these instead: Cost per booked job (CPBJ), not cost per lead. If CPL is $45 but only 20% book, your real CPBJ is $225. For a $450 pump-out that's thin; for a $12k drain field install that's a home run. Lead-to-booked rate by channel. LSAs typically book at 25-40%. Search Ads 15-25%. Meta 8-18%. If your numbers are half these benchmarks, the problem is either lead quality (agency's fault) or intake process (your fault — fix speed-to-lead and script). Revenue per lead by service line. Install leads are worth 20x pump-out leads. Make sure your agency is bidding and allocating budget accordingly, not optimizing for cheap pump-out clicks. ROAS by channel after 60 days. Target 4x-8x on paid media for established septic operators. Below 3x, something is broken. Call recording review. Listen to 10 inbound calls per week for the first month. You'll immediately spot whether your CSR is losing bookable jobs or whether the agency is sending junk.

When to hire an agency vs. build in-house

Hiring an agency makes sense when you're doing $500k-$8M in revenue and don't have a marketing hire who can run Google Ads at a senior level. The math: a competent in-house paid media manager costs $75k-$110k fully loaded. A $2.5k/month agency costs $30k/year and comes with a team. Build in-house when: you're over $8M revenue, running multiple locations, and need daily optimization that an agency juggling 20 accounts can't provide. At that stage, hire a Director of Marketing and keep the agency as a specialist (e.g., just for Meta creative or SEO). Hybrid works for most operators in the $3M-$10M range: in-house marketing coordinator who handles GBP, reviews, email, and vendor management, plus an agency running paid media. This gives you continuity if the agency underperforms and lets you fire them without losing institutional knowledge. One warning: do not try to run Google Ads yourself as the owner while also running the business. Every septic owner who tries this spends $40k on wasted clicks before admitting defeat. If you don't have 15 hours a week to dedicate to campaign optimization, outsource it.

The bottom line

Hiring a lead generation agency for septic tank services is a straightforward decision when you know what to look for: exclusive leads, owned assets, transparent pricing in the $1.5k-$4k/month management-fee range (plus real ad spend), and a contract that lets you leave in 30 days if performance tanks. The agencies worth hiring will welcome every item on the vetting checklist. The resellers will dodge. Your next action: pull three agency proposals, run them through the 12-point checklist, and reject anyone who won't give you admin access to the ad accounts and landing pages they build. That single filter will eliminate 80% of bad options before you ever sign a contract.

faq.question: How much should I expect to pay a lead gen agency for septic services?
faq.answer: Management fees run $1,500-$4,000/month depending on channel scope and service tier, with separate ad spend of $2k-$25k/month paid directly to Google and Meta. Anything under $1,500/month is likely a reseller or freelancer who won't deliver sustained results.

faq.question: What's the difference between an agency and a shared-lead service like Angi or HomeAdvisor?
faq.answer: A real agency builds you exclusive lead flow on your own ad accounts, domain, and tracking. Shared-lead services sell the same lead to 3-5 contractors competing on speed. If an agency charges per-lead instead of a monthly management fee, they're a reseller in disguise.

faq.question: How long before I see results from a septic lead generation agency?
faq.answer: Google LSAs can produce leads in week one. Google Search Ads typically stabilize at target CPL by day 30-45. Meta Ads need 60-90 days to optimize. Local SEO takes 6-12 months. Judge performance at the 90-day mark, not the 30-day mark.

faq.question: Should the agency or I pay for ad spend?
faq.answer: You pay Google and Meta directly on your own credit card attached to your own ad accounts. Any agency that wants ad spend routed through their accounts is either marking it up for hidden margin or hiding the fact they're running a shared-lead operation.

faq.question: What's a realistic cost per lead for septic services?
faq.answer: Google Local Services Ads typically run $20-$45 per lead, Google Search Ads $45-$120, and Meta Ads $25-$70. These vary significantly by market competition and service type — install leads cost more than pump-out leads but are worth 10-20x the revenue.

articles.title: Lead Generation for Commercial Flooring Contractors That Works
articles.description: Why LinkedIn outbound and Google Ads beat Facebook for $50k+ commercial flooring jobs. A tactical playbook for contractors chasing GC decision-makers.
articles.keyword: lead generation for commercial flooring contractors
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Here's the uncomfortable truth most commercial flooring contractors won't say out loud: the $3,000 you dumped into Facebook lead ads last quarter brought you tire-kickers, bad phone numbers, and one homeowner who wanted laminate in her basement. For a company bidding on $50k–$500k build-outs, that's not a lead problem — it's a channel problem. Commercial flooring is a B2B sale with a long cycle, multiple decision-makers, and specs written months before the award. The people who sign off — GC project managers, estimators, facility directors, and tenant improvement leads — don't scroll Facebook looking for a flooring contractor. They search Google when a bid is live, and they live on LinkedIn the rest of the time. This article lays out a lead generation system built for that reality: LinkedIn outbound to the right job titles, Google Ads for high-intent commercial queries, and a follow-up stack that doesn't let a $75k opportunity die in a voicemail inbox.

Why Facebook ads fail for commercial flooring

Facebook (and Instagram) are interest and demographic platforms. Meta's targeting is excellent at finding a 42-year-old homeowner in Dallas who likes HGTV. It is awful at finding the project manager at a mid-market GC who's bidding a 60,000 sq ft medical office fit-out next month. Three structural problems kill Meta performance for $50k+ commercial work: - Audience mismatch. B2B job-title targeting on Meta is thin and self-reported. You cannot reliably target "Senior Project Manager at ENR Top 400 GC." You can on LinkedIn.

  • Intent mismatch. Commercial flooring is bought when a project is specced, not when someone sees a pretty epoxy floor in their feed. Meta is a disruption channel; commercial flooring is a demand-capture game.
  • Lead quality collapse. Lead-form ads optimize for cheap submissions. Our audits of contractor accounts routinely show 70–85% of Meta leads are residential, out-of-area, or unqualified. Your estimator burns four hours a week disqualifying noise. Meta can work for residential refinishing, retail-adjacent services, or recruiting installers. For commercial GC relationships, it's the wrong tool. Stop measuring cost-per-lead and start measuring cost-per-qualified-bid-opportunity. The math changes immediately.

The commercial flooring buyer map

Before you touch a channel, map the actual buying committee. For a typical $50k–$500k commercial flooring job, five roles matter: 1. GC Project Manager / Project Executive — owns subcontractor selection on build-outs. 2. GC Estimator / Chief Estimator — pulls bids during preconstruction. 3. Facility Director / Director of Facilities — owns re-flooring, repairs, and recurring maintenance for property owners. 4. Tenant Improvement (TI) Coordinator — common at REITs and large property managers. 5. Architect / Interior Designer — specs the product; influences who gets invited to bid. Each role has a different trigger. The estimator needs you in their vendor list before an ITB (invitation to bid) goes out. The facility director needs you when a floor fails. The architect needs to trust your product knowledge months before a project breaks ground. Build a target account list of 200–500 GCs, property managers, and architecture firms in your service radius. Pull it from Dodge Construction Network, ConstructConnect, or BuildingConnected. This list is the backbone of everything that follows — LinkedIn outbound, email sequences, retargeting audiences, and even your Google Ads location modifiers all key off it.

LinkedIn outbound: the backbone of the system

LinkedIn Sales Navigator is non-negotiable. Budget $99/month per seat and build saved searches around: - Job titles: Project Manager, Senior PM, Estimator, Preconstruction Manager, Director of Facilities, VP of Construction, TI Coordinator.

  • Companies: Your target account list of 200–500 firms.
  • Geography: Your actual service radius — not "United States."
  • Seniority: Manager and above. Run outreach through a tool like HeyReach, Expandi, or Dripify at 20–25 connection requests per day per seat (stay under LinkedIn's weekly 100-invite limit). Use a 4-touch sequence: 1. Connection request, no pitch. One line referencing their company or a recent project.
  1. Day 2 after accept: short message introducing your company, specific project types, and one proof point ("We just finished 48,000 sq ft of LVT at [recognizable project]").
  2. Day 7: send a one-page capabilities PDF — union status, bonding capacity, product lines, recent projects.
  3. Day 14: direct ask for a 15-minute intro call via Calendly link. Expect 25–35% connection acceptance, 8–12% reply rates, and 1–3% booked-meeting rates. On a list of 500 contacts, that's 5–15 meetings with actual decision-makers per quarter — each potentially worth six figures in bid opportunities.

Google Ads for high-intent commercial queries

LinkedIn builds the relationship. Google Ads captures the moment someone needs a contractor now. The mistake most flooring contractors make is bidding on broad terms like "flooring contractor" and getting flooded with homeowners. Structure your account around commercial-intent keywords only: - "commercial flooring contractor [city]"

  • "epoxy flooring contractor [city]"
  • "warehouse flooring installation"
  • "commercial vinyl flooring installation"
  • "commercial polished concrete [city]"
  • "ESD flooring contractor"
  • "MMA flooring installation" Use exact and phrase match only. Broad match will burn your budget on residential searches. Add aggressive negatives: "home," "residential," "DIY," "near me cheap," "home depot," "lowes," "laminate," "carpet cleaning." Set location targeting to your service radius with bid adjustments favoring commercial zip codes (industrial parks, medical districts, downtown cores). Run separate campaigns per product line — epoxy, resinous, LVT, polished concrete, sports flooring — because conversion rates and cost-per-click vary 3–5x between them. Send traffic to dedicated landing pages, not your homepage. Each page should feature: specific product, 3–5 project photos with square footage, named client logos, bonding/insurance info, and a short form (name, company, project location, square footage, timeline). Expect $80–$180 cost-per-lead and 15–30% lead-to-opportunity rates on well-built campaigns.

The follow-up stack that closes six-figure jobs

Most flooring contractors lose more revenue to bad follow-up than bad marketing. A $75k lead that calls on Tuesday and doesn't hear back until Friday is already talking to your competitor.
