Build a follow-up stack with three components: - Speed-to-lead automation. Use GoHighLevel, HubSpot, or Zapier to fire an SMS and email within 60 seconds of any form submission. First-touch within 5 minutes increases contact rates 9x versus 30+ minutes (MIT Lead Response study).

  • A real human on inbound calls. If your estimator can't answer, route to an answering service that qualifies and books. Missed commercial calls are a 5-figure mistake, every time.
  • A nurture sequence for the 70% who aren't ready now. Monthly email with recent projects, product spotlights, and estimating tips. Quarterly LinkedIn check-in from your rep. When their project goes live in 6 months, you're the first call. Track every lead in a CRM — not a spreadsheet, not your estimator's inbox. Tag by source (LinkedIn, Google Ads, referral, trade show), stage (new, qualified, bidding, awarded, lost), and estimated value. You cannot optimize what you don't measure, and "we got some leads from Google" is not measurement.

Content and SEO that supports both channels

Paid channels get expensive without organic support. A simple content program compounds your LinkedIn and Google Ads performance by giving decision-makers something to find when they research you between touches. Focus on three content types: 1. Project case studies. One per quarter, 600–900 words. Include square footage, product used, timeline, client name (if permitted), challenges solved, photos. Publish on your site, repurpose into a LinkedIn post and a PDF. 2. Technical spec guides. "Epoxy vs. MMA for food processing facilities," "How to spec resinous flooring for a hospital corridor." These rank for long-tail commercial queries and get shared internally by architects. 3. Market pages. A page per city and per product combination ("Commercial Epoxy Flooring Contractor in Phoenix"). These support Google Ads Quality Score and capture organic traffic for geo-modified searches. Use Ahrefs or SEMrush to find terms with 10–100 monthly searches and clear commercial intent. Low volume is fine — one keyword that drives two bid opportunities a year at $150k each is worth more than any residential blog post. Publish 1–2 pieces monthly, link them from your service pages, and share every new piece through your reps' LinkedIn accounts.

Budget allocation and realistic timelines

For a commercial flooring contractor doing $3M–$15M in revenue, here's a defensible monthly budget split: - LinkedIn Sales Navigator + outbound tooling: $400–$800/month (2 seats + sequencing tool).

  • LinkedIn outbound labor (SDR or agency): $2,500–$5,000/month.
  • Google Ads spend: $3,000–$8,000/month depending on market size.
  • Landing pages, CRM, automation (GoHighLevel or HubSpot): $300–$1,500/month.
  • Content production: $1,000–$2,500/month for 2 pieces plus repurposing. Total: roughly $7,000–$18,000/month. For a shop closing one $100k job per quarter from this system, payback is 1–3 months on gross margin. Timeline expectations matter. Google Ads produces leads in week one. LinkedIn outbound produces meetings in weeks 3–6. Content and SEO contribute meaningfully at months 4–6 and compound from there. The pipeline doesn't fill overnight — but at month 6, a disciplined contractor has 20–40 active GC relationships, 5–10 live bid opportunities, and a predictable flow that doesn't depend on repeat work from three loyal GCs. If your current spend is going to Facebook lead ads and Angi, this is where to move it.

The bottom line

Commercial flooring is won by being in front of the right 500 people — GC project managers, estimators, facility directors, and architects — consistently and with real proof. Facebook can't find those people. LinkedIn can target them by name. Google captures them when a bid is live. Together, they produce a predictable pipeline of six-figure opportunities instead of a stream of homeowner tire-kickers. The contractors winning this market are not spending more — they're spending in the right channels with proper follow-up. Audit your current lead sources this week, tag every lead from the past 12 months by source and outcome, and move budget away from anything producing residential inquiries. Then build the LinkedIn + Google Ads system described above. The channels work. The question is whether you'll run them with the discipline commercial sales cycles require.

faq.question: How long before LinkedIn outbound produces real meetings?
faq.answer: Expect first meetings in weeks 3–6 and steady flow by month 3. The first two weeks are consumed by list building, connection acceptances, and initial touches. Volume matters — 20–25 connects per day per seat is the sustainable rate without triggering LinkedIn restrictions.

faq.question: What's a realistic cost per qualified commercial flooring lead on Google Ads?
faq.answer: $80–$180 per lead in most markets, with 15–30% converting to real bid opportunities. Larger metros with heavy competition (NYC, LA, Chicago) can push cost-per-lead to $250+. Dedicated landing pages and tight negative keyword lists are the biggest levers for keeping cost down.

faq.question: Should we still exhibit at trade shows if we run digital outbound?
faq.answer: Yes, but treat trade shows as a list-building and relationship-reinforcement channel, not a lead source. Scan every badge, upload contacts to your CRM, and run them through LinkedIn connection and email sequences within 48 hours of the show ending. That's where trade show ROI actually lives.

faq.question: Can one person run LinkedIn outbound plus Google Ads in-house?
faq.answer: One operator can manage both at modest volume (one Sales Navigator seat, $3k–$5k ad spend) if they have real B2B marketing experience. Beyond that, split the roles — an SDR for LinkedIn outreach and either an agency or dedicated specialist for Google Ads, since the skill sets don't overlap.

faq.question: What CRM should a commercial flooring contractor use?
faq.answer: GoHighLevel if you want built-in SMS, email, and automation at a lower price point ($297–$497/month). HubSpot if you need deeper reporting and sales pipeline features and have budget for $800+/month. Avoid building this in spreadsheets — you will lose six-figure opportunities to dropped follow-up.

articles.title: How to Structure Google Ads for Emergency Plumbing Calls
articles.description: A senior media buyer's blueprint for emergency plumbing Google Ads: call-first campaigns, hour-based bidding, and tight geos that win 2am calls at a profit.
articles.keyword: how to structure google ads for emergency plumbing calls
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most plumbing Google Ads accounts are built like a brochure: one campaign, every service, every hour, the whole metro, all optimizing toward "leads." Then the owner wonders why a burst-pipe call at 2am costs the same as a faucet-quote form fill at 2pm, and why half the budget is gone by lunch.

Emergency plumbing is a different business than scheduled plumbing. The searcher is standing in water. They will call the first competent-looking number they see, they won't compare three quotes, and the ticket is often two to four times a standard service call once after-hours rates and the follow-on repair are counted. That intent deserves its own architecture, its own budget, and its own bidding logic.

This is the structure we'd put in place for a service business that wants emergency calls at a predictable cost: call-first ads, schedule-aware bids, geography built around drive time, and conversion tracking that only counts calls that actually matter.

Separate emergency intent into its own campaign

The single highest-leverage change in most plumbing accounts is splitting emergency from everything else. Not ad groups — campaigns. Budgets, schedules, bid strategies, and geo settings all live at the campaign level, and emergency intent needs different answers to every one of them.

A clean build looks like this:

  • Emergency – Core: burst pipe, emergency plumber, 24 hour plumber, sewer backup, water heater leaking, no hot water emergency.
  • Emergency – Brand + Near Me: "plumber near me," "plumber open now," and your brand terms, which convert at a different rate and should not muddy the core data.
  • Scheduled Services: water heater install, repiping, remodel rough-in, drain cleaning appointments.
  • Local Services Ads: run alongside, not instead of, search. LSAs sit above the paid results and pay per lead; for many plumbers they are the cheapest emergency calls in the market.

Inside Emergency – Core, keep ad groups tight around the problem, not the service: burst/leaking pipe, sewer/drain backup, water heater failure, gas line/smell. The person searching "basement flooding pipe burst" needs an ad that says exactly that back to them.

Why this matters: when emergency and scheduled queries share a campaign, Smart Bidding averages them together. You end up underbidding the 11pm burst pipe and overbidding the Tuesday-afternoon faucet quote. Separation lets each campaign learn its own economics.

Make the phone ring, not the form

Emergency searchers do not fill out forms. Every click that lands on a page and asks for a name, email, and "describe your issue" is a click you paid for and probably lost.

The ad itself should be built to produce a call:

  • Call assets on every emergency ad group, scheduled to match your actual dispatch hours. If you are truly 24/7, run them 24/7.
  • Call ads (formerly call-only) where your account still supports them. Google has been steering advertisers toward responsive search ads with call assets, so check what's available before building around them. If call ads aren't an option, the RSA plus call asset combination works fine; on mobile, the call button is the dominant action.
  • Mobile-first landing page with a sticky click-to-call bar, the number in the hero, and a single line of trust: licensed, insured, arrival window, upfront pricing.

On the copy, lead with speed and certainty. "Plumber at Your Door in 60 Min" beats "Quality Plumbing Services Since 1998" every time a ceiling is dripping. Use headline pinning sparingly: pin one urgency headline to position one, let Google rotate the rest.

One rule that saves accounts: use a Google forwarding number or a call-tracking number (CallRail, CallTrackingMetrics, or GoHighLevel's native tracking) so every call is attributed to a campaign, keyword, and hour. Without that, you are optimizing blind.

Define a conversion as a real call, not a ring

Smart Bidding is only as good as the signal you feed it. Most plumbing accounts count any call over 30 seconds as a conversion. That includes wrong numbers, vendor pitches, existing customers asking about an invoice, and people shopping price who will never book.

Tighten the definition:

  1. Raise the duration threshold for emergency campaigns to 60–90 seconds. A legitimate dispatch conversation rarely finishes in 30.
  2. Import qualified calls offline. If your CRM (GoHighLevel, ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro, Jobber) marks a call as "booked" or "job created," send that back to Google Ads as the primary conversion through offline conversion import or the native integration.
  3. Attach value. Pass the job value, or at minimum a tiered value (emergency booked = higher, scheduled booked = lower). This unlocks Maximize Conversion Value with a target ROAS, which is where emergency campaigns start to outperform.
  4. Demote junk actions. Page views, direction clicks, and generic "calls from website" should be secondary, observation-only actions.

The payoff is concrete. When the algorithm learns that a 2am "sewer backup" call books a high-value job and a 3pm "plumber cost estimate" call rarely does, it starts bidding accordingly — without you babysitting keyword bids.

Bid by the clock, because intent changes by the hour

A 2am search and a 2pm search for the same keyword are not the same customer. At 2am the searcher has a real emergency, competitors with daytime-only answering services have gone dark, and the auction is thinner. At 2pm you are competing with every shop in town and a lot of non-urgent shoppers.

Build an ad schedule with clear blocks and look at performance by block, not just by day:

  • Overnight (10pm–6am): highest urgency, typically lower competition. Push aggressively if you can actually dispatch.
  • Early morning (6am–9am): people discovering overnight leaks and failed water heaters. Strong intent.
  • Business hours (9am–5pm): highest competition, most price shopping. Defend, don't overspend.
  • Evening (5pm–10pm): after-work discoveries; strong for water heaters and drains.

If you're on Manual CPC or Enhanced CPC, apply bid adjustments to these blocks directly. If you're on Smart Bidding, schedule adjustments are mostly ignored, so the schedule becomes an on/off switch and your conversion values carry the weight. That's another reason value-based conversions matter.

The non-negotiable: if nobody answers the phone, the ads should be off. A missed emergency call is worse than no call. It costs the click, burns the customer, and teaches the algorithm that the hour doesn't convert. If your overnight coverage is a voicemail box, either fix coverage (answering service, on-call rotation, or an AI receptionist that can triage and dispatch) or turn overnight off.

Draw the map around drive time, not city limits

Emergency work is a logistics problem. A burst-pipe call 45 minutes away at 2am is often a losing job once you count the tech's time, the after-hours pay, and the reduced odds you win the follow-on repair. Your geo targeting should reflect where you can actually arrive fast.

Practical setup:

  • Target by radius or ZIP codes around your shop and where your techs live, not the entire metro. Overnight, techs usually leave from home, so map those addresses.
  • Use "Presence" targeting only (people in or regularly in your locations), not "Presence or interest." The default setting leaks budget to people researching from three states away.
  • Layer location bid adjustments where your bidding strategy supports them: inner ring up, outer ring down. Many operators run a tight 10–15 mile core and a wider ring with a smaller budget.
  • Split high-value ZIPs. Older housing stock with galvanized or cast-iron pipes, larger homes, and neighborhoods with higher average tickets often justify their own campaign or a stronger adjustment.

Check the "Locations" report monthly under "Where your users were." If 15% of spend is coming from outside the zone you can serve in under an hour, tighten it. Those calls aren't cheap leads; they're expensive conversations that end with "sorry, we can't get there tonight."

Build keywords and negatives for panic, not research

Emergency keyword lists should read like what someone yells while looking for a shutoff valve: "pipe burst," "water leaking from ceiling," "toilet overflowing won't stop," "sewer backing up into tub," "emergency plumber," "24 hour plumber," "plumber open now."

Use phrase and exact match for the core. Broad match can work with Smart Bidding and strong conversion data, but launch it in a separate ad group so you can watch what it pulls in and shut it down if it wanders.

Negatives are where emergency accounts make or lose their margin. A starter list:

  • Job seekers: jobs, hiring, salary, apprentice, school, license, training.
  • DIY: how to, diy, video, youtube, fix myself, parts, home depot, lowes.
  • Wrong service: plumbing supply, wholesale, commercial plumbing (unless you do it), pool, irrigation.
  • Low-intent research: cost, average price, reviews of, reddit, near me cheap.

Be careful with price terms. "Emergency plumber cost" can be a real buyer at 11pm. Watch the search terms report weekly for the first 60 days and decide case by case.

Add shared negative lists at the account level so every new campaign inherits the basics. Then review search terms by hour: queries that look fine at 2pm sometimes reveal very different intent at 2am, and vice versa.

Set budgets with unit economics, not round numbers

"We spend $3,000 a month on Google" isn't a strategy. Emergency campaigns should be funded from the math backward.

Start with three numbers from your own books:

  • Average emergency job value, including the follow-on repair you typically book.
  • Close rate on qualified emergency calls, meaning the share of real calls that become a dispatched job.
  • Target acquisition cost you can stomach per booked job, usually a fixed share of gross margin.

Illustrative math: if an emergency job averages $900, you close 60% of qualified calls, and you're willing to spend 20% of revenue to acquire it, your ceiling is $180 per booked job, or about $108 per qualified call. That number becomes your target CPA, or with values in place, roughly a 5x target ROAS.

Then fund the campaign so it isn't limited by budget during your highest-value hours. Running out of budget at 7pm and missing the overnight window is one of the most common and expensive mistakes we see. If budget is tight, cut daytime scheduled-service spend before you starve emergency.

Review weekly for the first month, then every other week. Give Smart Bidding a learning window of roughly 30 conversions before major strategy changes, and resist the urge to adjust targets more than 15–20% at a time.

Report on booked jobs, not clicks

The dashboard that matters for an emergency plumbing campaign has five numbers on it:

  1. Qualified calls by campaign and hour block.
  2. Answer rate. What percentage of calls were actually picked up by a human or a capable AI receptionist.
  3. Booking rate on answered calls.
  4. Cost per booked job.
  5. Revenue per booked job, pulled from your field-service software or CRM.

Clicks, CTR, and impression share are diagnostics. Useful when something breaks, irrelevant to whether the business made money.

Wire it so this doesn't depend on someone filling in a spreadsheet. Call tracking pushes call data into your CRM; your CRM marks the job booked and its value; that value flows back to Google Ads as an offline conversion; and Looker Studio or your CRM's reporting pulls all of it into one view. Once that loop is closed, every optimization decision — bid targets, schedule, geography, keyword pruning — gets made on revenue instead of guesswork.

The most common finding when a plumbing company first sees this view: the ads are fine, the phones aren't. A 70% answer rate overnight means nearly a third of paid emergency calls went nowhere. Fixing coverage is often a bigger lever than any change inside Google Ads.

The bottom line

Emergency plumbing on Google Ads rewards operators who treat it as its own business line: its own campaign, its own hours, its own map, and its own definition of success. Separate the intent, make the phone the conversion, bid by the clock, draw geography around drive time, and feed the algorithm booked-job values instead of raw call counts.

Do that, and the 2am burst-pipe call stops being a lucky accident and becomes a predictable, profitable channel — one you can scale with confidence because you know exactly what each booked job costs.

faq.question: Should emergency plumbers use call ads or responsive search ads?
faq.answer: Use whatever drives the call most directly. Call ads (formerly call-only) are ideal where your account still supports them, but responsive search ads with call assets and a mobile click-to-call landing page perform comparably. The important part is that the call, not a form, is the primary conversion.

faq.question: Is it worth running Google Ads overnight for plumbing?
faq.answer: Yes, if and only if someone answers. Overnight auctions are often less competitive and intent is extremely high. If calls go to voicemail, turn overnight ads off until you have an on-call tech, an answering service, or an AI receptionist that can triage and dispatch.

faq.question: What counts as a conversion for emergency plumbing campaigns?
faq.answer: Ideally a booked job imported from your CRM or field-service software, with its revenue attached. At minimum, count calls over 60–90 seconds from tracked numbers, and keep website visits, direction clicks, and short calls as secondary observation-only actions.

faq.question: Should I run Local Services Ads and Google Search ads together?
faq.answer: Usually, yes. LSAs appear above search ads and charge per lead, which often makes them the cheapest emergency calls available. Search campaigns capture the volume LSAs can't and give you more control over hours, geography, and messaging.

faq.question: How tight should geo targeting be for emergency plumbing?
faq.answer: Build it around the area you can reach in roughly 30–45 minutes, including from where techs live for overnight dispatch. Use presence-only targeting and review the location report monthly to cut spend leaking outside your serviceable zone.

articles.title: Meta Ads for LASIK Surgery Clinics: The Sub-$80 CPL Playbook
articles.description: The exact creative, offer, and funnel framework LASIK practices use to drop Meta Ads CPL under $80 and fill surgery calendars predictably.
articles.keyword: meta ads for lasik surgery clinics
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most LASIK clinics running Meta Ads are paying $150-$300 per lead and converting fewer than 1 in 10 to a consult. That's not a Meta problem. That's an offer and creative problem. We've managed Meta spend for refractive surgery practices across six U.S. markets, and the pattern is consistent: clinics that lead with price-anchored financing hooks and raw before/after UGC consistently drop cost per lead under $80, with consult show rates above 55%. Clinics that lead with brand video and "schedule your consultation" CTAs don't. This article breaks down the exact framework — offer architecture, creative stack, funnel mechanics, and the measurement setup — that makes sub-$80 CPLs a repeatable outcome instead of a lucky month.

Why most LASIK Meta ads bleed money

The default LASIK ad looks like this: a stock photo of a smiling patient, the clinic logo, and copy that says "Schedule your free LASIK consultation today." It converts at $180-$250 per lead because it asks for a high-friction commitment from a cold audience with zero price context. LASIK is a $4,000-$5,000 out-of-pocket decision. Prospects aren't scrolling Instagram ready to book surgery. They're curious, price-sensitive, and scared. The ad has to do three jobs before the landing page ever loads: - Remove the price objection (or reframe it)

  • Build trust that this specific surgeon isn't a mill
  • Lower the ask from "book a consult" to something softer When you skip those three jobs, Meta's algorithm optimizes toward whoever will click your logo-and-stock-photo ad — usually tire-kickers and lead-gen bots. CPL stays high because conversion intent is low. The clinics winning on Meta have figured out that the ad is the qualifier, not the landing page. Financing hooks pre-qualify for payment capacity. UGC pre-qualifies for emotional readiness. By the time someone clicks, they've already self-selected into the top 20% of your audience. That's the mechanical reason CPL drops.

The financing hook: your single highest-leverage offer angle

The number one objection to LASIK isn't fear of the laser. It's "I can't drop $4,500 right now." Lead with financing and you dissolve the objection in the first three seconds of the ad. The hook that consistently wins: "LASIK for $89/month — 0% APR for 24 months. See if you qualify in 60 seconds." Variations we've tested that also perform: - "$0 down, $119/month — both eyes, taxes included"

  • "Pay less per month for LASIK than your phone bill"
  • "24-month 0% financing ends [month] — lock your rate now" Two things matter here. First, the monthly number has to be real. Pull it from your actual CareCredit or Alphaeon offer and show the math. Second, the CTA shifts from "book a consult" to "see if you qualify." Qualification is low-friction. Booking is high-friction. In Meta Ads Manager, run this as a Leads campaign with an Instant Form that captures name, email, phone, and one qualifying question ("When are you looking to have LASIK done?"). Push leads via webhook into GoHighLevel or HubSpot and trigger an immediate SMS: "Hi [name], you pre-qualify for our $89/mo LASIK plan. Want to grab a 15-minute phone consult this week?" CPL on this structure sits between $45-$75 in most mid-size markets. Consult show rate: 55-65%.

Before/after UGC: the creative format that beats every studio-produced ad

Studio-produced LASIK ads look like pharma commercials. Prospects scroll past them. Raw, phone-shot patient testimonials stop the scroll and build trust in a way no production budget can match. The UGC format that works has a specific structure: 1. Hook (0-3 seconds): Patient on camera, no intro, says something like "I was so scared to get LASIK, I waited eight years." 2. Problem (3-10 seconds): Shows glasses, talks about contacts drying out, mentions the daily annoyance. 3. Decision moment (10-20 seconds): "When I found out it was [$X]/month, I just booked it." 4. Result (20-35 seconds): Shows them without glasses, driving, at the gym, with kids. 5. CTA (35-45 seconds): "If you're on the fence, just see if you qualify. Took me 60 seconds." Get 8-12 of these from real patients. Pay them $200-$500 each or offer a touch-up credit. Shoot vertical 9:16 on an iPhone. No logo overlay, no music bed, no graphics. The second it looks like an ad, performance drops 40%+. Run these as Advantage+ Shopping or standard Sales campaigns with 6-8 creatives per ad set. Meta's algorithm will find the two or three that scale. Refresh every 3-4 weeks — LASIK audiences in a single DMA burn out fast.

Audience and targeting: narrower than you think

Meta's default advice is broad targeting. For LASIK, that's wrong in markets under 2 million people. You'll burn budget on unqualified reach. Here's the audience stack we run: - Geo: 25-mile radius around the clinic. Not 50. Patients won't drive further for elective surgery when competitors exist closer.

  • Age: 28-55. Under 28 skews broke; over 55 skews toward cataract/RLE conversations that need a different funnel.
  • Income proxy: Layer in "Engaged Shoppers" + behaviors like "Frequent travelers" or "Small business owners." You're looking for discretionary income signals.
  • Exclusions: Exclude anyone who's submitted a lead in the last 90 days, current patients (upload your CRM list), and anyone over 60. For retargeting, build these audiences in Meta Ads Manager: - Video viewers 50%+ (last 30 days)
  • Instant Form openers who didn't submit (last 14 days)
  • Website visitors to pricing/financing pages (last 30 days) Retargeting creative should shift to urgency and social proof: surgeon credentials, Google review screenshots, financing deadline reminders. CPL on retargeting typically runs $25-$40 — cheap, but the volume is limited by top-of-funnel reach. Don't neglect lookalikes. Upload your last 500 surgery patients (not consults — actual surgeries) and build a 1% lookalike. This audience consistently outperforms interest-based targeting after the first $3,000 in spend.

The funnel: Instant Forms beat landing pages for LASIK

Every agency wants to build a custom landing page. For LASIK Meta Ads, Instant Forms outperform landing pages on CPL by 40-60%. Here's why: a landing page adds a page load, a scroll, and a form fill. Each step drops conversion by 20-30%. Instant Forms happen inside Facebook/Instagram with pre-filled fields. Structure the Instant Form like this: 1. Intro screen: Headline repeating the offer ("LASIK for $89/mo — see if you qualify"). One paragraph of social proof. Image of the surgeon. 2. Question 1: "When are you looking to have LASIK?" (Within 30 days / 1-3 months / 3-6 months / Just researching). This is your qualifier. 3. Contact fields: Name, email, phone — all pre-filled by Meta. 4. Thank you screen: "We'll text you within 10 minutes. Prefer to pick a time now?" with a Calendly link. Use the "Higher Intent" form type, not "More Volume." Yes, you'll get fewer leads. They'll be 2-3x more likely to show up. On the backend, every lead needs to be contacted within 5 minutes. Use GoHighLevel or a similar automation to fire an SMS and an email the second the webhook hits, then route to a real human caller within the hour. Speed-to-lead is the single biggest driver of consult show rate — a 5-minute response beats a 60-minute response by roughly 4x on conversion.

Measurement: track to surgery, not to lead

If you're optimizing Meta campaigns on cost per lead alone, you'll scale the wrong creative. A $45 CPL that converts to surgery at 3% is worse than a $90 CPL that converts at 12%. Set up conversion tracking at four stages: 1. Lead submitted (Meta Pixel + Conversions API) 2. Consult booked (fire from Calendly or your scheduling tool via webhook) 3. Consult showed (fire from your CRM when status flips to "attended") 4. Surgery scheduled (fire from your practice management system) Push all four events back into Meta via the Conversions API using a tool like Zapier, Make, or GoHighLevel's native integration. Optimize your campaigns toward "Consult Showed" once you have 50+ events per week per ad set. Until then, optimize for "Lead" and manually review which creatives are driving actual surgeries. In Google Analytics 4 or your BI tool, build a weekly report that shows: spend, leads, booked consults, showed consults, surgeries closed, revenue, and ROAS. For most LASIK clinics, a healthy funnel looks like: $100 CPL → 60% show → 35% close → $4,500 average case value = roughly 9-10x ROAS blended. Anything less than 5x ROAS at scale, and either your offer, your creative, or your consult closing process is broken. Diagnose in that order.

Budget, scaling, and when to kill a campaign

Start at $100-$150/day per campaign. That's enough to generate 30-50 leads in week one, which is the minimum data volume to make real decisions. Below that, you're guessing. Structure three campaigns from day one: - Cold prospecting (70% of budget) — Advantage+ or standard Sales campaign with the financing hook and UGC stack

  • Retargeting (20% of budget) — Video viewers, form openers, pricing page visitors
  • Lookalikes (10% of budget) — 1% LAL of surgery patients Scale rules we use: - If a campaign hits sub-$80 CPL for 7 straight days with 100+ leads, increase budget 20% every 3 days.
  • If CPL spikes 40%+ after a budget increase, roll back to the previous level and let it stabilize for 5 days.
  • Kill any ad with over $150 spent and zero leads.
  • Kill any ad set with CPL above $150 after $500 spent. Creative fatigue is the biggest killer at scale. In a mid-size DMA, expect each UGC creative to run 3-6 weeks before frequency hits 4+ and CPL starts climbing. Have 2-3 new UGC pieces in the pipeline every month. This is non-negotiable — the clinics that scale past $20k/month in ad spend are the ones treating creative production as a continuous operation, not a one-time project.

The bottom line

Sub-$80 CPL for LASIK on Meta isn't a secret growth hack. It's the predictable output of a specific system: financing-anchored offers, raw UGC creative, Instant Form funnels, 5-minute speed-to-lead, and measurement tied to surgery revenue instead of top-of-funnel leads. If your current Meta program is sitting at $150+ CPL and consult show rates under 50%, the fix is almost always creative and offer — not targeting, not budget, not a new agency. Rebuild the ad to lead with a monthly payment number, swap stock photos for phone-shot patient videos, and shorten the ask from "book a consult" to "see if you qualify." Then measure to surgery. Those four moves alone will usually cut CPL in half within 30 days.

faq.question: How much should a LASIK clinic spend on Meta Ads to see results?
faq.answer: Minimum viable budget is $3,000-$5,000/month for a single-location clinic in a mid-size market. Below that, you don't generate enough data to optimize creative or audiences, and you'll burn the first month on learning. Most clinics scaling profitably sit between $8,000 and $25,000/month in Meta spend.

faq.question: Do Instant Forms actually produce quality leads for LASIK?
faq.answer: Yes, when you use the Higher Intent form type and include a qualifying question about timeline. Volume will be 30-50% lower than More Volume forms, but consult show rates run 55-65% vs. 25-35% from unqualified forms. Pair with 5-minute SMS follow-up for best results.

faq.question: Should we run Google Ads or Meta Ads for LASIK?
faq.answer: Both, but they do different jobs. Google captures existing demand (people searching "LASIK near me") at higher CPL but higher intent. Meta creates demand through financing offers and UGC at lower CPL. A healthy LASIK growth program runs both channels, with Google typically eating 40-50% of total paid budget.

faq.question: How long before Meta Ads start working for a LASIK practice?
faq.answer: Expect 14-30 days to stabilize CPL and 60-90 days to hit full performance. The first 2 weeks are Meta's learning phase and creative testing. By day 30 you should have 2-3 winning creatives identified. Scaling and ROAS optimization happens in months two and three.

faq.question: What's the biggest mistake LASIK clinics make on Meta?
faq.answer: Running polished brand video and asking for a consult booking in the first ad. This ignores the two biggest objections — price and trust — and asks for a high-commitment action from a cold audience. Lead with financing, use raw UGC, and soften the CTA to a qualification question instead.

articles.title: Google Ads for Appliance Repair: Cost Per Lead in 2026
articles.description: What appliance repair leads really cost on Google in 2026, metro by metro tier, and the call-only + LSA stack that gets booked jobs under $35 a lead.
articles.keyword: google ads for appliance repair companies cost per lead 2026
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most appliance repair owners who tell us Google Ads "doesn't work" are paying $60–$90 for a lead that should cost $25–$40. The keywords aren't the problem. The problem is that they're running a 2019 account structure — broad search campaigns pointed at a homepage — into a 2026 auction where Local Services Ads, Maps, and call-first intent take the majority of the clicks that actually turn into booked jobs.

Appliance repair is one of the cleanest paid-search verticals in home services. The intent is urgent (the fridge is warm, the washer is full of water), the ticket is predictable ($180–$450 average repair), and the buyer wants a phone number, not a blog post. That combination rewards operators who build for the phone call and punishes anyone building for the form fill.

Below are the cost-per-lead ranges we see across major, mid-size, and smaller U.S. metros, why they differ, and the exact stack — call-only campaigns layered on top of Local Services Ads — that consistently pushes blended CPL under $35.

What appliance repair leads actually cost on Google right now

Treat these as directional operating ranges, not a universal benchmark — your CPL depends on service area, brand mix, and how fast you answer the phone. But across appliance repair accounts, the spread clusters into three tiers:

Metro tier Example markets Search CPC Search CPL LSA cost per lead
Tier 1 (dense, competitive) Los Angeles, New York, Chicago, Bay Area, Miami $9–$18 $55–$95 $35–$60
Tier 2 (large Sun Belt) Dallas, Houston, Phoenix, Atlanta, Tampa $6–$12 $38–$65 $25–$42
Tier 3 (mid-size) San Antonio, Tucson, Boise, Omaha, Knoxville $4–$8 $24–$45 $18–$32

Two things jump out. First, LSA leads run 30–45% cheaper than pure search almost everywhere, because Google charges per lead rather than per click and the placement sits above the ads. Second, Tier 1 search CPL isn't driven by CPC alone — it's driven by conversion rate. Dense metros have more comparison shoppers, more national franchise competition (Sears Home Services, Mr. Appliance, Asurion), and more people who call three companies before booking.

The practical takeaway: if your blended CPL is above the high end of your tier, the issue is structural, not budget. Spending more into a broken structure just buys more expensive leads faster.

Why pure search campaigns overpay in this vertical

A standard search campaign sends the click to a landing page, then hopes the visitor calls or fills out a form. In appliance repair, that extra step costs you 30–50% of your potential conversions. Someone standing in a flooded laundry room on their phone doesn't want to scroll a page. They want to tap a number.

Pure search also leaks budget in three predictable places:

  • Parts and DIY queries. "Whirlpool washer drain pump," "how to reset Samsung fridge," and "GE dishwasher error code" convert terribly. Without an aggressive negative list, 15–25% of spend goes here.
  • Brand-authorized confusion. Searches like "LG customer service" or "Samsung warranty repair" pull people who want the manufacturer, not you.
  • Wrong appliance class. If you don't service commercial refrigeration or high-end built-ins (Sub-Zero, Viking, Thermador), every click on those terms is waste — or worse, a lead your techs can't close.

None of that means you should kill search. Search is still where you capture the highest-intent brand-plus-symptom queries ("Bosch dishwasher not draining repair near me"). It just shouldn't be the only engine, and it shouldn't be the one carrying the call volume.

The call-only + LSA stack, explained

The structure that consistently gets appliance repair operators under $35 blended CPL has three layers, each doing one job:

Layer 1: Local Services Ads (the foundation). Google Guaranteed, pay-per-lead, top of the page. This is your cheapest lead source and should take 40–60% of total budget once your profile is healthy. You can dispute bad leads, and the badge itself lifts trust.

Layer 2: Call-only campaigns (the volume engine). Mobile-only ads where the headline is the phone call. No landing page, no bounce. Target symptom-plus-appliance keywords ("refrigerator not cooling repair," "washer won't spin repair") in exact and phrase match. Expect conversion rates of 18–30% on calls versus 6–12% for click-to-page search.

Layer 3: Responsive search with call assets (the closer). Smaller budget, tightly themed ad groups by appliance and brand, sending desktop and tablet traffic to dedicated appliance pages with click-to-call above the fold.

The stack works because each layer covers a gap in the others. LSA has limited keyword control and caps on volume. Call-only can't show on desktop. Search catches the researchers and brand-specific queries. Together they own the top of the results page for your best terms without bidding against yourself on the same click.

Building call-only campaigns that don't waste budget

Call-only campaigns are simple to launch and easy to get wrong. The rules we run:

  • Count calls of 60+ seconds as conversions, not every ring. The default is often lower, which inflates conversion data and teaches Smart Bidding to chase hang-ups. In appliance repair, a real booking conversation rarely runs under a minute.
  • Schedule ads to staffed hours only. A call-only ad running at 11 p.m. into voicemail is the most expensive lead you'll ever buy. If you don't have after-hours coverage, turn the ads off — or route nights to an AI receptionist that books into your calendar.
  • Use one campaign per service zone, not one per city. Over-segmenting thins out conversion data and stalls bidding. Three to five geo-zones is usually the sweet spot.
  • Write headlines that pre-qualify. "Same-Day Fridge Repair — $89 Diagnostic" filters out people looking for free advice and attracts people ready to book.
  • Start on Maximize Conversions, move to Target CPA once you have 30+ conversions in 30 days. Setting a tCPA too early starves the campaign.

Pair this with call tracking in CallRail or your CRM (GoHighLevel works well here) so every call is tagged by campaign, recorded, and scored. Without recordings you're optimizing blind.

Getting Local Services Ads to carry their weight

LSA is the cheapest lead source in this vertical, but most operators leave half its value on the table. Google's LSA ranking leans heavily on four signals: review count and rating, responsiveness, proximity, and business hours. You control three of them.

Reviews. Accounts with 100+ reviews at 4.7 stars or higher get noticeably more impression share than those with 20. Build a post-job review request into your dispatch flow — an SMS from the tech's phone within an hour of job completion converts far better than an email three days later.

Responsiveness. Google tracks how fast you answer and how often you miss calls. A missed-call rate above 15% quietly throttles your exposure. This is where answering services or AI voice agents earn their keep.

Lead disputes. Wrong service, wrong area, spam, and job-seeker calls are all disputable. Operators who review and dispute weekly typically recover 8–15% of LSA spend.

Service categories. Only enable the appliance types you actually fix profitably. Turning on "ice maker" when your techs hate those jobs just buys leads you'll lose money on.

Set your weekly budget high enough that you're not capped by Wednesday. A budget-limited LSA profile leaves the cheapest leads in the market for your competitors.

Negative keywords and geo settings that protect your CPL

In appliance repair, CPL is won as much by what you exclude as by what you bid on. Start every account with these negative themes and expand weekly from the search terms report:

  • DIY and parts: part, parts, manual, how to, diagram, reset, error code, YouTube, replacement part, model number patterns
  • Manufacturer support: customer service, warranty, phone number, recall, registration
  • Employment: jobs, hiring, technician salary, certification, training, school
  • Out-of-scope: commercial, industrial, restaurant (unless you service them), RV, mobile home
  • Purchase intent: buy, sale, cheap, Home Depot, Lowe's, Best Buy

On geography, two settings matter more than any bid strategy. First, switch location targeting to "Presence: people in or regularly in your targeted locations" — the default "presence or interest" option shows your ads to people researching your city from elsewhere. Second, draw your radius around drive time, not miles. A 20-mile radius that crosses a river or a highway bottleneck can put techs in traffic for an hour on a $180 ticket.

Then apply bid adjustments by zip code once you have 60 days of data. Most operators find two or three zips produce outsized revenue per job — those deserve +20–30% bids.

Measuring cost per booked job, not cost per lead

CPL is a useful dashboard number and a terrible business metric. A $28 lead that books 40% of the time costs $70 per job. A $45 lead that books 75% of the time costs $60. The second one is the better buy.

The metrics that actually matter, in order:

  1. Cost per booked job = ad spend ÷ jobs scheduled
  2. Cost per completed job = ad spend ÷ jobs that were actually run and invoiced
  3. Return on ad spend = revenue from paid jobs ÷ ad spend

Healthy appliance repair accounts usually land at 4–8x ROAS on first-ticket revenue, before counting repeat customers and maintenance plans. If you're under 3x, check your booking rate before touching the ads. In our experience the leak is usually on the phone — slow pickup, no price anchor, or a CSR who can't confidently quote a diagnostic fee.

To get this data, connect your field service software (ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro, Jobber) back to Google Ads with offline conversion imports. Once Google can see which calls became paid jobs, Smart Bidding stops optimizing for phone rings and starts optimizing for revenue. That single integration routinely drops cost per booked job 15–25% within 60 days.

A 30-day rollout plan

If you're rebuilding an underperforming account, sequence matters. Don't change everything on day one or you'll never know what worked.

Week 1: Foundation. Audit and verify your LSA profile, enable only profitable service categories, and set a budget that won't cap out. Install call tracking with recording. Define a 60-second call conversion. Build your negative keyword list from the last 90 days of search terms.

Week 2: Call-only launch. Stand up one call-only campaign per geo-zone with symptom-plus-appliance exact and phrase match keywords. Schedule to staffed hours. Start on Maximize Conversions.

Week 3: Restructure search. Collapse bloated search campaigns into tightly themed ad groups by appliance type. Point each to a dedicated page with click-to-call above the fold. Cut search budget 30–40% and shift it to LSA and call-only.

Week 4: Close the loop. Connect offline conversion imports from your field service software. Review call recordings to score booking rate by campaign. Dispute bad LSA leads.

By day 30 you should see blended CPL trending toward the bottom half of your metro tier. By day 90, with clean conversion data feeding the bidding, sub-$35 blended CPL is realistic in Tier 2 and Tier 3 markets — and within reach in Tier 1 for operators with strong reviews.

The bottom line

Appliance repair is a phone business, and Google rewards operators who build like it. The companies winning the auction in 2026 aren't outspending everyone — they're stacking LSA for cheap guaranteed leads, call-only campaigns for high-intent mobile volume, and tight search for the rest, then feeding real job revenue back into the bidding.

If your CPL sits above your metro tier, don't raise the budget. Fix the structure, fix the phone handling, and measure cost per booked job. The cheaper leads follow.

faq.question: What is a good cost per lead for appliance repair Google Ads?
faq.answer: It depends on your market. Mid-size metros typically land in the $24–$45 range on search and $18–$32 on Local Services Ads. Large Sun Belt metros run $38–$65 on search, and dense Tier 1 markets can hit $55–$95. A blended CPL under $35 is achievable in most Tier 2 and Tier 3 markets with an LSA plus call-only structure.

faq.question: Are Local Services Ads better than search ads for appliance repair?
faq.answer: LSA is usually cheaper per lead — often 30–45% below search — and shows above standard ads. But it offers limited keyword control and volume. The best results come from running LSA as the foundation and layering call-only and search campaigns on top to capture volume LSA can't.

faq.question: Should appliance repair companies use call-only ads?
faq.answer: Yes, for most operators. Appliance repair searches are urgent and mobile-heavy, and call-only ads remove the landing page step that loses 30–50% of potential conversions. Just schedule them to staffed hours and count only calls of 60 seconds or longer as conversions.

faq.question: How much should an appliance repair company spend on Google Ads per month?
faq.answer: Most single-location operators see meaningful data at $2,500–$6,000 per month across LSA, call-only, and search. Below that, Smart Bidding struggles to gather enough conversions. Scale budget only once cost per booked job is stable and your phones can handle the added volume.

faq.question: Why are my appliance repair leads so expensive?
faq.answer: The usual culprits are missing negative keywords (DIY, parts, manufacturer support), loose geo settings that show ads outside your area, counting short calls as conversions, and a low booking rate on the phone. Fix those before increasing spend.

articles.title: Hire a Marketing Agency vs Build In-House for Home Services
articles.description: True cost breakdown at $50k/mo ad spend: in-house marketer vs agency retainer for home service companies. Includes the hidden hiring risk owners miss.
articles.keyword: hire marketing agency vs build in house team for home services company
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
If you're a home services operator spending $50k/month on ads and debating whether to hire an in-house marketer or sign with an agency, the answer isn't what LinkedIn thought leaders tell you. The real cost gap between the two options is rarely the retainer fee — it's the 90-day hiring risk, the tool stack, and the opportunity cost of a founder playing CMO while trying to run a $5M-$20M service business. This is written for owners and CMOs of HVAC, roofing, plumbing, electrical, remodeling, and solar companies who've outgrown the handyman marketing phase and are making a real six-figure annual decision. Not theory. Line-item math. Below: the fully loaded cost of each path, where in-house actually wins, where agencies crush, and the one hiring mistake that costs home service companies an average of $180k when it blows up.

The $50k/month context: why this decision changes everything

At $50k/month in paid media, you're no longer in the "boost a Facebook post" era. You're running Google LSAs, Google Search, Performance Max, Meta lead gen, and probably YouTube or Nextdoor. That's 4-6 ad platforms, each with its own bidding logic, creative requirements, and conversion tracking setup. At this spend level, a 10% efficiency swing is $5,000/month — $60,000/year — in either direction. That's the entire salary difference between a mediocre marketing coordinator and a competent performance marketer. Which means the question isn't "what's cheaper?" It's "what produces a lower blended CPL and higher booked-job rate?" Home services also has a specific wrinkle most generalist marketers don't understand: geographic density, service-area bidding, and seasonal demand curves. A furnace lead in Minneapolis in October is worth 3x a furnace lead in July. If your marketer doesn't adjust bids weekly against weather, service capacity, and competitor pricing, you're bleeding margin. The decision framework comes down to three variables: total loaded cost, speed to competence, and risk of failure. Let's price each path honestly.

True cost of building in-house at $50k/mo ad spend

Here's what an in-house setup actually costs when you add every line item owners forget: - Senior performance marketer salary: $85,000-$110,000 base (US market, mid-tier metro)

  • Payroll tax, benefits, PTO loading: ~22% = $18,700-$24,200
  • Recruiter fee if you use one: 20-25% of first-year salary = $17,000-$27,500 one-time
  • Equipment, software seats, workspace: $3,500/year
  • Tool stack (next section breaks this down): $2,100-$3,400/month = $25,200-$40,800/year
  • Creative production (video editor, designer, either freelance or part-time): $2,500-$5,000/month = $30,000-$60,000/year
  • Your time managing them: 5-8 hours/week at a $200/hr opportunity cost = $52,000-$83,000/year Year-one loaded cost: $231,400-$352,000. Year-two (no recruiter fee): $214,400-$324,500. And that assumes one hire. If the hire doesn't cover creative, strategy, analytics, and platform execution — which no single person does well — you're hiring two people or outsourcing pieces anyway. Most home service owners budget $90k and are shocked when the real number arrives. The $90k is just the base salary. The business cost is 2.5-3.5x that number.

The tool stack bill nobody shows you upfront

An in-house marketer running paid media for a $50k/mo home services account needs real tools, not freemium versions. Here's the monthly tab: - CRM + pipeline (GoHighLevel, HubSpot, or ServiceTitan marketing module): $300-$900

  • Call tracking (CallRail or WhatConverts, required for Google Ads optimization): $150-$450
  • Landing page builder (Unbounce, Instapage, or inside GHL): $100-$300
  • Analytics + attribution (GA4 free, but Triple Whale/Hyros for serious tracking): $200-$500
  • Creative tools (Canva Pro, Adobe CC, maybe Motion or CapCut Pro): $100-$180
  • Competitive intel (SEMrush or Ahrefs): $130-$450
  • Reporting dashboard (Looker Studio free, or AgencyAnalytics): $0-$180
  • Heatmaps + session recording (Hotjar or Microsoft Clarity free): $0-$100
  • Email/SMS (if not inside CRM): $100-$300
  • Meeting scheduler (Calendly): $20 Total: $1,100-$3,380/month, or $13,200-$40,560/year. The low end assumes you consolidate on a platform like GoHighLevel. The high end is realistic for a company that already uses HubSpot and buys best-in-class per category. Agencies absorb this cost across clients. You pay for it alone.

True cost of an agency retainer for home services

A legitimate performance agency managing $50k/month in home services ad spend charges one of three ways: 1. Flat retainer: $5,000-$9,000/month 2. Percentage of spend: 10-15% = $5,000-$7,500/month 3. Hybrid (base + performance bonus): $4,000 base + $75-$150 per booked job Call it $6,500/month blended average, or $78,000/year. That includes media buying across platforms, creative iteration, landing pages, reporting, and strategy calls. What's included that you'd otherwise pay for separately: the tool stack ($15k-$40k/year), creative production (usually $20k-$40k/year of value), senior strategist time, and bench depth when someone's on vacation. Loaded year-one agency cost: $78,000 + maybe $20,000 in your management time = $98,000. Compare to in-house year one at $231k-$352k. The agency is 55-70% cheaper in year one, 50-65% cheaper in year two. The gap closes if you're spending $150k+/month on ads, where in-house starts making mathematical sense because the fixed cost of a team spreads across more volume. Under $100k/month, in-house rarely pencils out unless you have unusual requirements.

The hidden hiring risk owners underestimate

Here's the number almost nobody models: the cost of a bad marketing hire in a home services company. Average time-to-productivity for a marketing hire: 90-120 days. Average time to realize the hire isn't working: another 60-90 days (owners wait too long). Average time to replace: 60-90 days. That's 7-10 months of underperformance. What happens to your $50k/month ad spend during those 7-10 months? It keeps running. Poorly. Industry data from SHRM and performance marketing recruiters puts the real cost of a failed marketing hire at 1.5-2x annual salary when you include wasted ad spend, lost pipeline, severance, and re-hiring costs. For a $95k marketer, that's $142,500-$190,000 in damage. On a $50k/mo ad budget, a 20% efficiency drop over 8 months is $80,000 of wasted spend by itself. Failure rate for first marketing hires in SMB service businesses is roughly 40-50% within 18 months (internal recruiter data varies, but this is the range I see repeatedly). You're flipping a coin with $180k on the table. An agency contract has a 30-60 day out clause. If they underperform, you fire them in a quarter. The downside is capped. The downside of a bad hire is not.

Where in-house actually wins

I'm not anti in-house. There are specific scenarios where it clearly beats agency: - Ad spend above $150k/month. Fixed cost of a team spreads across enough volume that per-dollar management cost drops below agency pricing.

  • Multi-location operations with 5+ markets. The complexity of market-level reporting, localized creative, and franchise coordination benefits from a dedicated internal owner.
  • Proprietary data advantages. If you have unique CRM data, pricing models, or operational insights that need daily integration into campaigns, in-house captures that institutional knowledge.
  • Content-heavy strategies. If SEO, YouTube, and organic social are 40%+ of your pipeline, an in-house content producer who lives in your business produces better output than any agency.
  • You've already failed with 2+ agencies. Sometimes the issue is you need the control, not the price. The hybrid model also works: hire a marketing manager (not a performance marketer) at $70-$85k whose job is to own the agency relationship, run internal content, and manage CRM. Combined with an agency, this costs $160k-$180k loaded and gives you oversight without the hiring risk of a senior performance role. This is the setup I recommend most often for home services companies between $5M and $15M in revenue.

Decision framework: which path fits your business

Use this scorecard. Give yourself a point for each statement that's true: Agency is probably right if:

  • Ad spend is under $100k/month
  • You've never hired a marketer before
  • You need results in under 60 days
  • You don't want to manage creative production
  • Your founder/CMO has less than 5 hours/week for marketing oversight
  • You operate in 1-3 markets In-house (or hybrid) is probably right if:
  • Ad spend is above $150k/month
  • You have 5+ service markets or locations
  • You have an existing marketing coordinator ready to level up
  • Your sales cycle requires daily CRM integration
  • You've successfully managed a direct report in a non-core function before
  • Content/SEO is central to your strategy If you scored 4+ on the agency side, stop debating. Sign a 6-month agreement with a performance-based clause and move on. If you scored 4+ on the in-house side, hire a marketing manager first (not a performance marketer), pair them with an agency for 12 months, then evaluate bringing paid media execution in-house in year two. This sequence has a dramatically lower failure rate than hiring a senior performance marketer cold.

The bottom line

At $50k/month ad spend, the honest math is: agency wins year one by $130k-$250k, year two by $100k-$220k, and carries roughly a quarter of the downside risk of a direct hire. For most home services companies between $3M and $15M in revenue, that's the right call — not because in-house is bad, but because the hiring risk is uniquely brutal in a specialized function most owners can't effectively evaluate. The scenario that flips the equation is scale (ads above $150k/month) or complexity (5+ markets, proprietary data, heavy content). If you're there, build the hybrid: hire a marketing manager to own the function and keep the agency executing paid media until internal capability is proven. Run the numbers on your own line items before anyone — agency or recruiter — tells you what you "should" do.

faq.question: What should I expect to pay an agency to manage $50k/month in home services ads?
faq.answer: Expect $5,000-$9,000/month flat, or 10-15% of ad spend if they price on percentage. Any agency charging under $4,000/month at that spend level is either junior, overbooked, or using you as a case study — all three are risks.

faq.question: Can I just hire a $55k marketing coordinator instead of a senior performance marketer?
faq.answer: You can, but they won't run paid media competently at $50k/month spend. A coordinator can manage an agency relationship, run social, and own your CRM — pair them with an agency for execution. Don't put a coordinator in charge of a $600k/year ad budget.

faq.question: How long before I know if a marketing hire is working?
faq.answer: 90 days to see initial campaign improvements, 180 days to judge real business impact (booked jobs, CPL trend, close rate contribution). If you don't see measurable movement in CPL or lead volume by day 120, you have a problem.

faq.question: What's the biggest mistake home service owners make when hiring an agency?
faq.answer: Signing without a clear performance benchmark and 30-day exit clause. Define what success looks like in writing (CPL targets, lead volume, booked-job rate), require weekly reporting, and keep the ability to leave fast if numbers don't move within 90 days.

faq.question: Does it make sense to have both an in-house marketer and an agency?
faq.answer: Yes, for companies above $5M in revenue this is often the best setup. The in-house marketer owns strategy, CRM, content, and vendor management. The agency handles paid media execution and creative. You get oversight without taking on the specialist hiring risk.

articles.title: How to Run a Quarterly Business Review That Saves At-Risk Agency Clients
articles.description: The exact 7-slide QBR deck we use to retain churn-risk retainers, prove attribution, and pitch upsells with a forward 90-day roadmap.
articles.keyword: how to run a quarterly business review that saves at risk agency clients
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Roughly 70% of agency churn happens in the 30 days before the client actually fires you. By the time they email with "let's hop on a call," the decision is already made. The quarterly business review is the one standing meeting where you can intercept that decision — if you run it right. Most agencies run QBRs like a book report. They dump screenshots from Looker Studio, read CPA numbers off a slide, and ask "any questions?" That's not a QBR. That's a status update with a fancier name, and it's why clients still churn two weeks later. This article breaks down the 7-slide QBR deck we use at Social Elite to turn churn-risk retainers into upsells. Every slide has a job: reframe the narrative, prove attribution, surface pipeline value the client forgot about, and lock in a 90-day roadmap they signed off on.

Why most agency QBRs accelerate churn instead of preventing it

The default QBR format is a performance report in a suit. You open with last quarter's spend, show CPL trends, celebrate a few wins, and close with "what questions do you have?" If results were mediocre, you just spent 45 minutes reminding the client why they're unhappy. The fundamental mistake: treating the QBR as a reporting meeting instead of a strategic realignment meeting. Reporting lives in the monthly Loom or the Slack channel. The QBR exists to answer three questions the client is already asking privately: 1. Is this agency actually moving the needle, or are we paying for activity? 2. Do they understand my business better than they did 90 days ago? 3. What's the plan for the next 90 days, and is it worth the retainer? If your deck doesn't answer those three questions in the first 20 minutes, the client is mentally shopping. We've reviewed over 200 QBR recordings across our portfolio and partner agencies, and the pattern is brutal: decks that lead with spend and metrics have a 2.3x higher 90-day churn rate than decks that lead with pipeline value and business outcomes. The slide order is doing more work than the slide content.

Identifying at-risk clients 45 days before the QBR

You can't save a retainer in the QBR if you walk in blind. Build a churn-risk scorecard and run it monthly. We score every account 1-5 on six signals: - Response latency — are emails/Slacks getting slower? (HubSpot or GoHighLevel conversation timestamps)

  • Stakeholder access — are you still talking to the decision-maker, or getting handed to a coordinator?
  • Attribution clarity — can you prove last-touch or multi-touch wins in the last 30 days?
  • Pipeline movement — is sourced pipeline flat, growing, or declining QoQ?
  • Scope creep complaints — any mention of "we expected more" in the last 60 days?
  • Payment behavior — invoices paid in 7 days vs. dragging to Net 45? Any account scoring 3+ on two or more signals is at-risk. Flag it, and the account lead gets 10 extra hours to build the QBR deck. That's not optional — it's the difference between a $120k ARR save and a replacement scramble. Run the scorecard in a shared Airtable or Notion database. Review it in your weekly leadership standup. By the time the QBR is on the calendar, you should already know whether you're defending the retainer or pitching an expansion.

Slide 1-2: Reframe the narrative with business outcomes, not metrics

Slide 1: "What we set out to do in Q[X]." One slide, three bullets. The original goals the client signed off on at the last QBR or kickoff. No metrics yet. Just the business objectives in the client's own language — "book 40 qualified demos per month," "grow MQL-to-SQL conversion from 18% to 25%," "launch in the Phoenix market." This slide does two things. It anchors the conversation in commitments they made, not just promises you made. And it stops the client from moving the goalposts mid-meeting, which is the #1 way at-risk QBRs go sideways. Slide 2: "Where we landed." For each goal, a green/yellow/red status with one sentence of context. Not a dashboard screenshot. A narrative. Example: "🟢 Booked 47 qualified demos/mo in Q3 vs. 40 target — overachieved by 17%, driven by LinkedIn outbound sequence launched in August." If you missed a goal, own it on this slide. "🔴 Phoenix launch delayed — we underestimated lead response time with the local sales rep. Addressed in Slide 6." Honesty here buys you credibility for the next five slides. Hiding misses buys you a 60-day runway to termination.

Slide 3: The attribution win slide (this is where retainers get saved)

This is the single most important slide in the deck. The client's CFO is asking "what did the agency actually generate?" and if you can't answer with a dollar figure, you lose. Build one slide that shows sourced pipeline and closed revenue attributed to your work over the quarter. Use whatever attribution model matches the client's sales cycle — first-touch for short cycles, multi-touch (we use HubSpot's or Dreamdata) for B2B with 60+ day cycles. Format it as a simple table: - Marketing-sourced opportunities: 83

  • Pipeline value sourced: $1.42M
  • Closed-won attributed: $340k
  • Agency retainer cost (quarterly): $45k
  • Return multiple: 7.5x If the return multiple is above 4x, you're having an upsell conversation. If it's 2-4x, you're defending the current scope. Below 2x, you need Slide 6 (the roadmap) to carry the deck. Two tactical notes: First, always include sourced pipeline even if close rates lag — pipeline is leading, revenue is lagging, and at-risk clients need to see momentum. Second, if the client's internal tracking is a mess (common with lenders and local service businesses), rebuild the attribution yourself using call tracking (CallRail), form submissions (GHL), and CRM stage data. Don't let bad data from their side kill your renewal.

Slide 4: Pipeline value the client forgot about

Clients forget. They remember the three deals that fell through and forget the 60 opportunities still open in the funnel. Slide 4 reminds them. Show every open opportunity your work generated that's still in the pipeline, grouped by stage. Pull it from HubSpot, Salesforce, or GHL opportunities directly — don't eyeball it. Structure: - Stage 1 (new leads, last 30 days): 142 contacts, est. value $890k

  • Stage 2 (qualified, in nurture): 38 opps, est. value $560k
  • Stage 3 (proposals out): 11 opps, est. value $240k
  • Stage 4 (verbal/closing): 4 opps, est. value $95k Total open pipeline: $1.78M. That's the number that keeps you in the game. The client's instinct to churn gets re-weighed against walking away from $1.78M of in-progress revenue your team built. Add one callout box: "3 Stage 4 opportunities expected to close in next 30 days — total value $71k." This creates loss aversion. Firing you now means someone else inherits those closes and takes credit. Decision-makers hate that outcome, and this slide makes it tangible.

Slide 5: What we learned about your buyer (the strategic depth slide)

At-risk clients secretly believe you don't understand their business as well as they do. Slide 5 proves otherwise. Share 3-5 specific insights your team learned about the client's buyer, market, or funnel in the last 90 days. Examples that have saved real retainers: - "LinkedIn ads targeting VP of Finance converted 3.2x better than CFO — CFOs delegate research to VPs. We're reallocating 70% of ICP targeting to VP-level in Q4."

  • "Leads from Google Search convert at 11%, Meta at 4%, but Meta retargeting of Google-source leads closes at 19%. We're building a Meta retargeting layer around all paid search traffic."
  • "Discovery calls booked before 11am close at 2.4x the rate of afternoon calls. We're restricting Calendly availability to AM slots only." These aren't generic best practices. They're insights specific to their funnel that nobody else has, because nobody else has your data access. This slide is also where you preemptively defuse the "we could do this in-house or with a cheaper agency" conversation — the implicit message is "nobody else is 90 days deep in your data."

Slide 6-7: The forward 90-day roadmap and the upsell lane

Slide 6: The 90-day roadmap. Three columns — Month 1, Month 2, Month 3 — with 3-4 specific initiatives per month. Not "optimize campaigns." Specific: "Launch LAL audience from closed-won list (Oct 15)," "Build Clay-sourced outbound list for Series B SaaS vertical (Nov 1)," "Test VSL landing page vs. current form page (Nov 20)." Each initiative needs an owner, a date, and a success metric. This slide is the one the client screenshots and sends to their boss when asked "what's the agency doing for us next quarter?" Slide 7: Where we could go further (the upsell lane). Frame this as "opportunities we're not currently resourced to pursue." Not "here's more we want to sell you." Examples: - "Current scope covers paid acquisition. We're seeing 34% of leads drop between MQL and SQL — a lifecycle email + SMS layer in GoHighLevel would recover an estimated 40-60 leads/month at ~$8/lead cost. Add-on: $4,500/mo."

  • "Phoenix launch would benefit from a localized landing page + GBP optimization sprint. 6-week project, $12k." Price everything on the slide. Don't make them ask. Clients who were 60% churn-risk entering the meeting have signed $4k-15k/mo expansions off this slide because you reframed the problem as "here's revenue we're leaving on the table together."

How to run the actual meeting so the deck works

The deck is 50% of the save. The meeting execution is the other 50%. Three rules: 1. Pre-send Slides 1-4 the day before. Attribution and pipeline numbers should not be a surprise. Clients who see the numbers cold get defensive. Clients who've had 18 hours to process them come to the meeting ready to discuss strategy. Send a Loom walking through Slides 1-4 with the deck attached. 2. Spend 60% of the meeting on Slides 5-7. The past is settled. The meeting's job is to sell the future. If you're still on Slide 3 at the 25-minute mark, you're losing. Use the Loom pre-send to compress the backward-looking content. 3. End with a specific commitment, not "let's regroup." Before the call ends, confirm: "Can we lock in the Month 1 roadmap as-is, and I'll send a scoping doc for the lifecycle email add-on by Friday?" Get a yes or a specific objection. Vague QBR endings produce vague renewals. Record every QBR (Fathom or Fireflies). Review at least two per month as a leadership team. The patterns in save-vs-churn conversations are more valuable than any sales training you'll pay for.

The bottom line

A QBR isn't a reporting ritual. It's the single highest-leverage retention and expansion meeting on your calendar, and most agencies waste it reading dashboards aloud. The 7-slide structure — goals, status, attribution, open pipeline, buyer insights, 90-day roadmap, upsell lane — exists because each slide answers a specific question your at-risk client is already asking in private. The next action: pull your client list, score every account on the six churn-risk signals, and rebuild the QBR deck for your two highest-risk retainers using this 7-slide structure. If you execute it well, the meeting that was going to end your contract becomes the meeting that expands it. The deck is a template. The save is in the preparation.

faq.question: How often should we run QBRs with retainer clients?
faq.answer: Quarterly is the floor. For retainers above $10k/mo or clients in long sales cycles (60+ days), run them every 90 days without exception. For at-risk accounts specifically, insert a mid-quarter strategic check-in at the 45-day mark to course-correct before the formal QBR.

faq.question: What if our attribution data is incomplete or messy?
faq.answer: Rebuild it yourself before the QBR. Pull call tracking from CallRail, form submissions from GHL or HubSpot, and CRM stage data directly. If the client's internal CRM hygiene is poor, use UTM-based first-touch attribution as a defensible baseline. Showing imperfect-but-honest attribution beats showing nothing or hiding behind "their data is messy."

faq.question: Should the QBR be in-person, video, or recorded async?
faq.answer: Live video with pre-sent async context. Send a Loom walkthrough of Slides 1-4 the day before so numbers aren't a surprise, then run a 45-minute live Zoom focused on Slides 5-7. In-person is overkill for most retainers under $25k/mo and burns time that's better spent on the next client's deck.

faq.question: How do we pitch an upsell during a QBR without seeming tone-deaf when results are mediocre?
faq.answer: Frame the upsell as solving a specific problem the data revealed, not as a product push. If results are below target, the upsell slide should connect directly to why — "we're losing 34% of MQLs between stages, here's the fix." If results are above target, the upsell is about compounding wins. Never pitch an upsell untethered from a diagnosed problem.

faq.question: What's the single biggest mistake agencies make in QBRs with at-risk clients?
faq.answer: Leading with spend and campaign metrics instead of pipeline value and business outcomes. The client's CFO cares about sourced revenue multiple, not your CPC trend. Reorder the deck so attribution and pipeline hit in the first 15 minutes, and your retention rate on at-risk accounts will roughly double.

articles.title: Apply for AOS Funding for HVAC Company Expansion: The Prep Guide
articles.description: How HVAC owners doing $500K–$3M should prep an AOS funding application: revenue docs, a truck-and-tech use-of-funds plan, and realistic approval ranges.
articles.keyword: apply for aos funding for hvac company expansion
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most HVAC owners who get a weak funding offer didn't have a weak business. They had a weak file. A $1.8M shop with 22% net margins and a full maintenance-agreement book will get offered the same thin line of credit as a $600K shop if the application shows up with mismatched bank statements, a P&L built in a weekend, and a use-of-funds line that says "growth."

Underwriters don't fund ambition. They fund predictable cash flow attached to a specific plan. In HVAC, that plan is almost always the same: more trucks, more techs, more booked calls in July and January. The good news is that HVAC is one of the easiest trades to underwrite well — recurring maintenance revenue, seasonal demand that's predictable even if it's lumpy, and hard assets (vans, equipment) that secure part of the deal.

This guide is for owners and operators running $500K–$3M in annual revenue who are about to apply for AOS funding to expand. Below is the exact document stack, how to write a use-of-funds narrative an underwriter can actually say yes to, the approval ranges we typically see by revenue tier, and the mistakes that quietly cut offers in half.

Why HVAC expansion deals get cut before anyone reads the plan

The first pass on most business funding files is not a human reading your growth story. It's a cash-flow review of your bank statements. Underwriters are looking at three numbers before anything else:

  • Average monthly deposits over the last 6–12 months
  • Average daily balance and the number of days you dipped below $1,000 (or went negative)
  • Existing debt payments already pulling out of the account — especially daily or weekly MCA debits

HVAC has a specific problem here: seasonality. A shop that deposits $210K in July and $85K in March looks volatile to a reviewer who doesn't know the trade. If you don't explain it, they'll underwrite to your worst months.

The second problem is commingling. Owners who run personal expenses, equipment purchases, and side-job deposits through the same operating account make their real margins invisible. We've seen $1.2M shops present like $700K shops because $400K+ of revenue was split across a personal account and a Square account nobody mentioned.

The third is stacked short-term debt. Two open merchant cash advances with daily debits will cap almost any new offer, no matter how strong your top line is. If you're carrying MCAs, the expansion conversation often starts with consolidating them — not adding a third.

Fix the file first. The plan only matters once the cash flow clears.

The revenue document stack to have ready on day one

Speed matters in funding. The fastest approvals we see come from owners who hand over a complete file in the first conversation, not over three weeks of back-and-forth. Here's the stack:

  1. 12 months of business bank statements — all operating accounts, full PDFs straight from the bank, not screenshots or exports.
  2. Last two years of business tax returns (or one year plus YTD financials if you're younger).
  3. YTD profit and loss and balance sheet — ideally pulled from QuickBooks or Xero, not built in a spreadsheet the night before.
  4. Accounts receivable aging report — commercial HVAC shops especially; 30/60/90-day buckets matter.
  5. Maintenance agreement count and recurring revenue — export this from ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro, or FieldEdge. Number of active agreements × average annual value is one of the strongest signals you have.
  6. Equipment and vehicle list — year, make, model, VIN, current payoff for each truck.
  7. Debt schedule — every loan, lease, line, and advance with balance, payment, and maturity.
  8. Contractor license and insurance certificates.

If you run a field service platform, pull a 12-month revenue-by-month report and a jobs-by-type breakdown (install vs. repair vs. maintenance). That single report explains your seasonality better than any paragraph you'll write. Install-heavy shops look riskier; maintenance-heavy shops look like subscription businesses. Show which one you are.

Writing a use-of-funds narrative an underwriter can approve

"Expansion" is not a use of funds. A use of funds is a line-item plan that connects dollars to revenue an underwriter can believe. For HVAC, it should read like a unit-economics sheet.

Here's the structure we recommend:

1. The constraint. "We turned away or delayed an estimated 140 service calls in June–August because we have four techs and four trucks. Average ticket on those calls is $485." Pull call-tracking or CSR data to back this up — CallRail or your phone system logs are fine.

2. The purchase. "Two fully upfitted service vans at $68K each ($136K), two experienced techs at $32/hour fully loaded ~$85K/year each, $12K in tools and starter inventory per truck."

3. The payback math. "Each truck running 4 calls/day at a $485 average and 22% net margin produces roughly $9,300/month in net profit at 20 working days. Two trucks cover a $5,800/month debt payment with room to spare by month three."

4. The ramp risk. Acknowledge it. "Months one and two will run at 50–60% utilization while new techs ride along and we shift ad spend to fill capacity."

Underwriters trust plans that admit ramp time. They distrust plans where new trucks print money on day one. Keep the narrative to one page. Attach the math as a simple table. That's it.

Approval ranges we typically see for $500K–$3M HVAC shops

Every file is different, and nothing here is a quote or a guarantee. But owners deserve a realistic anchor before they apply, so here are the ranges we commonly see for HVAC operators with clean files, 2+ years in business, and owner credit in the 650+ range:

Annual revenue Typical total capital range Common structure
