Gemini was cheapest but required significantly more editing. If cost matters most, GPT-4o-mini is workable with tighter prompts.

faq.question: How long until the workflow produces publishable output?
faq.answer: Expect 4-6 weeks of iteration before the output is genuinely publishable without heavy edits. The first two weeks will produce recognizable AI slop no matter what you do. Voice-matching gets better as you build up the reference document of approved posts.

faq.question: What if my founder won't record a weekly podcast?
faq.answer: Then this workflow won't work for you — full stop. The entire system depends on a consistent, opinionated source input. If the founder won't record 45 minutes a week, either find a different source (a sales call recording, a Loom, an internal all-hands) or hire a writer to interview them.

faq.question: Does Google penalize AI-generated content produced this way?
faq.answer: Google's stance is that they penalize unhelpful content, not AI-assisted content. Because this workflow is human-reviewed, sources original founder POV, and includes specific examples and quotes, it reads as high-quality content. We've had zero ranking issues on articles produced through it — but blindly publishing raw AI output without QA will hurt you.

articles.title: How to Use AI to Score Inbound Leads in Real Time (Under 30s)
articles.description: A tactical guide to scoring inbound leads with GPT-4o and webhooks in under 30 seconds — plus a fitness studio case study that tripled show rates.
articles.keyword: how to use ai to score inbound leads in real time
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most inbound leads die in the first five minutes. Not because they aren't interested — because your sales team is on another call, your rep pipeline is a Slack channel, and your CRM's "lead score" is a static number based on form field length. By the time someone actually looks at the lead, they've already booked with a competitor who called back in 90 seconds. This is fixable. With a webhook, a GPT-4o API call, and about 40 lines of glue code, you can classify inbound lead intent in under 30 seconds and route the hot ones to a live rep's phone while the cold ones drop into a nurture sequence. No new CRM. No six-figure enterprise contract. Below is the exact architecture we deployed for a 4-location fitness studio that took their inbound-to-booked-consult rate from 22% to 61% in six weeks — including the prompts, the scoring rubric, and the numbers.

Why static lead scoring is dead weight in 2026

The old model — HubSpot's built-in scoring, Salesforce's grade/rating fields, Marketo's behavioral points — was designed for a world where sales reps followed up within a business day and prospects were patient. That world is gone. Static scoring rules break for three reasons: - They can't read language. A form message that says "my husband and I are moving to Austin in March and need a gym before we sign our lease" scores identically to "just looking, thanks" if both check the same dropdowns.

  • They lag. Points-based systems require someone to log the activity, then the score updates on a nightly refresh. By then the lead is cold.
  • They optimize for the wrong signal. Time on site, email opens, and pages viewed correlate weakly with buying intent for high-consideration services. What actually correlates: specificity of the ask, urgency language, and stated timeline. AI scoring reads the actual content of the inbound message — free-text, context, urgency, buying signals — and returns a score in seconds. That's the shift. You're no longer scoring behavior after the fact; you're scoring intent at the moment of arrival.

The 30-second architecture: webhook + GPT-4o + router

The stack is deliberately boring. Boring is fast to build and easy to debug. 1. Form fires webhook. Any form platform works — Typeform, Gravity Forms, GoHighLevel forms, native site forms. On submit, POST the payload to a webhook endpoint (we use Make.com or n8n; a Cloudflare Worker also works). 2. Webhook calls GPT-4o API. Payload includes the raw form fields plus any enrichment you have (source URL, UTM params, IP-based location from Clearbit or IPinfo). Prompt returns a JSON object: {score: 1-100, intent_tier: hot/warm/cold, reasoning: string, recommended_action: string}. 3. Router dispatches based on tier. Hot leads (score 80+) trigger a Twilio call to the on-duty rep AND a text to the lead: "Hey [name], this is Sarah from [studio] — saw you just reached out, calling you in 60 seconds." Warm leads (50-79) go to a same-day callback queue. Cold leads (<50) drop into a 14-day email nurture. 4. Log everything. Every score, prompt, and outcome goes to a Google Sheet or Airtable base for weekly prompt tuning. End-to-end latency in production: 8-14 seconds from form submit to rep phone ringing. GPT-4o is fast enough that the bottleneck is Twilio's call initiation, not the model.

The scoring prompt that actually works

Prompts that ask the model to "rate this lead 1-100" without a rubric produce garbage. You need a scoring rubric embedded in the system prompt. Here's the structure we use: ``` You are a senior sales qualifier for [BUSINESS TYPE]. Score this inbound lead on intent to buy within 30 days. Rubric:

  • 90-100: Explicit timeline within 30 days, specific pain, budget signal, or asks about pricing/availability directly.
  • 70-89: Strong problem statement, timeline 30-90 days, or referral mention.
  • 50-69: Curious, researching, no timeline stated but relevant fit.
  • 30-49: Information gathering, generic questions, no urgency signals.
  • 0-29: Job seeker, vendor pitch, spam, or wrong ICP. Return strict JSON: {score, intent_tier, reasoning (max 2 sentences), recommended_action}. Lead data: [INSERT FORM FIELDS]
- **Constrain the output.** Use OpenAI's `response_format: json_object` parameter. Never parse free-text — you'll hit edge cases weekly. Run the prompt in batch against 200 historical leads with known outcomes before you go live. If the score doesn't correlate with actual closes, tune the rubric, not the model.

Case study: how a fitness studio 3x'd show rates in 6 weeks

The client: a boutique strength training studio with 4 locations across Denver, running $18K/month in Meta and Google Ads driving free-trial consult bookings. Baseline (before AI scoring):

  • Inbound leads: ~340/month
  • Lead-to-booked-consult: 22%
  • Consult show rate: 54%
  • Trial-to-membership close: 41%
  • Cost per member: $312 The problem: front desk staff triaged leads between class check-ins. Average response time was 47 minutes. Hot leads with clear buying intent got the same drip email as tire-kickers. What we built: Gravity Forms → Make.com webhook → GPT-4o scoring → GoHighLevel routing. Hot leads (80+) triggered a Twilio call to the location manager's cell within 30 seconds and a personalized SMS. Warm leads went into a same-day callback list sorted by score. Cold leads got a 14-day nurture with content matched to their stated goal. Results after 6 weeks:
  • Median response time on hot leads: 71 seconds
  • Lead-to-booked-consult: 61% (from 22%)
  • Consult show rate: 78% (from 54%)
  • Trial-to-membership close: 44%
  • Cost per member: $118 (down 62%) The scoring model correctly identified 87% of leads that eventually became members within the top two tiers. The single biggest lift came from calling hot leads within 90 seconds — the AI just made that triage possible without hiring another SDR.

What to feed the model beyond form fields

The form fields are the floor, not the ceiling. Enrichment before the GPT-4o call materially improves scoring accuracy. Cheap, fast additions: - UTM and referrer data. A lead from a branded search query ranks differently than one from a cold display ad. Feed the full UTM string into the prompt.

  • Time and day of submission. Leads that submit at 11pm on a Tuesday behave differently than 9am Monday. Include timestamp context.
  • IP-based location and company. IPinfo ($0.50/1K lookups) or Clearbit Reveal returns company name for B2B and city for B2C. For local service businesses, distance-from-location is a huge signal.
  • Page path history. If you have a segment.io or PostHog session, pass the last 5 page URLs. A lead who viewed pricing three times before submitting is a different animal.
  • Previous interactions. If the email exists in your CRM, pull the last touchpoint summary. Returning leads should score higher. Don't dump raw JSON at the model — summarize enrichment into a plain-English context block. GPT-4o performs meaningfully better on natural language than on nested JSON. Total added latency for enrichment: 2-4 seconds if you parallelize the API calls.

Routing hot leads to a live rep without dropping the ball

Scoring is worthless if the handoff fails. The routing layer is where most implementations quietly break. The pattern that holds up in production: 1. On-duty rep detection. Maintain a simple availability schedule in Airtable or GoHighLevel. The webhook checks who's actually on shift before firing the Twilio call. Nothing kills trust like ringing a rep's phone on their day off. 2. Failover chain. If the primary rep doesn't answer within 20 seconds, roll to secondary. If nobody picks up, send an immediate SMS to the lead: "Missed you — booking link here so you can grab a slot right now: [Calendly link]." Never leave a hot lead hanging. 3. Context brief on the call. When Twilio connects the rep, play a short whispered brief: "Hot lead, score 92, wants strength training, moving to Denver next month." We do this by piping the GPT-4o reasoning field into a text-to-speech intro. The rep walks into the call already briefed. 4. Auto-log the outcome. After the call, the rep gets a one-tap SMS: "Booked / No answer / Not fit — reply with number." That outcome writes back to the scoring log for weekly model tuning. The fitness studio saw a 40-point jump in show rates specifically because reps were prepped on the lead's context before they said hello.

Cost, tooling, and what this actually costs to run

Real monthly costs for a business doing 500-1,500 inbound leads/month: - GPT-4o API: ~$0.008 per lead scored (input + output tokens for a typical prompt). 1,000 leads = $8/month. Use gpt-4o-mini for the first-pass filter if volume is much higher; it's ~10x cheaper and adequate for cold/warm classification.

  • Make.com or n8n: $29-99/month depending on operation volume. n8n self-hosted is free if you have a $5 VPS.
  • Twilio: ~$0.013/minute for calls, $0.008/SMS. Budget $50-150/month.
  • Enrichment (IPinfo/Clearbit): $50-200/month depending on volume.
  • CRM (GoHighLevel/HubSpot): whatever you already pay. All-in: $150-500/month for the infra. For a business spending $10K+/month on ads, this pays back inside the first week almost always. Build time with a competent developer or automation specialist: 15-25 hours for v1, another 10-15 hours of tuning over the first month. If you're building it yourself with Make.com and don't code, budget 40-60 hours and expect to break it twice. Do not try to build this on Zapier — the latency and error handling aren't good enough for a 30-second SLA.

The mistakes that kill these builds in month two

Most AI lead scoring projects work great in week one and quietly decay by week eight. The failure modes are predictable: - No feedback loop. If you never compare AI scores against actual closed outcomes, the model drifts and you don't notice. Weekly review of the top 20 and bottom 20 scored leads against outcomes is non-negotiable.

  • Prompt sprawl. Someone adds a rule, then another, and six weeks later the prompt is 800 tokens of contradictory instructions. Version your prompts in Git. Change one thing at a time.
  • Ignoring the reps' feedback. Your best-closing rep knows things the model doesn't. Set up a Slack channel where reps flag misscored leads. Feed those into your few-shot examples monthly.
  • Over-automating cold leads. The cold tier is where you lose long-tail revenue. A lead scored 35 today might be a 90 in three months. Nurture them like humans, not like list fodder.
  • Not monitoring latency. GPT-4o occasionally spikes to 8-12 seconds. Set up a Datadog or Better Stack alert if end-to-end time exceeds 45 seconds. A slow hot-lead alert is a broken hot-lead alert. Treat this like the piece of infrastructure it is. It's not a set-and-forget tool — it's a scoring engine that needs quarterly tuning, same as your ad accounts.

The bottom line

Real-time AI lead scoring isn't a nice-to-have anymore — it's the difference between capturing intent while it's hot and paying to generate that same intent twice. The stack is cheap, the build is measured in weeks, and the compounding effect on close rate is larger than almost any other optimization you can make to a paid acquisition funnel. Start with 200 historical leads and a scoring prompt. Batch-score them, compare to actual outcomes, and tune the rubric until the correlation is real. Then wire the webhook. Then wire the router. Ship v1 in a month, not a quarter.

faq.question: How accurate is GPT-4o at scoring lead intent compared to a human sales rep?
faq.answer: In our benchmarks across ~2,000 scored leads, GPT-4o with a tuned rubric and few-shot examples agrees with senior sales reps' scoring roughly 84-89% of the time. It's not better than a great human — it's just consistent, instant, and available at 3am. That's the whole value prop.

faq.question: Do I need to switch CRMs to build this?
faq.answer: No. This layer sits between your form and your CRM. It works with HubSpot, Salesforce, GoHighLevel, Pipedrive, or a Google Sheet. The webhook writes the score back to whatever fields you have. Don't let a vendor sell you a platform migration to get AI scoring — it's a plumbing job, not a rip-and-replace.

faq.question: What happens if the GPT-4o API is down or slow?
faq.answer: Build a fallback. If the API doesn't respond in 15 seconds, default the lead to the 'warm' tier and notify a rep. Never block the lead from entering your CRM because the AI call failed. Log the failure and investigate — but the lead moves forward either way.

faq.question: Can this work for low-volume, high-ticket B2B like consulting or M&A?
faq.answer: Yes, and arguably it works better there. When each lead is worth $50K+, missing a hot one is catastrophic. Feed the model deeper enrichment (LinkedIn data via Clay, company revenue, tech stack) and the scoring becomes qualitative research at machine speed. The 30-second SLA matters even more when your competitor is charging the same rates.

faq.question: How often should I retune the scoring prompt?
faq.answer: Review it weekly for the first month, then monthly. Retune formally every quarter or whenever your offer, ICP, or ad channels shift materially. Keep a changelog — you'll want to know which version of the prompt produced which scoring behavior when outcomes start drifting.

articles.title: Best CRM Automation for Roofing Companies: JobNimbus vs GHL vs AccuLynx
articles.description: Comparing JobNimbus, GoHighLevel, and AccuLynx on lead-to-appointment automation, call tracking, and cost per user for a 10-rep roofing sales floor.
articles.keyword: best crm automation for roofing companies
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most roofing companies lose 40-60% of inbound leads before the first appointment is even booked. Not because the leads are bad — because the CRM sits there like a filing cabinet while a rep is on a roof or driving between jobs. The lead ages, the competitor's auto-responder fires in 90 seconds, and you eat a $75-$150 CPL for nothing. If you're running a 10-rep sales floor and spending $8K-$40K/month on leads (Meta, Google LSA, storm-chasing lists), your CRM isn't a database problem — it's a speed-to-lead and appointment-setting problem. The three names that dominate this conversation are JobNimbus, GoHighLevel (GHL), and AccuLynx. They are not equivalent tools. This breakdown compares all three on the only three things that actually move revenue: lead-to-appointment automation, integration with call tracking, and true cost per user at 10 seats.

The real job of a roofing CRM (and why most fail at it)

A roofing CRM has to do three things well before anything else matters: catch a lead in under 60 seconds, book an appointment without a human touching it, and track which ad source produced the booked job — not just the lead. JobNimbus and AccuLynx were built as production and job management platforms first. They handle photos, measurements (EagleView, HOVER), material orders, and insurance supplements beautifully. Their front-end lead automation was bolted on later, and it shows. GoHighLevel was built as a marketing automation and communication platform. It has no idea what a supplement is, but it will fire an SMS, ringless voicemail, and email inside 8 seconds of a form submission and keep hammering the lead across 14 touchpoints until they book or opt out. Here's the operator's take: - If your bottleneck is production chaos after the sale, JobNimbus or AccuLynx wins.

  • If your bottleneck is leads dying before the appointment, GHL wins — and it's not close.
  • Most 10-rep floors have both problems, which is why the smart stack is GHL on the front + JobNimbus on the back, connected via webhook or Zapier. The rest of this article assumes you already know which bottleneck is costing you more.

JobNimbus: strong on production, average on lead speed

JobNimbus runs about $75/user/month on the Growing plan (annual billing), which puts a 10-rep floor at roughly $750/month plus onboarding. It integrates natively with EagleView, CompanyCam, QuickBooks, Beacon, and SRS — the roofing production stack. On lead-to-appointment automation, JobNimbus has Automation Engine which fires workflows on triggers (new contact, status change, tag added). You can send templated emails and texts, assign reps by territory, and create tasks. It works. It's not fast. Where it lags: - No native power dialer. Reps click-to-call or use a third party.

  • Two-way SMS is functional but not conversational-AI ready. No native AI booking agent.
  • Speed-to-lead automations typically fire in 30-90 seconds, not sub-10-second like GHL.
  • Call tracking integration is limited — CallRail works via Zapier, but attribution back to ad source at the job-won level requires manual tagging. JobNimbus shines once the appointment is set. Job costing, material ordering, subcontractor management, and supplement tracking are best-in-class for roofing. If your close rate is fine but your production margin is leaking, this is your tool. If your problem is that 50% of leads never pick up the phone, you're solving the wrong problem with it.

AccuLynx: the enterprise pick, priced accordingly

AccuLynx doesn't publish public pricing, but based on quotes across the industry it lands around $99-$150/user/month depending on modules, with a mandatory onboarding fee ($1,500-$5,000). A 10-rep floor is realistically $1,200-$1,500/month all-in. What you get for that: the deepest roofing-specific feature set on the market. Aerial measurement integrations, insurance scope-of-work builders, SumoQuote proposal integration, labor & material tracking, and a very mature job pipeline. Larger roofing companies ($10M+ revenue) tend to standardize on AccuLynx because it scales operationally. On automation and lead handling: - Automated Workflows module handles status-triggered emails and SMS.

  • AccuLynx has a native call tracking add-on — better than JobNimbus here — plus CallRail integration.
  • Lead Insights ties calls and forms to ad sources, which is genuinely useful for a media buyer.
  • Booking automation is still human-in-the-loop. No native AI SDR. The honest assessment: AccuLynx is a superior operations platform to JobNimbus, but the price premium is hard to justify unless you're above 15 reps or doing complex insurance/commercial work. For a 10-rep floor focused on retail residential, you're paying for capacity you won't use. And it still doesn't solve the sub-60-second lead response problem.

GoHighLevel: built for lead speed, weak on roofing production

GHL is not a roofing CRM. It's a marketing automation platform that agencies white-label. But for the specific job of turning an inbound lead into a booked appointment on the calendar, nothing in the roofing space touches it at the price point. At the Agency Pro (SaaS) plan of $497/month, you get unlimited users and unlimited sub-accounts. A 10-rep floor pays the same as a 2-rep floor. That math alone changes the conversation. What GHL does that the others don't: - Sub-10-second SMS/email response on form fill, triggered by webhook.

  • Native AI conversation bot (Conversation AI add-on, ~$97/mo) that qualifies and books directly to a rep's calendar.
  • Native power dialer and 2-way SMS inbox with unified conversation view.
  • Built-in call tracking with dynamic number insertion, plus CallRail/Twilio integration.
  • Attribution reporting at the source/campaign/ad level for booked appointments and closed deals — assuming you set UTMs correctly.
  • Missed call text-back — recovers 15-25% of missed inbound calls automatically. What GHL doesn't do: material ordering, EagleView-to-order pipelines, supplement tracking, QuickBooks-grade job costing. Which is why the operator move is to run GHL as the front-end lead engine and push booked appointments into JobNimbus via webhook for production.

True cost per user at 10 reps: the number that actually matters

Sticker price is misleading. Here's the fully-loaded monthly cost for a 10-rep sales floor, including the add-ons you actually need: JobNimbus (Growing plan):

  • 10 users × $75 = $750
  • CallRail (essentials): $50
  • Zapier (professional): $50
  • Total: ~$850/month, or $85/user AccuLynx:
  • 10 users × ~$125 avg = $1,250
  • Call tracking add-on: included or $75
  • SumoQuote integration: $99
  • Total: ~$1,400/month, or $140/user
  • Plus $2,500 one-time onboarding GoHighLevel (Agency Pro):
  • Flat $497/month, unlimited users
  • Conversation AI: $97
  • Twilio usage (SMS/voice at volume): $150-$300
  • Total: ~$800-$900/month, or $80-$90/user Cost per user is roughly a wash between GHL and JobNimbus. AccuLynx is 60-75% more expensive. But cost per user is the wrong metric — the right one is cost per booked appointment. If GHL's sub-10-second response and AI booking add 15-20 more appointments per month at a $150 booked-appointment value, that's $2,250-$3,000 of monthly revenue lift for the same tool spend.

Call tracking integration: where deals get won or misattributed

If you're spending real money on Google LSA, Meta Ads, and Google Search, you cannot run a roofing sales floor without call tracking wired into the CRM. Otherwise you're optimizing ad spend blind. CallRail is the industry standard. Here's how each CRM handles it: - JobNimbus + CallRail: Zapier-based integration. Calls create contacts, but ad-source attribution requires manual UTM tagging and a source field mapping. Serviceable, not elegant.

  • AccuLynx + CallRail (or native): Deeper integration. Lead Insights ties calls to campaigns and shows source in the pipeline view. Best-in-class for reporting.
  • GHL + CallRail (or native Twilio): Full dynamic number insertion, call recording, whisper messages, and source attribution stored on the contact record. AI can transcribe and tag calls automatically. GHL also does something the others don't: missed-call text-back. When a lead calls and no rep picks up (which happens 30-40% of the time on a 10-rep floor with reps on roofs), GHL fires an SMS within 30 seconds: "Hey — sorry we missed you. This is Mike with [Company]. Want me to text you a free inspection quote?" Recovery rate is typically 15-25% of missed calls. On 200 missed calls a month, that's 30-50 recovered opportunities that would have gone to voicemail purgatory.

The stack most 8-figure roofers actually run

After looking at dozens of roofing operations doing $5M-$30M in revenue, the pattern is clear. Nobody wins with a single tool. The stack looks like this: 1. GoHighLevel on the front: form intake, sub-10-second response, AI booking, missed call text-back, nurture sequences, review requests. 2. JobNimbus or AccuLynx on the back: once appointment is booked and rep runs it, deal moves to production CRM for measurements, material orders, job costing. 3. CallRail or GHL native tracking feeding call data to both systems. 4. Zapier or native webhook connecting GHL → production CRM on "appointment set" or "contract signed" trigger. Setup cost is real: budget $3,000-$8,000 for a proper build (GHL snapshot, calendar setup, automation workflows, integration mapping, phone numbers, AI training). Monthly ongoing at 10 reps is roughly $1,200-$1,700 all-in including both platforms. The ROI math: if this stack recovers even one additional deal per rep per month at $8,000-$15,000 average job size and 35% gross margin, you're looking at $28K-$52K in additional gross profit against ~$1,500 in software. That's the reason the operators running this dual-stack are consistently outrunning single-CRM competitors on the same ad budget.

The bottom line

The best CRM automation for roofing companies is not a single tool — it's a stack. If forced to pick one, GHL wins for lead-to-appointment automation and cost at 10 reps, JobNimbus wins for balanced production and price, and AccuLynx wins only if you're above 15 reps or heavy on insurance/commercial work. Before you switch anything, audit two numbers this week: your average lead response time, and your inbound call answer rate. If response time is over 60 seconds or answer rate is under 70%, no amount of pipeline management software will fix your problem. Fix the front end first, then optimize production.

faq.question: Can I run GoHighLevel and JobNimbus at the same time?
faq.answer: Yes, and it's the most common setup for roofing companies doing $3M+ in revenue. GHL handles lead intake, response, and booking on the front end. JobNimbus handles job production on the back end. They connect via Zapier or native webhook when a lead becomes a booked appointment or signed contract.

faq.question: Is AccuLynx worth the extra cost over JobNimbus?
faq.answer: For most 10-rep residential roofing operations, no. AccuLynx is the better platform if you're above 15 reps, doing complex insurance work, or need deep production reporting. Below that scale, JobNimbus delivers 85% of the value at 55% of the cost.

faq.question: What's the fastest way to improve lead-to-appointment conversion?
faq.answer: Cut your response time to under 60 seconds and add missed-call text-back. Nothing else moves the number more. Speed-to-lead studies consistently show a 5-8x conversion difference between sub-1-minute and 5-minute response times.

faq.question: Does GoHighLevel have EagleView or HOVER integration?
faq.answer: No, and it won't. GHL is a marketing and communication platform, not a production tool. If you need EagleView or HOVER integration, you need JobNimbus or AccuLynx running alongside GHL for the production side of the business.

faq.question: How long does it take to migrate from one roofing CRM to another?
faq.answer: Plan on 4-8 weeks for a clean migration at 10 reps, including data export, custom field mapping, automation rebuild, phone number porting, and rep training. Rushing the switch typically costs more in lost leads and rep confusion than the entire annual software savings.

articles.title: How to Hire a Lead Generation Agency for Medical Spa: Vetting Checklist
articles.description: Vetting a med spa lead gen agency? Here's the CPL benchmarks, red-flag guarantees to avoid, and contract terms that actually protect operators.
articles.keyword: hire lead generation agency for medical spa
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Roughly 40% of med spa operators I talk to have been burned by at least one lead gen agency. The story is always similar: a slick pitch deck promising 100 booked appointments a month, a $5,000/month retainer, and 90 days later they've got 400 junk leads, a burned Meta ad account, and no shows on the calendar. This isn't a lead generation problem. It's a vetting problem. Med spa lead gen is one of the most competitive verticals in paid media — CPMs on Meta for aesthetics keywords have climbed steadily, and the market is flooded with agencies who learned the playbook from a $997 course and are now selling it to you at $5K/month. This article is for med spa owners and marketing directors about to sign an agency contract. Below: the CPL and CPA ranges that are actually realistic by treatment category, the guarantee language that should make you walk, and the seven contract clauses that keep the operator (not the agency) in control.

What a realistic CPL and CPA actually look like for med spas

Before you vet anyone, calibrate your expectations. Agencies weaponize your ignorance of benchmarks. Here's what I see across active med spa accounts running Meta Ads and Google Ads in 2026: - Botox / filler leads: $18–$45 CPL, $60–$140 CPA (booked and showed)

  • Body contouring (CoolSculpting, Emsculpt): $45–$95 CPL, $180–$400 CPA
  • Laser hair removal: $12–$30 CPL, $50–$120 CPA
  • Weight loss / GLP-1 (semaglutide, tirzepatide): $35–$80 CPL, $110–$260 CPA
  • Medical-grade skincare / HydraFacial: $20–$40 CPL, $70–$160 CPA These vary by market. Miami, LA, and NYC will run 30–50% higher. Secondary markets (Tulsa, Boise, Grand Rapids) can run 20% lower. If an agency quotes you a $6 CPL for Botox in Dallas, they're either running incentive-heavy giveaways that attract deal-hunters who never rebook, or they're counting form fills that are 80% junk. A qualified, phone-verified lead with intent costs what it costs. Any agency that can't quote a range in this ballpark either doesn't work in the vertical or is lying. Ask them to show you a live dashboard from an active client (redacted) before you sign anything.

Red-flag guarantees that should make you walk

Guarantees sell contracts. They also expose the agency's business model. Here are the specific ones to flag: "We guarantee 100 leads per month." A lead is a form fill. Form fills are trivially cheap to generate if you don't care about quality. This guarantee means nothing without a definition of qualified lead, source verification, and a duplicate/bot filter. "We guarantee X booked appointments or we work for free." Read the fine print. "Booked" usually means anyone who clicks a Calendly link — not showed. And "work for free" typically means they continue running your ads (badly) at your ad spend cost until they hit the number. "Pay per show." Sounds great, but almost always priced at $300–$500 per show, which locks you into a CPA that's higher than what you'd pay a competent agency running the ads directly. It also incentivizes the agency to over-promise on the phone to get butts in seats. "Exclusive territory." Meaningless in paid social. Meta doesn't care about your zip code exclusivity agreement. "Our proprietary AI." 99% of the time this is ChatGPT wrapped in a GoHighLevel snapshot. Ask them to demo it live. If they dodge, walk.

The seven contract clauses that protect the operator

This is where most operators lose. The agency drafts the contract, and you sign a 12-month lockup with 30-day-out language buried on page four. Non-negotiable clauses to demand: 1. Month-to-month after 90 days. Give them a 90-day ramp, then you should be able to exit with 30 days notice. Any agency confident in their work agrees to this. 2. You own the ad accounts. Meta Business Manager, Google Ads, and any tracking pixels must live under your business. They get admin access, not ownership. 3. You own the CRM data. If they build you a GoHighLevel or HubSpot instance, you get an export of all contacts, conversation histories, and automations at termination. 4. You own the creative. All ad creative, video, and copy produced during the engagement transfers to you. Get this in writing. 5. Transparent ad spend. Ad spend goes on your card, not theirs. No markups, no "managed spend" fees hidden inside a bundled retainer. 6. Defined KPIs and reporting cadence. Weekly reports with CPL, CPA, show rate, and close rate. Not vanity metrics like impressions and reach. 7. Kill clause on performance. If CPL exceeds X or show rate drops below Y for 60 consecutive days, you exit with no penalty. If they push back on any of these, the answer is no.

How to audit their case studies in 15 minutes

Every agency has a highlight reel. Here's how to stress-test it: Ask for the client's phone number. Not a testimonial video, not a screenshot. A reference call with a current client who's been with them 6+ months. Agencies with real results have a stack of references. Agencies without will stall. Verify the numbers with source data. "We generated 847 leads for Glow Med Spa in Q2" — cool, show me the Meta Ads Manager screenshot with the account name visible and the date range. Photoshopped screenshots are common. Ask them to share their screen live. Check attribution. A lot of agencies claim credit for leads that came from Google organic, direct traffic, or referrals. Ask specifically: "What percentage of these leads were tracked with UTM parameters back to your specific ad campaigns?" If they don't know what a UTM is, end the meeting. Look at close rate and LTV, not just lead count. A good agency asks about your average ticket, rebook rate, and package upsell rate before they pitch. If they only talk about lead volume, they don't understand the business. Search their client list on Google Reviews. If their case study client has a 3.2-star rating and reviews mentioning "pushy sales," the leads might be volume-driven junk that damaged the brand.

What their tech stack tells you about their capability

The tools an agency uses are a fast credibility check. Here's what a competent med spa lead gen operation looks like under the hood: - Meta Ads Manager + Google Ads — table stakes. If they don't run both, they're missing half the funnel.

  • GoHighLevel or HubSpot for lead capture, SMS/email nurture, and appointment booking. GoHighLevel is the industry default for med spa lead gen because of the built-in SMS automation.
  • Calendly, Vagaro, or Boulevard integration for actual booking into your calendar system. Ask specifically: how do leads get from the ad to a confirmed appointment in [your booking software]?
  • A call tracking tool (CallRail, WhatConverts) if phone calls are a lead channel.
  • A UTM/attribution layer — Google Analytics 4 with conversions, or a paid tool like Hyros or Triple Whale for multi-touch.
  • An AI voice or SMS speed-to-lead tool — leads that aren't contacted within 5 minutes convert 80% worse. Ask how they handle first-touch response time. If an agency's answer to "how do you track and follow up on leads" is "we send them to your email inbox," they're 10 years behind. Speed-to-lead automation is non-negotiable in this vertical.

Pricing structures and what you should actually pay

Agency pricing in this space ranges from $1,500/month freelancers to $15K/month full-service. Here's what each tier gets you: $1,500–$3,000/month: Freelancer or small shop. Usually one channel (Meta only), basic reporting, minimal CRM setup. Fine if you're doing under $50K/month in revenue and just need lead flow. $3,500–$6,000/month: Mid-tier agency. Multi-channel (Meta + Google), managed CRM in GoHighLevel, weekly reporting, dedicated account manager. This is the sweet spot for most med spas doing $50K–$200K/month. $6,000–$10,000/month: Full-service with creative production, SMS/email nurture management, and appointment show-rate optimization. Worth it if you're doing $200K+/month and need real operational lift. $10,000+/month: Should include in-person shoots, monthly strategy, dedicated media buyer, and multi-location support. Ad spend is separate. Budget minimum $3,000/month in ad spend to get meaningful data; $5,000–$15,000/month is where most performing accounts sit. Avoid percentage-of-ad-spend pricing (10–20% of spend). It incentivizes the agency to burn budget. Flat retainer plus performance bonus is the cleanest structure.

The 20-minute discovery call script that filters out bad agencies

When you get on a sales call, run this sequence. It takes about 20 minutes and it filters out 80% of pretenders: 1. "Walk me through the last med spa client you onboarded — from day one to first booked appointment. Timeline?" Legit answer: 14–30 days. If they say "leads within 48 hours," they're running junk traffic. 2. "What's your average CPL for Botox in a market my size?" They should give you a range with context. Vague answers = no experience. 3. "Show me a live dashboard from a current client." Not a case study PDF. Live Meta Ads Manager, redacted. 4. "Who actually runs my account day-to-day, and can I talk to them before signing?" If the person running your ads is a $12/hour VA in Manila, you deserve to know. 5. "What happens in month one if the numbers aren't hitting?" Answer should include a specific optimization framework, not "we'll test more creative." 6. "What's your termination policy?" If it's not 30-day out after ramp, negotiate or walk. 7. "Can you send me the contract before our next call?" Read the whole thing. Twice.

The bottom line

Hiring a lead generation agency for your medical spa is a bet on the operator, not the pitch. The agencies worth working with are the ones that show you real dashboards, quote realistic CPLs, agree to month-to-month terms, and let you keep your ad accounts and data. Everyone else is renting you outcomes they can't sustain. Use the vetting checklist above on your next three sales calls. You'll be surprised how many agencies fail question two. The right agency will pass all seven — and they won't need a hard-sell to close you, because their track record does it for them.

faq.question: How long before a med spa lead gen agency starts producing results?
faq.answer: Expect a 14–30 day ramp for Meta and Google campaigns to exit the learning phase and start producing consistent qualified leads. If an agency promises leads in 48 hours, they're running low-quality giveaway traffic that won't convert to paying patients.

faq.question: Is it better to hire a med spa lead gen agency or bring it in-house?
faq.answer: Under $100K/month in revenue, an agency is almost always cheaper than a full-time media buyer ($75K+ salary plus tools). Above $300K/month, a hybrid model — in-house strategist plus specialist agency — usually wins on speed and cost.

faq.question: What's a fair contract length for a med spa lead gen agency?
faq.answer: A 90-day initial commitment is reasonable to let campaigns ramp. Anything beyond that should convert to month-to-month with 30-day notice. Any agency requiring a 12-month lockup is protecting themselves from being fired for underperformance.

faq.question: Should the agency use my Meta and Google ad accounts or their own?
faq.answer: Always yours. You own the pixel data, ad account history, and audience seed data — all of which stay with you at termination. Agencies that insist on running through their accounts are protecting their leverage, not your interests.

faq.question: How much ad spend do I need to make a med spa lead gen agency worth it?
faq.answer: Minimum $3,000/month in ad spend to generate enough data to optimize. Under that, you're paying agency fees on volume too small to move the needle. Sweet spot for most single-location med spas is $5,000–$10,000/month in spend.

articles.title: Best Lead Generation Strategy for Commercial HVAC: The ABM Play
articles.description: Stop burning budget on Meta ads. Here's the ABM, LinkedIn, and direct mail framework that fills commercial HVAC pipelines in 90 days.
articles.keyword: best lead generation strategy for commercial hvac
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Commercial HVAC is not a Meta ads business. If you're running lead-gen for a mechanical contractor targeting property managers, facility directors, or REIT asset managers and someone is pitching you Facebook lead forms — fire them. The buying committee for a $180K rooftop unit replacement or a $40K/year preventive maintenance contract is not scrolling Reels between meetings. Commercial HVAC has three unusual traits that break most lead-gen playbooks: a tiny total addressable market per metro (usually 800–3,000 named accounts), a 6–18 month sales cycle, and a buying committee of 3–5 people who all need to say yes. That combination demands account-based marketing (ABM), not spray-and-pray digital. Below is the exact 90-day framework we deploy for commercial mechanical contractors: how to build the target list, sequence LinkedIn and direct mail, layer in intent data, and structure the sales motion so property managers actually respond. No fluff, no vanity metrics — just the pipeline math.

Why Meta ads fail for commercial HVAC (and what actually works)

Meta's targeting was built for consumer intent and B2C lookalikes. When you try to reach a Director of Facilities at a 400-property REIT, you're paying to serve ads to their 12-year-old's iPad because the household algorithm can't tell them apart. Here's the math problem. If your true addressable market in a metro is 1,800 commercial properties over 50,000 sq ft, and each has 2–3 decision-makers, you have ~5,000 humans to reach. Meta's minimum viable audience is 50,000+ for the algorithm to optimize. You will either bleed money on a tiny custom audience or waste 90% of impressions on plumbers, homeowners, and HVAC techs looking for jobs. What works instead is a narrow, named-account motion: - Build a target list of 500–1,500 named commercial properties

  • Identify 3–5 buying-committee contacts per account (facility director, property manager, COO, VP of operations, chief engineer)
  • Sequence them across LinkedIn, email, direct mail, and phone over 60–90 days
  • Layer in intent signals from Bombora, 6sense, or LinkedIn Sales Navigator's buyer intent This is ABM 101, but almost no HVAC contractor executes it. That's your opening.

Building the target account list (the foundation nobody gets right)

Your list is 70% of the outcome. Get this wrong and no amount of clever creative saves you. The goal is a defensible, ranked list of accounts where a single won deal pays back your annual marketing spend. Start with these data sources: 1. CoStar or Reonomy for commercial property data — pull every building over 50,000 sq ft in your service radius, filtered by property type (Class A/B office, industrial, medical, multifamily 100+ units, hospitality). 2. LinkedIn Sales Navigator to overlay decision-makers by title: Facilities Director, Property Manager, Chief Engineer, VP Operations, Director of Real Estate. 3. Public permit data from your city — buildings that pulled mechanical permits in the last 24 months signal equipment turnover. 4. Building age filters — target properties with rooftop units 12+ years old. Replacement cycles are predictable. Rank the list into three tiers: - Tier 1 (100 accounts): Perfect fit, high urgency signals, deals worth $250K+ lifetime. Full ABM treatment.

  • Tier 2 (400 accounts): Good fit, standard treatment.
  • Tier 3 (1,000 accounts): Nurture with lower-touch email and retargeting. Load this into HubSpot or GoHighLevel with account-level custom properties. Every contact must be tagged to their parent account so you can see committee-level engagement.

The LinkedIn play: content plus outbound, not one or the other

LinkedIn is where commercial real estate operators actually live during business hours. But posting generic "5 tips for HVAC maintenance" content will get you 40 impressions and zero meetings. Run two parallel motions: Motion 1 — Executive thought leadership. Your owner, VP of Sales, or top service manager posts 3x per week. Content pillars: total cost of ownership math (real numbers on deferred maintenance costs), building code changes affecting commercial mechanical, case studies with named property types ("How we cut a 180K sq ft Class B office's HVAC opex by 22%"), and hot takes on industry issues (refrigerant phaseouts, electrification mandates). Motion 2 — Sales Navigator outbound. Your BDRs run sequences to Tier 1 and Tier 2 contacts: - Day 1: Connection request, no pitch, referencing their specific property or portfolio

  • Day 4: Voice note (LinkedIn now supports these) — 45 seconds, one specific observation about their building
  • Day 10: InMail with a case study PDF relevant to their property type
  • Day 18: Comment thoughtfully on one of their posts
  • Day 25: Direct message with a specific meeting ask tied to a trigger event Expected reply rates: 12–18% on Tier 1, 6–10% on Tier 2. That's 10–25x better than cold email alone. Track everything in Sales Navigator plus your CRM.

Direct mail is the unlock (yes, in 2026)

Property managers get 200 emails a day and zero interesting mail. A tactile, high-value piece to a named account cuts through in a way pixels can't. We consistently see 8–15% meeting rates on well-executed direct mail into Tier 1 lists. What works — and what doesn't: Don't send: postcards, brochures, tri-folds, anything with a stock photo of an HVAC unit. It gets thrown out with the pizza flyers. Do send: dimensional mail with a specific, personalized artifact. Options that hit: - A printed, bound building energy audit summary using public utility and permit data for that specific address, with 3 flagged inefficiencies and a note from your VP

  • A hardcover book on commercial building operations (Nordhaus, Rocky Mountain Institute reports) with a handwritten card and dog-eared page
  • A small toolkit (thermal imaging phone attachment, ~$180) with a card that says "scan any suspect duct — call us with what you find" Budget: $40–120 per Tier 1 account, sent in waves of 25–50. Follow up with a LinkedIn message and a phone call within 72 hours referencing the piece. Tools like Sendoso, Reachdesk, or Postal.io handle the logistics and CRM integration.

The 90-day pipeline framework, week by week

Here's the calendar we run. This assumes a two-person sales/BDR team and a marketing lead running list-building and content. Days 1–14: Foundation

  • Pull and enrich Tier 1/2/3 account list in HubSpot
  • Identify 3–5 contacts per Tier 1 account (500 contacts total)
  • Build 4 case study one-pagers by property type
  • Set up LinkedIn Sales Navigator sequences and warm up sending domains Days 15–30: Air cover
  • Launch executive LinkedIn content cadence (3 posts/week)
  • Begin retargeting to your Tier 1/2 list via LinkedIn Matched Audiences ($3K–5K/month)
  • Send first direct mail wave to 50 Tier 1 accounts Days 31–60: Outbound push
  • BDRs run full LinkedIn + email sequences to all Tier 1 contacts
  • Second direct mail wave to next 50 Tier 1 accounts
  • Host a virtual roundtable for property managers (10–15 attendees is a win)
  • Book target: 25–40 first meetings Days 61–90: Convert and expand
  • Second-meeting rate should hit 55%+ if first meetings were qualified
  • Site walks and proposals on 15–20 accounts
  • Begin outbound to Tier 2 with lower-touch email + LinkedIn
  • Signed contracts or LOIs: 3–6 by day 90; pipeline of $2M–5M in flight Measure account-level engagement, not lead-level. The right dashboard shows accounts moving from "aware" to "engaged" to "meeting booked" to "proposal."

Intent data and trigger events: how to know when to strike

Timing kills or makes commercial HVAC deals. A property manager who just took over a portfolio, a building that just changed hands, a REIT that announced an ESG target — these are your buying windows. Miss them and you're stuck in a beauty contest against the incumbent. Triggers to monitor and automate alerts for: - Property ownership changes — Reonomy and CoStar push transaction alerts

  • New facilities/property manager hires — LinkedIn Sales Navigator alerts on job changes at target accounts
  • Building permits pulled for mechanical, electrical, roofing — city open-data portals or BuildingConnected
  • Utility rate case filings in your state — signals opex pressure
  • ESG or decarbonization announcements from REITs and large tenants — Google Alerts + press release monitoring
  • 6sense or Bombora intent surges on topics like "chiller replacement," "building automation," "HVAC RFP" When a trigger fires on a Tier 1 or Tier 2 account, that account jumps the queue. BDRs get a same-day Slack alert with a suggested outreach angle. Meeting rates on trigger-based outreach run 3–5x cold baseline. Don't overbuild this. Start with 3 trigger types, prove the motion, then layer more in. A shared spreadsheet and Zapier can run this before you invest in 6sense.

What the sales motion looks like when leads land

You can generate perfect meetings and still lose if the sales motion doesn't match how commercial buyers actually decide. Three principles. First meeting is not a pitch — it's a diagnostic. Send a pre-meeting form via Calendly asking for their top 3 building pain points, current maintenance provider, and equipment age. Show up with a hypothesis. Ask better questions than the incumbent. Leave with a signed site-walk agreement. Site walks are the real sales tool. No commercial deal closes without your senior tech physically walking their mechanical rooms. Charge for it if you have to ($500–1,500 as a paid assessment credited toward work) — it filters tire-kickers and creates commitment. Bring an iPad, take photos of every deficiency, and generate a branded findings report within 72 hours. Proposals need three tiers, always. Good/Better/Best with real numbers on payback, energy savings, and risk reduction. Property managers need to bring options to their boss or ownership. A single-option quote gets shopped; a tiered proposal gets negotiated. Finally, treat the buying committee as one target. Copy the CFO on the proposal email. Send a separate version to the facilities director focused on downtime risk. Never rely on your champion to sell internally for you — arm them with committee-specific one-pagers.

The bottom line

The best lead generation strategy for commercial HVAC isn't a channel — it's a system. Named accounts, buying-committee mapping, LinkedIn plus direct mail plus outbound, all wired to intent triggers and a diagnostic-first sales motion. Meta ads and Google Local Services are fine for residential replacement work. They are the wrong tool for a $250K rooftop deal decided by a committee of five. If you're currently running paid social for commercial work, kill it and redirect the budget to list-building, LinkedIn Sales Navigator, and dimensional mail. In 90 days you'll have a real pipeline instead of a lead list of unqualified homeowners. Measure account engagement, not cost per lead — that single reframe changes everything about how you allocate spend.

faq.question: How much should a commercial HVAC contractor spend on lead generation?
faq.answer: For a $10M–30M commercial mechanical contractor, expect to invest $15K–40K per month across list data, LinkedIn ads, direct mail, BDR salary, and content. That's 3–5% of revenue, weighted heavily to labor and data — not media spend. One won maintenance contract usually pays back a full year of the program.

faq.question: Do Google Ads work for commercial HVAC?
faq.answer: Google Ads work narrowly for high-intent commercial searches like "commercial chiller repair [city]" or "emergency rooftop unit service." They do not work for proactive maintenance contracts or capital equipment replacement — those buyers don't search Google, they ask their network and issue RFPs. Run Google for emergency service capture only, and keep the budget under 20% of your total demand-gen spend.

faq.question: How long does it take to see pipeline from an ABM motion?
faq.answer: First meetings start landing in weeks 4–6. Real qualified pipeline (proposals out) shows up around day 60–90. Closed contracts typically start month 4–6 given commercial sales cycles. If someone promises you closed deals in 30 days from a standing start, they're either lying or selling you emergency-service Google Ads.

faq.question: Should we hire a BDR in-house or outsource?
faq.answer: For your first motion, hire one BDR in-house at $55K–70K base plus commission. Outsourced SDR agencies rarely understand commercial mechanical enough to have credible conversations with facilities directors. Once the playbook is proven and documented, you can consider adding an offshore or agency SDR to handle Tier 2/3 volume.

faq.question: What CRM should we use to run this?
faq.answer: HubSpot Sales Hub Professional is the cleanest fit — strong account-based reporting, LinkedIn Sales Navigator integration, and sequence tooling. GoHighLevel works if you're smaller and want marketing automation bundled in. Salesforce is overkill unless you're above $50M in revenue with a dedicated ops person to manage it.

articles.title: How to Lower Cost Per Lead on Facebook Ads for Contractors
articles.description: A 5-lever teardown to slash Facebook Ads CPL for contractors. Real drops from roofing and remodeling accounts, with tactics you can ship this week.
articles.keyword: how to lower cost per lead on facebook ads for contractors
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
If your Facebook Ads CPL for roofing or remodeling sits above $80, you're leaving money on the table. We've taken accounts from $147 CPL down to $23 in under 60 days — and no, it wasn't a new audience hack or a magic Advantage+ setting. It was five levers pulled in the right order. This is written for contractors and the agencies running their paid social — founders spending $5K to $75K/month on Meta who are tired of vague optimization advice. If your leads are expensive, unqualified, or ghosting after form fill, one of these five levers is broken. Below: the exact teardown we run on every roofing, remodeling, siding, and window account we onboard — creative, offer, audience, form friction, and follow-up — with the CPL numbers we've actually hit.

Why contractor CPL is usually inflated (and what "good" looks like)

Most contractor accounts we audit are running CPLs between $75 and $200 for roofing, $60 to $150 for remodeling, and $40 to $90 for windows and siding. That's not a benchmark to celebrate — it's the ceiling of what happens when you run boosted posts, stock imagery, and a generic "Get a Free Quote" CTA. Here's what good looks like on accounts we run today: - Roofing (storm + retail mix): $18–$45 CPL, 25–35% lead-to-appointment rate

  • Full-home remodeling: $35–$70 CPL, 15–20% lead-to-consult rate
  • Bath/kitchen remodels: $22–$55 CPL, 20–30% lead-to-appointment rate
  • Windows/siding: $15–$35 CPL, 30–40% lead-to-appointment rate The delta between average and good isn't audience targeting — Meta's algorithm handles that better than any manual layer you'll build. The delta is the five levers below. Pull them in order: creative first, offer second, audience third, form friction fourth, follow-up fifth. Skip creative and you're optimizing a broken funnel. We've seen accounts cut CPL by 60% with nothing more than swapping stock hero images for iPhone-shot before/afters.

Lever 1: Creative — the 70% of your CPL problem

Meta's own data says creative drives 56% of ad performance. In our accounts, it's closer to 70%. Every account we've dropped CPL on started with a creative overhaul. The pattern that wins for contractors, tested across 40+ accounts: 1. UGC-style before/afters shot vertically on an iPhone. Not drone footage. Not polished agency reels. The homeowner or crew lead talking to camera for 8 seconds, then a crossfade to the finished job. 2. Static carousels with 5 slides: problem shot, mid-progress, finished result, price range or financing hook, CTA card. 3. "Neighbor testimonial" videos — 20-second clips of past customers naming the city or neighborhood. Local proof crushes generic reviews. One roofing client in Dallas: we killed 12 stock-image ads and replaced them with 6 iPhone-shot before/afters plus 2 crew-lead testimonials. CPL dropped from $94 to $31 in 18 days at the same $8K/month spend. Run creative testing inside Meta Ads Manager using dynamic creative with 4–6 hooks, 3 body copy variants, and 2 CTAs. Kill anything above 1.5x your target CPL after 50 impressions on the primary asset. Refresh top creative every 14–21 days — contractor audiences are geographically small and burn out fast.

Lever 2: Offer — stop selling "free quotes"

"Free estimate" is not an offer. Every contractor gives free estimates. When your ad says the same thing as your 40 competitors, you compete on CPM, and you lose. Offers that consistently cut CPL 30–50% in our accounts: - Roofing: "Free drone roof inspection + insurance claim review" (worked especially well post-storm in TX, FL, CO)

  • Bath remodel: "$1,500 off + 0% financing for 18 months if booked by [month end]"
  • Windows: "Buy 2 windows, get 2 free" (yes, it's price-inflated — it converts)
  • Full remodel: "Free 3D design consultation — see your kitchen before you commit" One Phoenix remodeling client was running "Get a Free Quote" at $128 CPL. We swapped to "Free 3D design mockup — $450 value, free through [month]" and CPL fell to $58 in three weeks. Same audience, same creative style, same budget. The offer needs three ingredients: a specific dollar value, a deadline, and a reason to act now. Vague benefits — "quality workmanship," "licensed and insured" — belong on your website, not your ad. Test 2–3 offers simultaneously in separate ad sets so Meta's algorithm doesn't blend the learnings.

Lever 3: Audience — go broader than you think

Contractors love to over-target. Homeowners 35–65, income $100K+, interested in "home improvement," layered with behavior filters. It's 2018 thinking, and it's why your CPL is high. Meta's algorithm in the Advantage+ era needs volume to optimize. Narrow audiences under 500K starve it. Here's the audience stack that works now: - Advantage+ Shopping/Leads campaigns with age 30–65, gender all, radius 25–50 miles around service area

  • One custom audience exclusion: past customers, current leads (last 90 days)
  • One lookalike: 1% LAL of closed customers (needs 200+ minimum in the source list — use GoHighLevel or HubSpot to export)
  • Zero interest layering at the campaign level We ran a controlled test on a Charlotte roofing account: interest-targeted audience (Home Improvement + Homeownership + income filter) hit $89 CPL. Same creative, same budget, Advantage+ broad targeting: $34 CPL. The algorithm found homeowners we would never have manually targeted — including a big pocket of renters who owned rental properties. For local contractors, radius is the only "targeting" that matters. Set your service radius, exclude past customers, and let Meta optimize. If you're spending under $3K/month, don't split into more than 2 ad sets — you'll fragment your data and inflate CPL.

Lever 4: Form friction — every field is a tax

Every extra form field costs you 5–15% of leads. Contractors routinely ask for name, email, phone, address, project type, timeline, budget, and "tell us about your project." That's an 8-field tax on your CPL. Here's the friction hierarchy from lowest to highest CPL: 1. Meta instant form, 3 fields (name, phone, zip): lowest CPL, lowest quality — expect 40–60% junk 2. Meta instant form, 3 fields + 1 qualifier question (e.g., "When are you looking to start?"): 15–25% higher CPL, 2x quality 3. Landing page, 4 fields + 1 dropdown: 30–50% higher CPL, 3x quality 4. Multi-step landing page (Typeform, Unbounce, Leadpages): 20–40% higher CPL than instant form, best quality The right answer depends on your close rate and sales team capacity. If your sales team is hungry and closes 8%+ of raw leads, run Meta instant forms with one qualifier. If your team is small and needs pre-qualified leads, run a 4–6 step landing page. We took a Denver siding contractor from a 7-field landing page ($112 CPL) to a Meta instant form with one qualifier ($38 CPL). Lead quality dropped modestly, but total booked appointments doubled because they were getting 3x the volume. Measure the metric that matters: cost per booked appointment, not cost per raw lead.

Lever 5: Follow-up — the invisible CPL killer

Follow-up doesn't literally lower your CPL number in Ads Manager. But it dramatically lowers your effective cost per booked job — which is the only number that pays your bills. The data on speed-to-lead is brutal: contact a Facebook lead within 5 minutes and you're 21x more likely to qualify them versus 30 minutes. Most contractors call the next morning. That's why their $60 leads feel like $180 leads. The follow-up stack that works: - Instant SMS within 60 seconds via GoHighLevel, Twilio, or HubSpot workflow: "Hey [name], this is Mike from [company] — got your request for [service]. Best number to reach you at?"

  • Auto-call to the sales rep's phone within 2 minutes with lead details
  • 7-day nurture sequence — 4 SMS, 3 emails — for anyone who doesn't answer
  • Retargeting audience built from lead form submitters, running testimonial creative for 30 days A Tampa roofing client had a $47 CPL but a 4% booking rate — effectively $1,175 per booked consult. We implemented GoHighLevel with 60-second SMS + auto-dial. Booking rate went to 22%. Effective cost per consult: $214. Nothing changed in Ads Manager. Everything changed in the P&L. If you're only measuring CPL, you're measuring the wrong thing. Measure cost per booked appointment and cost per signed contract.

The 30-day teardown sequence to actually run

Don't try to fix all five levers at once. You'll change too many variables and won't know what worked. Run them in order over 30 days: Week 1 — Creative + Offer. Shoot 6 iPhone-style creatives (3 UGC hooks, 3 before/after carousels). Rewrite offer with specific dollar value + deadline. Launch as new campaign, don't edit the existing one. Week 2 — Audience. Consolidate to one Advantage+ campaign, kill interest layers, exclude past customers, add 1% lookalike of closed customers. Kill old campaign once new campaign hits 50 leads. Week 3 — Form friction. A/B test Meta instant form (3 fields + 1 qualifier) against your current landing page. Measure cost per booked appointment, not raw CPL. Week 4 — Follow-up. Install GoHighLevel or equivalent. Sub-60-second SMS, auto-dial to rep, 7-day nurture, retargeting audience. Measure effective cost per booked appointment before and after. Across 40+ contractor accounts, this sequence has averaged a 58% CPL reduction and a 140% increase in booked appointments per ad dollar. The math isn't magic — it's five levers, pulled in order, measured properly.

The bottom line

Lowering CPL on Facebook Ads for contractors isn't about finding a new audience hack or a secret Meta setting. It's about pulling five levers — creative, offer, audience, form friction, follow-up — in the right sequence, and measuring cost per booked appointment instead of cost per raw lead. Start with creative this week. Shoot 4 iPhone-style before/afters and 2 crew-lead testimonials before you touch anything else. Then work down the list. If you do the full 30-day sequence, expect CPL to drop 40–60% and booked appointments to double at the same spend. Everything else is noise.

faq.question: What's a good CPL for a roofing contractor on Facebook Ads?
faq.answer: For retail roofing, $18–$45 CPL is achievable with strong creative and Advantage+ targeting. Storm and insurance-driven markets can hit $12–$25. If you're above $75, your creative or offer is broken — not your targeting.

faq.question: Should I use Meta instant forms or send traffic to a landing page?
faq.answer: Meta instant forms with one qualifier question win for most contractors — lower CPL, faster loading, and Meta's algorithm optimizes better with on-platform data. Use landing pages only if your sales team can't handle volume and needs heavier pre-qualification.

faq.question: How much should a contractor spend on Facebook Ads to see results?
faq.answer: Minimum $2,500–$3,000/month per market to give Meta's algorithm enough data to optimize. Below that, you'll get inconsistent results and won't be able to test creative properly. Most of our roofing and remodeling clients run $8K–$40K/month.

faq.question: How often should I refresh my Facebook ad creative?
faq.answer: Every 14–21 days for local contractors. Your service radius is geographically small, so audiences see the same ad quickly. Watch frequency in Ads Manager — when it hits 3.5+, CPL will spike and it's time for new creative.

faq.question: Why are my Facebook leads such low quality?
faq.answer: Usually one of three things: your form has zero qualifiers so anyone taps through, your offer is too broad ("free quote") and attracts tire-kickers, or your follow-up is slow so only bored leads answer. Add one qualifier question, tighten your offer, and install sub-5-minute SMS follow-up.

articles.title: The 4-Call Marketing Agency Sales Process for Cold Leads
articles.description: Turn cold booked calls into $3k-$8k/mo retainers at 35% close rates with this 4-call sequence: triage, audit, proposal, onboarding.
articles.keyword: marketing agency sales process for cold leads
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most agencies close cold leads at 8-12%. The good ones hit 20%. We run a 4-call sequence that consistently closes at 35% into $3k-$8k/mo retainers, and it works because it stops trying to close on the first call. If you're a founder or agency owner running paid cold traffic to a calendar, and your close rate is stuck under 20%, the problem isn't your offer or your ads. It's that you're compressing a 4-step buying decision into a 45-minute call and hoping the prospect self-qualifies, self-diagnoses, and self-closes. Below: the exact call sequence, what happens on each call, the scripts and assets we use, the CRM automations behind it, and the numbers you should expect at each stage.

Why the one-call close breaks on cold traffic

The one-call close was built for warm inbound. Referrals, podcast listeners, and people who read three blog posts before booking are already 60% sold. Cold Meta and Google traffic isn't. A cold lead who books off a $40 CPL Meta ad has zero context. They don't know your case studies, your process, or your price. When you jump into a 60-minute discovery-and-pitch on call one, three things happen: - Trust hasn't compounded. You're asking for $3k-$8k/mo from someone who met you 4 minutes ago.

  • You skip diagnosis. Without a real audit, your proposal is generic, so prospects push back on price.
  • No-shows tank your economics. Cold leads no-show at 40-55%. If your entire sales process depends on one call, half your pipeline evaporates. The 4-call sequence fixes all three. It separates qualification from diagnosis from proposal from onboarding. Each call has one job. Each has its own show-up rate, own conversion metric, and own script. And because the prospect invests time across 3-7 days, they self-select out early if they're not serious, meaning your later calls close at 55-70%.

Call 1: The 15-minute triage

The triage call is short, fast, and disqualification-heavy. Its only job: decide whether this lead deserves the audit. Book it as a 15-minute slot on Calendly or GoHighLevel. Never longer. The short slot signals seriousness and cuts no-shows because prospects feel the low commitment. What you cover: 1. Current revenue and margin (are they big enough to afford you?) 2. Current marketing spend and channels (do they have budget?) 3. What they've tried and why it failed (pain baseline) 4. Decision-maker and timeline (can they actually buy?) 5. Your one-sentence positioning and what the audit will deliver Disqualify hard. If they're under $30k/mo revenue, no ad budget, or not the decision-maker, end the call politely and move on. Roughly 40-50% of cold-booked calls should fail triage. If you're qualifying everyone, you're wasting your closer's time on call 2. Book the audit call live at the end, calendar open on screen. Don't say "I'll send a link." Send a confirmation SMS via GoHighLevel workflow the moment the call ends, then email a short pre-work form asking for ad account access, website URL, and current offer. If they don't complete pre-work 24 hours before the audit, cancel it. This alone lifts show rate on call 2 from 55% to 80%+.

Call 2: The audit call (where 70% of the selling happens)

The audit is a 45-minute working session where you present a custom teardown of their current marketing. This is where trust gets built and where the real close begins. Before the call, spend 30-45 minutes in their Meta Ads Manager, Google Ads, GA4, and their website. Build a Google Slides or Notion doc with: - Current state: spend, CPL, CPA, conversion rate, top and bottom performing ads

  • 3-5 specific problems with screenshots (bad creative, broken pixel events, no retargeting, wrong campaign objective, weak landing page)
  • What good looks like in their vertical (benchmarks from your other clients)
  • The gap in revenue terms: "You're leaving ~$47k/mo on the table" On the call, present the audit for 25 minutes. Do not pitch. Let them ask questions. When they say "so what would you do?"—that's the buying signal. Say: "That's exactly what I'd walk you through in a proposal. Let me put one together specific to your account and we'll review it Thursday." Book the proposal call live. Do not send a proposal by email. Emailed proposals close at 8-15%. Walked-through proposals close at 55-65%. This step alone is the single biggest lever in the entire sequence.

Call 3: The proposal walkthrough

The proposal call is 30 minutes and has a specific structure. You are not "presenting options." You are confirming a decision they've already started making. Structure: 1. Recap (3 min): Repeat the top 3 problems from the audit and the revenue gap. This re-anchors the pain. 2. The plan (10 min): Walk through exactly what you'll do in months 1, 2, and 3. Be specific: "Week 1 we rebuild your pixel and rewrite your 5 top-spending ads. Week 2 we launch a retargeting campaign to your last 90 days of site traffic." 3. Investment (2 min): Present one price. Not three tiers. One. "$4,500/month, 90-day initial term, then month-to-month." Say it, then shut up. 4. Handle objections (10 min): The two you'll hear are price and timing. For price: return to the revenue gap number. For timing: offer a start date two weeks out with a paid discovery sprint. 5. Close (5 min): "Do you want to move forward?" If yes, send the contract via PandaDoc or HelloSign live on the call and get it signed before hanging up. About 35-45% will sign on call 3. Another 15-20% will sign within 7 days with 2-3 follow-ups. Ghosts get a 14-day nurture sequence in HubSpot or GoHighLevel and a hard breakup email at day 21.

Call 4: The onboarding call (yes, it's part of the sales process)

Most agencies treat onboarding as operations. It's not. It's the last sales call, and it's where you prevent 30-day cancellations and set up the referral and upsell. Run it within 72 hours of contract signature. 60 minutes. Include the account manager and the media buyer who'll actually run the account. Cover: - Access checklist: Meta Business Manager, Google Ads, GA4, Shopify or CRM, domain, email tools. Use a Notion or ClickUp template so nothing gets missed.

  • Communication cadence: weekly Loom updates, monthly strategy call, Slack Connect channel for day-to-day.
  • The 90-day plan: written out, shared, agreed. Include specific KPIs and the review date.
  • Expectations on their side: creative approvals within 48 hours, one point of contact, no pausing campaigns without asking. The reason this is a sales call: buyer's remorse peaks between day 3 and day 10. A tight, professional onboarding kills remorse, gets them producing assets fast, and gives them a story to tell their business partner ("these guys are unbelievably organized"). Clients who go through structured onboarding retain 3.4x longer than those who get a Google Drive folder and a Slack invite.

The CRM and automation stack behind the sequence

The sequence only works if the operational plumbing is tight. Manual follow-up kills close rates because reps forget and leads go cold. Here's what we run: CRM: GoHighLevel or HubSpot. GHL if you're under 50 leads/month, HubSpot if you're scaling past 200. Pipeline stages: Booked Triage → Triage Complete → Audit Scheduled → Audit Complete → Proposal Scheduled → Proposal Sent → Closed Won / Closed Lost / Nurture. Automations: - SMS + email confirmation on booking, 24-hour reminder, 1-hour reminder

  • Pre-work form auto-sent after triage, with a cancel-if-incomplete rule
  • Missed call → automatic reschedule link + 3-touch text sequence over 48 hours
  • Post-proposal: day 1, 3, 7, 14, 21 follow-up sequence with different angles (case study, ROI calculator, breakup email)
  • Closed-lost → 90-day nurture into monthly newsletter Reporting: track show rate, triage-to-audit conversion, audit-to-proposal conversion, and proposal-to-close conversion separately. If your overall close rate drops, you need to know which call is leaking. Expected benchmarks on cold traffic: 60% triage show, 45% pass to audit, 80% audit show, 75% pass to proposal, 85% proposal show, 45% close. That math nets to roughly 12-15% booked-call-to-signed-client, at $3k-$8k/mo AOV.

What this sequence costs to run and when it pays back

The 4-call sequence takes real labor: roughly 3-4 hours of rep and analyst time per fully-qualified lead through proposal stage. On $3k-$8k/mo retainers with 12-month average client life, that's fine math. On $500/mo one-off projects, it isn't. This process only makes sense if your AOV is $2k/mo or higher. Team you need to run it: - SDR or founder handling triage (Call 1)

  • Senior strategist or founder handling audit and proposal (Calls 2 and 3)
  • Account manager handling onboarding (Call 4) In early-stage agencies, the founder runs calls 1-3. Once you're past 8-10 new clients a month, split triage off to an SDR making $50k base. The audit and proposal calls stay with a senior closer indefinitely because they're the highest-leverage hour in the business. Payback math: if you're spending $80 per booked call on cold traffic and closing at 35% through this sequence, your CAC lands around $230-$400. On a $4,500/mo retainer with 60% gross margin, you pay CAC back in month one and everything after month one is profit. That's the number you're building toward.

The bottom line

The reason cold leads close at 35% through this sequence isn't magic scripting or a better offer. It's that each call does one job well, the prospect self-qualifies across multiple touchpoints, and the CRM catches the leads that would otherwise fall through the floor. If you're running cold traffic and closing under 20%, don't rebuild your ads. Rebuild the sequence between the booked call and the signed contract. Map your current pipeline stages against the 4-call model, find the stage with the biggest drop-off, and fix that call first. Most agencies find their leak is at proposal—they're still emailing PDFs and hoping. Stop hoping. Get on the call, walk it through, and close it live.

faq.question: How long does the whole 4-call sequence take from first call to signed contract?
faq.answer: Typically 5-10 days. Triage day 1, audit day 3-4, proposal day 6-8, onboarding within 72 hours of signature. Compressing it faster hurts close rate; stretching it past 14 days lets prospects go cold.

faq.question: Can I skip the triage call and start with the audit?
faq.answer: Only if your traffic is warm (referrals, podcast, inbound). On cold paid traffic, skipping triage means you waste 40% of your audit prep on leads who can't afford you or aren't decision-makers. The 15-minute triage pays for itself in reclaimed strategist hours.

faq.question: What close rate should I expect in month one of implementing this?
faq.answer: Expect 20-25% in the first 30 days while you refine the audit deck and proposal walkthrough. Most agencies hit the 30-35% range by month three once the pre-work automation is dialed in and the closer has run 20+ proposal calls.

faq.question: Do I need a full-time SDR to make this work?
faq.answer: No, not until you're doing 8-10 new clients a month. Below that, the founder runs calls 1-3 and it's a better use of time than most other agency activities because it directly drives revenue. Hire the SDR once triage calls exceed 15 hours of founder time per week.

faq.question: How much should I spend building out the audit for each prospect?
faq.answer: Cap it at 45 minutes of analyst time. Build a repeatable template in Google Slides or Notion where 70% of the deck is prefilled and you're only customizing the screenshots, numbers, and specific problems. Any longer and the unit economics break on sub-$5k retainers.

articles.title: Business Credit Stacking for Contractors: $250K in 90 Days
articles.description: How trades operators stack $100K–$250K across 4–6 issuers in 90 days to fund trucks, crews, and lead flow — without personal guarantees killing them.
articles.keyword: business credit stacking for contractors
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most contractors are running six-figure operations on a personal Chase card and a prayer. Meanwhile, the operator down the street just pulled $180K in unsecured 0% credit across five issuers in under 90 days — and he's using it to add two trucks, a second crew, and $15K/month in Google LSA spend simultaneously. This isn't a hack. Business credit stacking is a documented funding stack used by HVAC, roofing, plumbing, electrical, and remodeling operators to bridge the gap between what SBA lenders will touch and what merchant cash advance sharks will charge you 40% APR for. Done right, it's the cheapest working capital a sub-$5M contractor can access. This guide breaks down exactly how contractors are stacking $100K–$250K across 4–6 issuers in 90 days, which banks to hit in which order, and how to deploy the capital so it actually returns 3–5x instead of becoming another liability.

Why credit stacking beats SBA and MCA for contractors

The average contractor's funding options look like this: an SBA 7(a) that takes 60–120 days and demands two years of tax returns, an equipment loan tied to a specific asset, or a merchant cash advance at 1.35 factor rate (that's ~50% APR when you actually math it out). Business credit stacking sits in the sweet spot. You're pulling unsecured revolving credit from 4–6 issuers — Chase Ink, Amex Business, Capital One Spark, US Bank Triple Cash, BofA Business Advantage, Navy Federal if you qualify — at 0% intro APR for 9–15 months. Total available: typically $100K–$250K for a 680+ FICO operator with a 2+ year old entity. The math is brutal in your favor: - MCA on $150K: ~$52,500 in cost over 12 months

  • SBA on $150K: ~$12,000/year interest, plus 60+ days waiting
  • Stacked 0% credit on $150K: $0 interest for 9–15 months if you clear balances or refinance The catch: it requires prep work most contractors skip. Miss the prep and you get denied across the board, hard pulls burning your score for 24 months. Do the prep, you walk in and walk out with a stack.

The 30-day prep window before you apply anywhere

Applying cold is how contractors end up with $25K in approvals instead of $200K. Underwriters at Chase and Amex are looking at 12+ specific signals.
