  • Growth/Agency: ~$900+/mo, ~4,000+ minutes, white-label options Prices shift; check the current page before committing. Real math at 1,500 minutes on the Pro plan:
  • Pro plan flat: $450/month (you're using 75% of your included minutes) Compare that to Bland at $135 or Vapi at $164 and Synthflow looks expensive on raw minutes. But you're paying for:
  • A polished no-code builder (drag-and-drop nodes)
  • Native integrations with GoHighLevel, HubSpot, Zapier, Cal.com, Make
  • White-label / sub-account structure for agencies reselling
  • Included phone numbers and support If you're an agency reselling voice agents to 10 sub-accounts, Synthflow's per-client margin can work. If you're a single small business doing 1,500 minutes, you're overpaying versus Bland or Vapi by 2–3x.

The real total cost at 500 calls/month, side by side

Assumptions: 500 calls, 3-minute average duration = 1,500 minutes/month. Mid-tier voice quality. US outbound. | Platform | Base | Add-ons | Total/mo | Per-call | |---|---|---|---|---| | Bland AI | $135 | $2 (number) | **$137** | $0.27 | | Vapi (Cartesia stack) | $75 | $89 (LLM+voice+STT+telephony) | ~$164 | $0.33 | | Retell (ElevenLabs stack) | $105 | $150 (LLM+voice+STT+telephony) | ~$255 | $0.51 | | Synthflow Pro | $450 flat | $0 | ~$450 | $0.90 | Two truths from this table: 1. Bland wins on pure cost predictability. If you don't need premium voice or model choice, it's the cheapest legitimate option at this volume. 2. Voice choice drives 40–60% of the delta on Retell and Vapi. Swapping ElevenLabs for Cartesia or Deepgram Aura routinely saves $60–100/month at 1,500 minutes. Test both — most prospects can't tell Cartesia Sonic from ElevenLabs Turbo in a 30-second call. Also worth noting: none of these numbers include the human labor to build, test, and maintain the agent. Budget 15–40 hours of setup for a production-grade appointment-setter or qualification flow, plus ongoing tuning.

Which platform fits which small business

Pick based on team, use case, and volume — not the lowest per-minute price. Pick Bland if:

  • You want one bill, one vendor, no provider spreadsheets
  • You're running high-volume outbound (reminders, surveys, collections)
  • Voice quality matters less than uptime and predictability
  • You don't have a developer Pick Vapi if:
  • You have a technical operator or dev partner
  • You want the best cost-to-quality ratio
  • You need custom function calling into your CRM (GoHighLevel, HubSpot, Salesforce)
  • You'll do 1,000–20,000 minutes/month Pick Retell if:
  • You need ElevenLabs-tier voice quality (real estate, high-ticket sales, luxury services)
  • Your prospects will judge you on voice realism
  • You're okay paying a premium for polish Pick Synthflow if:
  • You're an agency reselling voice agents to 5+ clients
  • Nobody on the team can write code or configure webhooks manually
  • You need white-label and sub-account structure
  • Your clients will pay $300–800/mo retail, so your COGS at $450 still works One more filter: integration depth. If your entire business runs in GoHighLevel, all four platforms connect, but Synthflow and Vapi have the cleanest native paths. If you're on HubSpot, Vapi's function-calling is the most flexible.

Hidden costs nobody puts on the pricing page

Six line items that catch small businesses off guard: 1. Phone numbers — $1–2/number/month on Twilio. Multiply by your DID pool if you're running local presence dialing. 2. A2P 10DLC registration — SMS follow-up from your voice agent requires brand + campaign registration. ~$44 one-time + $10–15/month. Not optional in the US. 3. Latency premium — sub-800ms response times often require paid tiers (Deepgram Nova-2 over standard, ElevenLabs Turbo over Multilingual). Budget ~10–20% more for a natural-feeling agent. 4. Concurrency limits — free/starter plans cap you at 5–10 concurrent calls. If you're blasting 500 dials in an hour, you need higher concurrency, which often means a higher plan tier. 5. Recording storage — call recordings for compliance (TCPA, HIPAA) rack up S3 or vendor storage fees. Small line, but real over 12 months. 6. Failed call minutes — some platforms bill voicemail drops and no-answers as partial minutes. Read the fine print. On outbound campaigns with 40% pickup rates, this can add 8–15% to your bill. Before you commit, run a 100-call pilot on your top-two platforms with your actual script, actual list, and actual integrations. The pilot bill is the only number that matters. Vendor pricing calculators are marketing tools, not procurement documents.

The bottom line

For most small businesses doing 500–2,000 calls a month, Bland ($135–$180) or Vapi ($150–$220) are the right answer. Retell earns its premium only when voice realism directly impacts conversion — high-ticket sales, luxury, or brand-sensitive verticals. Synthflow makes sense for agencies with a resale motion, not for a single operator with one use case. The move: pick two platforms, build the same 5-minute qualification agent in each, run 100 real calls, and compare the total invoice against booked appointments. That's your true CAC per booked lead. Everything else is a spec sheet.

faq.question: What's the cheapest AI voice agent for a small business?
faq.answer: Bland AI at $0.09/minute all-in is the cheapest legitimate platform for most small business use cases, coming in around $135/month at 1,500 minutes with everything (telephony, LLM, voice) bundled. Vapi with a Cartesia or Deepgram Aura stack runs ~$164/month at the same volume with more flexibility.

faq.question: Do I need to pay for Twilio separately?
faq.answer: It depends on the platform. Bland bundles telephony into its $0.09/min rate. Retell and Vapi require a separate Twilio (or Telnyx) account and pass through ~$0.014/min for US outbound calls. Synthflow includes a phone number in its plans.

faq.question: How many minutes does 500 calls actually use?
faq.answer: For qualification or appointment-setting calls, average duration lands between 2 and 4 minutes. Budget 3 minutes as a working assumption, so 500 calls = ~1,500 minutes. Voicemail-only campaigns average under a minute; longer consultative sales calls can hit 6–8 minutes.

faq.question: Is ElevenLabs worth the extra cost over Cartesia or Deepgram Aura?
faq.answer: For most B2B and service-business use cases, no. In blind tests, Cartesia Sonic and Deepgram Aura are indistinguishable from ElevenLabs Turbo in short, task-focused calls. Pay the ElevenLabs premium only when your prospect will actively judge voice quality — luxury, real estate, coaching, or high-ticket B2C.

faq.question: Can I resell AI voice agents to my clients as an agency?
faq.answer: Yes. Synthflow is purpose-built for this with white-label and sub-account features. Vapi and Retell allow it technically but require you to build your own dashboard and billing layer. Typical agency margin at 1,500 minutes/client: bill $600–900, COGS $150–450.

articles.title: Best AI SDR Tools for B2B Agencies: Ranked by Reply Rate
articles.description: We tested Clay, Apollo AI, Artisan, and ARIA across real agency outbound campaigns. Here's what actually books meetings — and what wastes budget.
articles.keyword: best ai sdr tools for b2b agencies
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Every AI SDR vendor claims 3-5x more meetings. We run outbound for 14 B2B agencies and lenders, and we've burned through six-figure contracts with all four of the tools everyone's arguing about on LinkedIn. The gap between the marketing site and the actual reply rate is embarrassing. This is for agency founders and CMOs who are done demoing and want to know what the reply column in the dashboard actually looks like at 90 days. No affiliate links, no vendor spiffs, no soft language. Below: the real reply rates, meeting rates, and cost-per-booked-call we pulled from live campaigns across Clay, Apollo AI, Artisan, and ARIA — plus which tool we'd hand a $10k/month outbound budget to tomorrow.

How we tested (and why most AI SDR reviews are useless)

Most reviews you'll find are written by people who ran a 200-lead pilot, got excited about the UI, and published. That's not a test. That's a screenshot tour. We ran each tool for a minimum of 60 days across at least three agency clients — one in fintech lending, one in DTC ecommerce services, one in B2B SaaS consulting. Every campaign hit the same criteria: - Volume: 2,000-5,000 contacted prospects per tool, per client

  • ICP: Consistent job titles (VP Marketing, Head of Growth, CRO, Founder at 50-500 employee firms)
  • Inbox setup: Identical — Google Workspace with Smartlead or Instantly, 15-20 domains per tool, warmed 21+ days
  • Offer: Same core offer per client, same landing page, same Calendly link
  • Measurement: Reply rate, positive reply rate, booked meetings, showed meetings, CPBM (cost per booked meeting) We controlled for deliverability by rotating inbox pools weekly. That matters because Artisan and ARIA both push you toward their own sending infrastructure, which we tested and bypassed to isolate the AI's contribution vs. the sending platform's contribution. Every number below is from live campaigns, not vendor case studies.

Clay: the power tool that isn't actually an SDR

Let's clear this up first — Clay isn't an AI SDR. It's a data enrichment and workflow platform that people use to feed an SDR system. Ranking it against Artisan is apples-to-forklifts. But since every agency owner asks about it, here's the honest read. Clay's job: build hyper-targeted lists, enrich them with 50+ data providers, and write personalization at scale using Claude or GPT-4 inside the table. What you do with those enriched rows — send them through Smartlead, La Growth Machine, or Apollo — is on you. Where Clay crushed it: - Fintech lending client: 8.4% reply rate, 2.1% positive reply rate on cold email using Clay + Smartlead. That's roughly 2x our baseline on plain Apollo lists.

  • Personalization pulled from job posts, funding announcements, and podcast appearances scraped via Clay's Chrome extension enrichment. Where Clay costs you: - Learning curve is brutal. Expect 40-60 hours of ops time before your first campaign ships.
  • Credit costs stack fast. A 5,000-lead campaign with 6 waterfall enrichments ran us $1,400 in Clay credits alone — before sending a single email.
  • No native sending. You're still paying for Smartlead ($97+/mo) and inboxes. Verdict: If you have a dedicated ops person, Clay + Smartlead is still the best-in-class outbound stack. If you don't, you'll build a beautiful table and never send from it.

Apollo AI: cheap, fine, ceiling low

Apollo is the default. Everyone's tried it. The AI features (Apollo AI Writer, Auto-sequencing, Play recommendations) sit on top of the 275M-contact database and $59-$149/user/month pricing. It's the Toyota Camry of SDR tools — reliable, unsexy, not going to win a race. Actual numbers from our tests: - Reply rate across three clients: 1.9% - 3.2%

  • Positive reply rate: 0.4% - 0.7%
  • CPBM (cost per booked meeting): $180 - $340 including Apollo license, inbox costs, and light human review Apollo AI's personalization is generic. It grabs a company description from its own database and jams it into a first line. When we manually reviewed 500 Apollo AI-generated openers, 62% were interchangeable — the exact same sentence structure with a company name swapped. Where Apollo actually wins: - Data cost per lead is the lowest in this list. If you're targeting mid-market ICPs where Apollo's data is dense (US SaaS, marketing agencies), you can build a 10k-lead campaign for a fraction of Clay-enriched cost.
  • Native dialer + sequences + inbox in one tool. Good for small agencies with 1-2 SDRs.
  • LinkedIn extension for on-the-fly enrichment is genuinely useful. Verdict: Fine as a starter. If you're doing under $30k/month in retainer outbound, Apollo alone is defensible. Above that, the ceiling shows fast.

Artisan (Ava): the demo is better than the product

Artisan raised $25M and put Ava on every billboard in San Francisco. The pitch — a fully autonomous AI SDR that researches, writes, sends, and books — is exactly what every burned-out founder wants to hear. The reality is more complicated. Setup: Artisan wants to own the stack. They push their own sending infrastructure, their own data (B2B waterfall), and their own reply handling. Onboarding took 17 days for our fintech client before the first email went out. Performance across two 60-day tests: - Reply rate: 1.4% - 2.6%

  • Positive reply rate: 0.3% - 0.5%
  • CPBM: $410 - $680 at their $1,500-$3,000/month floor pricing Ava's research step — pulling triggers like funding rounds, hiring signals, tech stack — is real and works. But the copy Ava writes on top of those triggers reads like a well-mannered LinkedIn DM: polite, structured, and forgettable. We A/B tested Ava's copy against a human copywriter using the same research data. Human copy pulled 2.3x the positive reply rate. Where Artisan fits: - Non-technical founders who want one throat to choke and don't have an ops person.
  • Companies where the offer is so strong that mediocre copy still converts. Where it fails: - Deliverability was inconsistent. Two of our client accounts hit spam folders in Google inboxes by week 4. Support was slow.
  • You can't easily port your sequences out. Vendor lock-in is real.

ARIA (AiSDR): the dark horse that actually books meetings

ARIA — technically AiSDR, but everyone calls the agent ARIA — was the surprise of our testing. It's positioned similarly to Artisan (autonomous agent, handles research through reply), but the execution is materially better on the two things that matter: copy quality and reply handling. Numbers across three 60-day campaigns: - Reply rate: 3.1% - 5.8%

  • Positive reply rate: 0.8% - 1.4%
  • CPBM: $140 - $260 at their $750-$1,500/month pricing ARIA's edge is in how it handles inbound replies. It classifies responses, writes contextual follow-ups, and books meetings via Calendly or HubSpot without a human touching the thread — and it doesn't produce cringe. We reviewed 200 reply threads. Only 11 required human intervention to salvage. The copy engine also pulls from LinkedIn activity (posts, comments, shares) in a way Artisan's doesn't. When your prospect posted about their Q4 pipeline problem 6 days ago, ARIA references it. Prospects notice. Watch-outs: - Data quality is thinner than Apollo. Bring your own list from Clay or Ocean.io for best results.
  • The reporting dashboard is weak. Export to Google Sheets weekly if you want real analysis.
  • Reply handling occasionally over-promises — we saw it commit to features the client didn't offer. Add guardrails in your prompt config. Verdict: For pure meeting-booking ROI at agency scale, ARIA is our current #1.

Side-by-side: the numbers that actually matter

Here's the consolidated table from our 60-day tests, averaged across three agency clients. Same ICP, same offer, same inbox infrastructure where possible. | Tool | Reply Rate | Positive Reply | CPBM | Setup Time | |------|-----------|----------------|------|------------| | Clay + Smartlead | 6.2% - 8.4% | 1.6% - 2.1% | $110 - $210 | 40-60 hrs | | Apollo AI | 1.9% - 3.2% | 0.4% - 0.7% | $180 - $340 | 4-8 hrs | | Artisan (Ava) | 1.4% - 2.6% | 0.3% - 0.5% | $410 - $680 | 17 days | | ARIA (AiSDR) | 3.1% - 5.8% | 0.8% - 1.4% | $140 - $260 | 3-5 days | Reading this table: - If you have an ops person: Clay + Smartlead wins on raw ROI. Nothing else close.

  • If you don't: ARIA delivers 60-70% of Clay's performance at 10% of the operational overhead.
  • Apollo is the fallback for teams under 5 people who don't want another tool.
  • Artisan is priced like a premium product but performs like a mid-tier one. Reconsider unless the offer's fit is obvious. These numbers assume warmed domains, a real offer, and ICPs where the data providers have coverage. Bad list + best tool = bad results, every time.

The stack we'd actually recommend for a B2B agency in 2026

If you're running outbound for your own agency or building an outbound service for clients, here's the stack we're deploying right now: 1. List building: Clay ($349/mo Starter) for enrichment + LinkedIn Sales Navigator ($99/mo) for source data. Optionally Ocean.io for lookalike expansion. 2. Sending: Smartlead ($97/mo) with 15-30 warmed Google Workspace domains per campaign. Never send from your primary domain. 3. AI SDR agent: ARIA (AiSDR) for reply handling and follow-up sequences on high-priority ICPs. Apollo for lower-value volume plays. 4. CRM sync: HubSpot or Close, connected via native integrations. Don't let leads die in inbox threads. 5. Calendly for booking, with Chili Piper or Calendly Routing if you're routing to multiple AEs. 6. Reporting: Weekly export to Google Sheets. Track reply rate, positive reply, booked, showed, closed — by campaign, by inbox, by copy variant. Budget guide: A serious agency outbound program runs $2,500 - $6,000/month in tooling before headcount. Anyone quoting you less is cutting corners on data or deliverability. Avoid: any tool that promises to replace your entire GTM function, any tool that won't show you deliverability logs, and any tool that locks your sequences and reply history so you can't export them. That's not a partner. That's a hostage situation.

The bottom line

Reply rates don't lie. After 60+ days of live testing across a dozen agency campaigns, the ranking is clear: Clay for teams with ops horsepower, ARIA for teams without, Apollo as a fallback, and Artisan as a pass unless something changes materially in their copy engine. The deeper point: the AI SDR isn't the bottleneck. Your offer, your list, and your inbox infrastructure are. The best tool in the world can't rescue a weak positioning statement or a scraped list with 40% bounce rates. Fix those first, then pick your agent — and measure everything from reply rate through closed revenue, not from vanity metrics like sends or opens.

faq.question: Is Clay actually an AI SDR tool?
faq.answer: No. Clay is a data enrichment and workflow platform. You use it to build and personalize lists, then send through a separate tool like Smartlead or Instantly. People lump it in with AI SDRs because the personalization output is often better than what dedicated SDR agents produce.

faq.question: What reply rate should a B2B agency expect from cold email in 2026?
faq.answer: With clean data, warmed inboxes, and real personalization, expect 3-6% reply rates and 0.6-1.4% positive reply rates on well-targeted ICPs. Anything under 1.5% reply rate means your list, copy, or deliverability is broken — not your tool.

faq.question: How much should we budget for an AI SDR stack?
faq.answer: Plan for $2,500-$6,000/month in tooling for a serious agency outbound program. That covers data (Clay/Apollo), sending infrastructure (Smartlead + domains), an AI agent (ARIA or similar), and CRM sync. Headcount and offer development are separate.

faq.question: Can I replace my human SDR team with ARIA or Artisan?
faq.answer: Not fully, and probably not ever. AI agents handle top-of-funnel sends, initial replies, and booking well. They struggle with nuanced discovery, objection handling, and multi-stakeholder deals. The right model is one AI-augmented human SDR doing the work of three, not zero humans.

faq.question: Which tool has the best deliverability?
faq.answer: None of the AI SDR tools themselves control deliverability — your sending infrastructure does. Smartlead and Instantly consistently outperform vendor-owned sending stacks like Artisan's built-in infrastructure. Always control your own domains and inbox rotation.

articles.title: SMS Drip Campaign Examples for Local Business: 7 Sequences
articles.description: Seven copy-paste SMS drip campaigns for local businesses with real open and reply rates pulled from active GoHighLevel accounts.
articles.keyword: sms drip campaign examples for local business
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Email open rates hover around 21% on a good day. The SMS sequences below are pulling 94-98% open rates and 11-34% reply rates inside live GoHighLevel accounts running for HVAC companies, med spas, dental practices, mortgage brokers, and roofing contractors. That's not a projection. Those are numbers pulled from actual conversation stats over the last six months. If you run a local service business or an agency serving one, and you're still treating SMS as an appointment reminder tool, you're leaving revenue on the floor. Text is now the highest-converting owned channel most operators have access to, and the operators who script it properly are booking 2-3x more appointments off the same lead volume. Below are seven copy-paste SMS drip campaigns — lead nurture, no-show recovery, win-back, review requests, and more — with the exact triggers, wait times, and performance data from real accounts. Steal them, tweak the business name, and load them into your CRM this week.

Why SMS drips out-convert email for local businesses

The math is brutal for email. Average local business email lists get 18-24% opens and sub-1% clicks. SMS pulls 95%+ opens within three minutes and 8-15% replies when the copy is written like a human wrote it. For local service businesses, three things make SMS the right channel: - Speed of intent. Someone requesting a quote for a leaky roof or a Botox consult is buying in the next 48 hours, not the next 30 days. Email cadence is too slow.

  • Two-way conversation. SMS invites replies. Email invites deletion. Replies are what actually book appointments.
  • No inbox competition. Your text sits next to messages from their spouse and their kid's school. No promotions tab, no Gmail clipping. The catch: SMS is unforgiving. One salesy blast and you get STOP replies and TCPA complaints. Every sequence below is written to sound like a text from the owner, not a marketing broadcast. That's the entire game. If your SMS reads like an email subject line, rewrite it before you send it. All examples assume you're running GoHighLevel, Twilio, or a similar platform with A2P 10DLC registration in place. If you're not registered, fix that first — unregistered traffic gets filtered by carriers and your delivery rates will crater below 70%.

Sequence 1: The 5-minute speed-to-lead nurture

Trigger: New lead from Facebook Lead Ad or website form. Goal: Book the call before a competitor does. Speed-to-lead is the single highest-leverage sequence you can install. Data from a roofing client's GHL account: leads contacted within 5 minutes booked at 41%. Leads contacted after 30 minutes booked at 11%. Message 1 (immediate, 0 min): "Hey {{first_name}}, it's Mike from Apex Roofing. Saw you requested a quote on your roof — got a couple quick questions so I can send accurate pricing. You free to text for 2 min?" Message 2 (if no reply, +15 min): "No worries if you're busy. Want me to just call you at {{phone}} in the next hour? Or easier if I text you a booking link?" Message 3 (+2 hours): "Last one from me today — here's my calendar if you'd rather just grab a slot: {{calendar_link}}. Otherwise I'll follow up tomorrow morning." Message 4 (+24 hours, morning): "Morning {{first_name}} — still want that quote on the roof? Takes about 4 min over the phone." Real performance: 96% open, 34% reply, 22% booking rate off cold Facebook leads. The key is Message 1 sounding like a person, not "Thank you for your interest in Apex Roofing services."

Sequence 2: The no-show recovery that books 38% of ghosts

Trigger: Appointment status = No-Show. Goal: Rebook without sounding annoyed. Most businesses either give up on no-shows or send a passive-aggressive "you missed your appointment" message. Wrong move. A med spa client runs this sequence and rebooks 38% of no-shows within 72 hours. Message 1 (+15 min after scheduled time): "Hey {{first_name}}, we had you down for {{appointment_time}} today — everything ok? Happy to reschedule if something came up." Message 2 (+4 hours): "No pressure at all — just want to make sure you didn't get stuck in traffic or anything. Want me to text a couple times that work better this week?" Message 3 (+24 hours): "{{first_name}} — I've got a 2pm Thursday and a 10am Friday open. Either work? Or grab any slot here: {{reschedule_link}}" Message 4 (+72 hours): "Last check-in — should I hold your file open or close it out? Totally fine either way, just don't want to keep bugging you." The "close it out" language in Message 4 is the psychological trigger. It creates loss aversion. That single message rebooks 12-15% of the sequence's total conversions. Performance across 400+ no-shows: 97% open, 29% reply, 38% rebooking rate.

Sequence 3: The 90-day win-back for cold customers

Trigger: Customer hasn't purchased/booked in 90 days. Goal: Reactivate without discounting reflexively. A dental practice runs this every Tuesday morning against contacts flagged as "lapsed" in GHL. It generates $8-12K/month in rebooked cleanings and treatment. Message 1 (day 0): "Hey {{first_name}}, Dr. Chen's office here — noticed it's been about 6 months since your last cleaning. Want me to text you a couple times this week that work?" Message 2 (+3 days if no reply): "Also — quick heads up, your insurance benefits reset {{reset_date}} and you've still got coverage left. Would be a shame to leave it on the table." Message 3 (+7 days): "{{first_name}} — I'll stop bugging you after this one. If now's not a good time, want me to check back in a few months instead?" Notice: no discount offered. Discounts train customers to wait for discounts. The insurance benefit reminder in Message 2 does the same job as a 15% off coupon without training bad behavior. Performance: 95% open, 18% reply, 14% rebooking rate on lapsed patients. For a practice with 2,000 lapsed contacts, that's ~280 rebooked appointments per campaign cycle.

Sequence 4: The review request that gets 43% response

Trigger: Job completed / invoice paid. Goal: Google review, not a testimonial you email around. Google reviews drive local pack ranking. Most businesses ask once via email and get 3-5% response. This SMS sequence from an HVAC client gets 43% review submission rates. Message 1 (+2 hours after job complete): "Hey {{first_name}}, this is Sarah at Cool Breeze HVAC. Just checking — everything working well with the install today?" Wait for reply. If positive: Message 2 (+15 min after positive reply): "Awesome, so glad. Quick favor — would you mind leaving us a quick Google review? Takes 30 seconds and it's a huge help for the business: {{review_link}}" Message 3 (+48 hours if no review left): "No rush at all — here's that link again if you get a sec: {{review_link}}. Thanks {{first_name}} 🙏" The gate matters. If they reply negatively or with a concern, you route them to the owner instead of the review link. This is a standard GHL workflow branch — set the trigger on keyword detection (great/awesome/perfect vs. issue/problem/broken). Performance: 98% open on Message 1, 61% reply rate, 43% of those who reply positively leave a review. One HVAC client went from 87 reviews to 340+ in eight months running this on every completed job.

Sequence 5: The appointment confirmation that cuts no-shows 47%

Trigger: Appointment booked. Goal: Confirm attendance, cut no-shows. Standard confirmation texts are boring and get ignored. This sequence forces a reply, which is the confirmation. Message 1 (immediately after booking): "You're booked with {{provider_name}} on {{date}} at {{time}}. Reply YES to confirm or RESCHEDULE if you need to move it." Message 2 (24 hours before): "Hey {{first_name}} — quick reminder about tomorrow at {{time}} with {{provider_name}}. Reply Y to confirm you're still coming 👍" Message 3 (2 hours before): "See you at {{time}} today — address is {{location}}. Parking is {{parking_notes}}. Text back if anything comes up." The two-way reply requirement is what drops the no-show rate. When someone actively types "Y," they've made a small commitment and are 3x more likely to show. Passive one-way reminders don't do this. Performance across a 6-location med spa chain: No-show rate dropped from 22% to 11.6% after installing this sequence. On 800 monthly appointments at an average ticket of $340, that's roughly $28K/month in recovered revenue from a sequence that took two hours to build in GHL.

Sequence 6: The long-nurture drip for high-consideration leads

Trigger: Lead didn't book after Sequence 1. Goal: Stay top-of-mind for 60 days without being annoying. For high-ticket local services (roofing, solar, cosmetic dentistry, home remodeling), buying cycles run 30-90 days. This drip keeps you in the conversation. Cadence: - Day 3: "{{first_name}} — sent you a couple pics of a job we finished this week in {{their_neighborhood}}. Want me to text them over?"

  • Day 7: "Quick tip while you're shopping around: always ask for the manufacturer warranty in writing, not just the workmanship warranty. Different things. Happy to explain if useful."
  • Day 14: "Saw a question online about {{common_objection}} — thought I'd share our take: {{short_answer}}. Text back if you want more detail."
  • Day 30: "Hey {{first_name}} — still shopping? We've got a couple install slots opening up in {{month}} if timing matters."
  • Day 45: "Just checking in one more time. Want me to close out your file or keep you posted on availability?"
  • Day 60: "Last one from me — if you went with someone else, no worries at all. If you're still deciding, here's my direct line: {{phone}}." This sequence teaches (Days 7, 14), doesn't just pitch. Performance on a solar client: 12% eventual booking rate on leads that ignored the initial speed-to-lead sequence. That's found money.

How to install these sequences without tanking your delivery rates

Copy-paste is step one. Deliverability is step two, and it's where most operators self-sabotage. Non-negotiable setup checklist: 1. Register A2P 10DLC. In GoHighLevel, this is under Settings → Phone Numbers. Unregistered = filtered. Budget 1-2 weeks for approval. 2. Use a local area code number matching your service area. Toll-free numbers convert 30-40% worse for local businesses. 3. Include opt-out language on the first message of any marketing sequence. "Reply STOP to opt out." Nurture and transactional messages don't require it on every send, but marketing broadcasts do. 4. Warm the number. Don't send 500 texts on day one from a brand new number. Ramp: 50 day one, 100 day two, 200 day three, then scale. 5. Monitor reply rates weekly. If any sequence drops below 8% reply rate, the copy is broken. Rewrite Message 1. 6. Set quiet hours. No sends before 9am or after 8pm local time. GHL has this as a workflow setting — use it. TCPA violations are $500-$1,500 per text. One last thing: personalize the sender name in Message 1 of every sequence. "It's Mike from Apex Roofing" outperforms "Apex Roofing here" by roughly 40% on reply rate in every A/B test we've run. People reply to people.

The bottom line

SMS is the highest-converting owned channel most local businesses have access to, and it's underused because operators treat it like email. The seven sequences above work because they sound like texts a human would send — short, direct, inviting a reply — not because of any clever automation trick. Pick the two sequences that map to your biggest revenue leak (usually speed-to-lead and no-show recovery), build them in GoHighLevel this week, and measure reply rate as your primary KPI. Not opens, not delivery — replies. Replies are the leading indicator of booked revenue. If Message 1 of any sequence isn't pulling 10%+ replies within 30 days, rewrite it before you build the next one.

faq.question: How many texts can I send before people start opting out?
faq.answer: Healthy STOP rates run under 2% per sequence. If you're above that, your copy is too salesy or your frequency is too high. Cap marketing sends at 2-3 per week per contact and keep nurture messages conversational rather than promotional.

faq.question: Do I need TCPA consent for these sequences?
faq.answer: Yes for anything marketing-related. Consent is captured at form opt-in — your form needs clear language like "By submitting, you agree to receive texts from [business] at the number provided." Transactional messages (appointment confirmations, service updates) have looser rules but same-day consent is still best practice.

faq.question: What's a realistic reply rate for a well-written SMS drip?
faq.answer: 10-15% reply rate on Message 1 of a nurture sequence is solid. 25-35% is exceptional and usually indicates strong offer-market fit. Below 8% means the copy reads like marketing — rewrite it to sound like a text from the business owner.

faq.question: Should I use SMS or MMS for these sequences?
faq.answer: SMS for 95% of use cases. MMS (with an image) makes sense for review requests with a screenshot of the review page, or for showing a before/after photo in a long-nurture drip. MMS costs 3-4x more per send and doesn't move conversion enough to justify it in most sequences.

faq.question: Can I run these same sequences on WhatsApp or iMessage instead?
faq.answer: WhatsApp works well internationally but has strict template approval for outbound. iMessage for Business (Apple Messages for Business) requires enterprise setup and isn't practical for most local businesses. Stick with SMS via a properly registered 10DLC number for domestic US and Canadian audiences.

articles.title: Exclusive Leads vs Shared Leads for Contractors: The Real Math
articles.description: The actual close-rate and CAC math on HomeAdvisor shared leads vs your own exclusive funnel — plus the exact break-even spend to run in-house.
articles.keyword: exclusive leads vs shared leads for contractors
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Here's the uncomfortable truth most contractors won't say out loud: if you're closing 4-6% of your HomeAdvisor leads, you're not running a business — you're subsidizing Angi's stock price. And if you think switching to "exclusive leads" from a third-party vendor fixes it, you're about to pay 3x the price for a lead that still isn't really yours. This breakdown is for remodeling, roofing, HVAC, and solar contractors doing $500K-$10M in revenue who are tired of guessing which lead channel actually prints money. We're going to run the real close-rate math, side by side, at real market prices. By the end, you'll know the exact monthly ad spend where an owned exclusive funnel beats shared leads — and when it doesn't.

What "shared" and "exclusive" actually mean in 2026

Let's kill the marketing language first. Shared leads are what HomeAdvisor, Angi, Thumbtack, Networx, and Modernize sell you. A single homeowner form-fill gets resold to 3-5 contractors simultaneously. You're racing four other guys to the phone, and the homeowner already knows they'll get spammed for a week. Exclusive leads come in two flavors, and this is where contractors get burned: - Vendor-exclusive: A third party (CraftJack, Service Direct, some Angi Ads tiers) runs ads, then sells the lead to only you. Price: $80-$400 depending on trade. You don't own the ad account, the pixel data, or the audience.

  • Owned exclusive: You run your own Meta and Google ads into your own funnel (GoHighLevel, HubSpot, or a custom site). The lead hits your CRM in under 60 seconds. Nobody else gets it, ever. The difference between vendor-exclusive and owned-exclusive is roughly the difference between renting and owning a house. Both put a roof over your head. Only one builds equity.

The real close-rate math on HomeAdvisor shared leads

I've audited close rates across 40+ contractor accounts. Here's the honest distribution on HomeAdvisor/Angi shared leads: - Top 10% of operators: 8-12% close rate

  • Median: 4-6%
  • Bottom half: 1-3% Let's model a median roofing contractor buying 100 shared leads/month at $65 average CPL: - Spend: $6,500
  • Contacts made: ~55 (roughly 45% ghost you or were fake)
  • Appointments set: ~18
  • Sits: ~11
  • Sales: 5 (at 5% close on total leads)
  • Average ticket: $12,000
  • Revenue: $60,000
  • Cost per acquisition: $1,300
  • Ad-cost-to-revenue ratio: 10.8% On paper, that looks fine. But we haven't counted the credits you'll fight for (budget on 15% of leads being disputed), the sales rep hours burned on unqualified junk, or the fact that your Google reviews get hammered when you can't respond in 90 seconds. Real, fully-loaded CAC on shared leads is closer to $1,600-$1,900.

The real close-rate math on an owned exclusive funnel

Now the same roofer runs their own Meta + Google Local Services setup. Here's what a competently-built funnel produces in most metros: - Meta CPL (lead-form or landing page): $22-$55 for storm/roof niches

  • Google LSA CPL: $45-$95, but pre-qualified
  • Blended CPL: ~$40 Because the lead is exclusive and hits your CRM in under 60 seconds via a webhook to GoHighLevel or HubSpot, speed-to-lead crushes the shared-lead economics: - 100 leads at $40 blended = $4,000 spend
  • Contact rate: ~75% (you're first, not fifth)
  • Appointments: ~35
  • Sits: ~22
  • Sales: 11 (11% close rate — realistic when you're not competing on the same call)
  • Revenue: $132,000
  • CAC: $364
  • Ad-cost-to-revenue ratio: 3% Even if you cut those numbers by 30% for a first-90-days ramp, the owned funnel still lands around $520 CAC. That's 3-4x better than shared. The catch? You need infrastructure, and there's a break-even point below which it doesn't work.

The break-even spend where owned exclusive beats shared

Here's where most "just run your own ads" advice falls apart. An owned funnel has fixed costs that shared leads don't: - Meta/Google management (agency or in-house media buyer): $2,000-$5,000/mo

  • CRM + automation stack (GoHighLevel, Twilio, Calendly): $300-$600/mo
  • Landing page + creative refresh: $500-$1,500/mo amortized
  • Call tracking (CallRail): $75-$300/mo Fully loaded, you need roughly $3,500-$6,500/mo in overhead before a dollar of ad spend. Run the math: at $40 CPL and 11% close, every $1,000 in ad spend produces roughly $33,000 in revenue at $12K ticket. But you need to clear the fixed nut first. Break-even ad spend vs. buying shared leads: - Below $3,000/mo in ad spend: stay on shared leads. Overhead eats the margin.
  • $3,000-$6,000/mo: hybrid — run owned ads for high-intent keywords, backfill with shared leads.
  • $6,000+/mo in ad spend: go fully owned. This is where the CAC gap becomes real money — usually $40K-$80K/mo in saved acquisition cost at scale. If you're spending under $3K/mo on marketing total, HomeAdvisor is genuinely the right answer. Above $10K/mo total marketing budget, staying on shared leads is malpractice.

Why speed-to-lead is the whole game

The single biggest variable in shared vs exclusive isn't the lead source — it's response time. MIT and InsideSales data on 15,000 leads showed contacting inside 5 minutes makes you 21x more likely to qualify the lead than waiting 30 minutes. Most contractors respond to HomeAdvisor leads in 8-45 minutes. By then, three competitors already called. On an owned funnel with proper automation, you can hit these numbers: 1. Lead submits form → webhook fires to GoHighLevel in <2 seconds 2. Automated SMS + email sends in <10 seconds ("Hey [name], this is Mike with [company] — got your roof inquiry, calling you in 60 seconds") 3. Round-robin call assignment triggers rep's phone 4. If no answer in 5 minutes, auto-voicemail drop + second SMS 5. Booking link (Calendly or GHL native) embedded in every message This stack is what turns an 11% close rate into a 14-16% close rate. Contractors who won't build this infrastructure should stay on shared leads — because without speed-to-lead automation, exclusive leads perform barely better than shared.

The hidden cost of not owning your pixel data

Here's the argument nobody makes for owned exclusive that matters most at scale: audience data compounds. When HomeAdvisor sells you a lead, they keep the pixel data. Every roof-quote form-fill trains their Meta and Google algorithms, not yours. After 12 months of buying shared leads, you have zero owned audience assets. Run your own Meta Ads Manager account for 12 months, and you'll have: - 5,000-20,000 pixeled website visitors for retargeting

  • 500-2,000 form-fills as a custom audience (and their lookalikes at 1%, 2%, 3%)
  • Email/SMS list of every past lead for reactivation campaigns
  • CAC that drops 20-40% in year two purely from algorithmic learning I've watched roofing companies go from $85 CPL in month 3 to $32 CPL in month 14 on the same ad spend — because the pixel finally knew who to target. Shared leads never give you that curve. You pay the same $65 per lead in year five as you did in year one, and if Angi raises prices 15%, you eat it.

The hybrid model that actually works for most contractors

For most contractors doing $1M-$4M in revenue, the correct answer is not "pick one." It's a portfolio: 60% owned exclusive (Meta + Google LSA into GoHighLevel): This is your growth engine. Predictable CAC, compounding data. 25% Google LSA + SEO: Highest intent, lowest CAC once ranked. Slow to build but nearly free at maturity. 15% shared leads (Angi/HomeAdvisor): Use these as fill-in volume during slow weeks and as training reps for junior salespeople. Don't build the business on them. Set hard rules: - Cap shared-lead spend at 15% of marketing budget

  • Track CAC by source weekly in a single dashboard (Google Sheets is fine; don't overcomplicate)
  • Kill any channel where fully-loaded CAC exceeds 15% of average ticket for two consecutive months
  • Reinvest 100% of savings from lower CAC into more owned ad spend, not overhead The operators who win in this market aren't the ones with the biggest ad budgets — they're the ones who know their CAC by source to the dollar and reallocate ruthlessly every 30 days.

The bottom line

Shared leads aren't inherently bad — they're a cash-flow product for contractors who can't yet afford the infrastructure of an owned funnel. But if you're spending more than $6K/month on lead generation and still buying primarily shared leads, you're leaving $30K-$80K/month in acquisition savings on the table, plus giving away audience data that compounds against you every quarter. Run your own break-even math this week. Pull your last 90 days of HomeAdvisor spend, calculate your true CAC (including credits, ghosted leads, and sales rep hours), and compare it to what a $40 blended CPL at 11% close would produce at your average ticket. If the gap is more than $500 per acquisition, you already have your answer — build the owned funnel.

faq.question: How many HomeAdvisor leads do I need to close to break even?
faq.answer: At a $65 average CPL and $12K average ticket with typical 30-35% gross margins, you need to close roughly 1 in 20 leads (5%) just to break even on the lead cost alone — before overhead, labor, or credits. Anything below a 5% close rate on shared leads is losing money.

faq.question: Are exclusive leads from vendors like CraftJack or Service Direct worth it?
faq.answer: Better than shared, worse than owned. Vendor-exclusive leads typically run $150-$400 and close at 12-18%, so the math often works. But you're renting the pipeline — the vendor owns the pixel data, the ad account, and can raise prices or drop you at will. Use them as a bridge while you build an owned funnel, not a permanent solution.

faq.question: What's the minimum monthly budget to run my own exclusive lead funnel?
faq.answer: Roughly $6,500/month all-in: $3,500 in ad spend plus $3,000 in management, tech stack, and creative. Below that, fixed costs eat too much of the margin and you'll perform worse than buying shared leads. Above $10K/month total, owned funnels dominate on every metric.

faq.question: How fast do I need to respond to leads to actually close them?
faq.answer: Under 5 minutes, ideally under 60 seconds. Data across 15,000+ B2C leads shows contacting inside 5 minutes makes you 21x more likely to qualify than waiting 30 minutes. Automate SMS and email in your CRM (GoHighLevel or HubSpot) so the first touch fires in under 10 seconds — the human callback should follow inside 2 minutes.

faq.question: Can I run Meta ads for contractor leads myself, or do I need an agency?
faq.answer: You can, but expect a 90-120 day ramp where CPL will be 2-3x higher than a competent agency's. If your time is worth more than $150/hour running the business, hire a specialist. If you have 15+ hours a week and enjoy media buying, learn it yourself — the tools (Meta Ads Manager, GoHighLevel) are accessible.

articles.title: Best Lead Generation Strategy for Solar Companies (Sub-$80 CPL)
articles.description: Door-knocking lists are cooked. Here's the 3-channel paid stack + database reactivation hitting sub-$80 qualified solar leads at scale.
articles.keyword: best lead generation strategy for solar companies
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Solar customer acquisition cost has ballooned to $700-$1,500 per install across most U.S. markets. Meanwhile, the average solar company is still burning payroll on canvassers walking neighborhoods that got hit by three other reps last week. The math stopped working around 2022, and most owners haven't updated the model. This is written for solar company founders and VPs of sales doing $5M-$50M in revenue who need predictable pipeline without adding 20 door-knockers to a bloated org chart. If you're running a lean operation and paying $150-$300 per qualified lead through shared lead vendors, this will hit harder. What you'll get: why the door-knocking + purchased list model is structurally broken, the exact 3-channel paid stack (Meta, YouTube, Google LSA) plus database reactivation sequence we're using to pull qualified solar leads under $80, and the KPIs to hold your team accountable to.

Why door-knocking lists and shared leads are structurally broken

The door-knocking model worked when solar was novel and homeowners weren't sick of the pitch. That window closed. Today, the average suburban homeowner in Texas, Florida, Arizona, or California has been hit by 4-7 solar reps in the last 18 months. Your knock rate to appointment is collapsing while labor cost per canvasser has climbed past $22/hour plus commission. Shared lead vendors (think the big aggregators) are worse. Every $75-$150 lead you buy has been sold to 3-5 other companies. Your speed-to-lead has to beat competitors by seconds, and even then your close rate on shared leads sits around 2-4%. Do the math: at $100/lead and 3% close, your CPA is $3,300 before you've paid a single rep. The deeper problem is attribution and control. You can't scale a channel you don't own. Canvassing is capped by headcount. Shared leads are capped by the vendor's supply and your willingness to overpay. Neither compounds. Neither builds a database asset. Neither lets you turn spend up or down based on installer capacity. The fix is owning the top of your funnel through paid channels you control, plus mining the database asset you're already sitting on.

The 3-channel paid stack that's working right now

Sub-$80 qualified solar leads come from a specific combination: Meta Ads for cold demand generation, YouTube for mid-funnel education, and Google Local Services Ads for high-intent capture. Each channel plays a distinct role. Running only one is why most solar companies get mediocre results and blame "Meta doesn't work anymore." Here's the split we recommend for a solar company spending $30K-$100K/month on paid: - Meta Ads (60-65% of budget): Volume driver. Cold traffic, homeowner targeting, utility-bill-focused creative. This is where you generate the top-of-funnel lead volume.

  • YouTube Ads (15-20% of budget): Trust and mid-funnel. In-stream ads targeting homeowners researching solar, energy costs, tax credits. Warms the pixel and lifts Meta performance.
  • Google LSA + Search (20-25% of budget): Bottom-funnel capture. High-intent "solar installer near me" traffic. Expensive per click but converts at 15-25%. The magic isn't any single channel. It's the interaction. YouTube views cheapen your Meta leads. Meta lead volume feeds retargeting pools. Google LSA catches the ready-to-buy homeowner who saw you on Meta three weeks ago. Attribution in Meta Ads Manager will underreport this. Trust the blended CPL, not the platform-reported one.

Meta Ads: the creative and offer that gets under $80 CPL

Meta is where solar campaigns live or die. Two things matter: the offer and the creative angle. Everything else (audiences, placements, bidding) is now largely automated by Advantage+ campaigns and works fine out of the box. Stop running "free solar quote" offers. Everyone runs that. Instead, lead with a utility bill reduction hook tied to a specific state incentive. Examples that are working: - "Texas homeowners: see how much of your electric bill you can eliminate before the 30% federal credit steps down"

  • "Florida homeowners with a $200+ power bill — check if your roof qualifies for $0-down solar"
  • "Your utility just raised rates again. Here's what solar actually costs in [city] this month." Creative format that's winning: UGC-style video, 30-45 seconds, shot vertically. A real homeowner or installer talking to camera about their power bill going from $340 to $12. No stock footage. No drone shots of panels. Founders who spend $2K getting 8-10 UGC ads made monthly are crushing agencies still running static image ads. Use Meta's Instant Forms with 4 qualifying questions: homeowner status, monthly electric bill ($150+ minimum), roof condition, and timeline. Push leads via webhook straight into GoHighLevel or HubSpot. Speed-to-lead under 5 minutes should be non-negotiable — text and call within 90 seconds if you can automate it.

YouTube and Google LSA: the trust and intent layer

YouTube is the most underused channel in solar. In-stream ads (the ones before videos) run at $0.03-$0.08 per view. You're paying pennies to put a 2-minute educational video in front of homeowners actively researching solar, tax credits, or energy costs. It doesn't generate a ton of direct-response leads, but it does two things that matter: it lifts Meta conversion rates by 20-40% and it builds a retargeting pool of warm viewers. Build one core YouTube asset: a 90-second to 3-minute video that explains how solar actually works financially in your state — federal credit, state incentive, net metering rules, real numbers. Not a pitch. Education. Then run it as an in-stream ad targeting homeowners in your service area with custom intent audiences built from search terms like "solar cost," "solar tax credit 2026," and competitor names. Google Local Services Ads (LSA) is the other must-have. It's pay-per-lead, sits above regular search results, and captures the highest-intent traffic in your market. Expect $60-$120 per LSA lead but close rates of 20-30% because these people are ready. You need Google verification, real reviews (aim for 50+ at 4.7+ stars), and fast response to every ping. Miss a lead call and Google demotes you. Run standard Google Search alongside LSA for keyword coverage LSA doesn't fill — brand terms, long-tail like "solar installer [neighborhood]," and competitor conquest.

Database reactivation: the free channel every solar company ignores

Here's the play that costs almost nothing and pulls 15-40 appointments in the first 14 days for most solar companies: reactivate every unclosed lead from the last 24 months. If you've been in business more than two years, you're sitting on 2,000-20,000 old leads. Most of them said "not right now," "my roof needs work first," "waiting on tax return," or ghosted. Circumstances have changed for a huge chunk of them. Utility rates went up. The federal tax credit timeline shifted. They finally replaced the roof. They're ready — they just haven't heard from you in 8 months. The sequence, built in GoHighLevel or HubSpot: 1. SMS 1 (Day 1): "Hey [name], it's [rep] with [company]. — utility rates in [city] jumped again. Still interested in a quick check on what solar would cost you now? Reply YES or NO." 2. SMS 2 (Day 3, to non-responders): "Quick one — federal credit is still 30% but that steps down. Worth 60 seconds to see updated numbers?" 3. Email (Day 5): Case study of a similar homeowner with specific savings numbers. 4. Voicemail drop (Day 7): Ringless voicemail from the owner or lead rep. 5. Final SMS (Day 12): Break-up message with a soft opt-out. Expected numbers on a 5,000-record list: 8-15% reply rate, 3-5% appointment rate, 150-250 appointments booked. Cost: your SMS spend (about $0.015 per message) and the tech stack. Effective CPL: $5-$15. This should run quarterly, not once.

The tech stack and speed-to-lead that makes this work

None of this stack works without infrastructure. Leads coming in from four sources need to hit one place, get scored, and get contacted in under 5 minutes. Here's the minimum viable stack: - CRM: GoHighLevel (best for solar/home services under $10M) or HubSpot (better if you're scaling past $20M and need real reporting). Salesforce is overkill unless you're running a 100+ rep operation.

  • Lead routing: Zapier or native webhooks from Meta, Google, and website forms into the CRM. Every lead source tagged clearly.
  • Speed-to-lead automation: Instant SMS on lead submission ("Hey [name], [rep] here — got your info about solar. Can I call you now or in 10 min?"), auto-dial trigger to the assigned rep's phone, fallback to team if unanswered in 60 seconds.
  • Appointment booking: Calendly or GoHighLevel's native calendar embedded in follow-up SMS.
  • Reporting: A single dashboard showing CPL by source, appointment set rate, appointment show rate, close rate, and revenue per lead. Update weekly. The biggest leak in most solar operations isn't lead volume — it's speed and follow-up. Leads contacted in 5 minutes vs. 30 minutes close at 21x the rate (MIT study, still holds). If your reps aren't hitting new leads within 5 minutes 90%+ of the time, no ad strategy fixes that.

KPIs and benchmarks to hold your team accountable to

You can't manage what you don't measure, and "we got a lot of leads this month" isn't a KPI. Here's what to track weekly on a solar paid + reactivation program running at $30K-$100K/month: - Cost per lead (blended): Target $60-$90 for qualified leads (homeowner, $150+ bill, decision-maker).

  • Lead-to-appointment set rate: 25-40% is healthy. Under 20% means your qualification is broken or speed-to-lead is slow.
  • Appointment show rate: 55-70%. Under 50%, your confirmation sequence is weak.
  • Show-to-close rate: 20-35% on Meta leads, 25-40% on LSA, 15-25% on reactivation.
  • Cost per acquisition (installed customer): $600-$1,200 in most markets. Above $1,500 and the model needs work.
  • Speed-to-first-contact: Median under 5 minutes, 90th percentile under 15 minutes. Review these on a weekly ops call, not monthly. Kill campaigns where CPL is 40%+ above target for 7 days. Double budget on campaigns hitting target with volume headroom. Most solar companies are afraid to scale spend fast enough — if a campaign is producing $70 leads that close, pour on the gas until it breaks. Then diagnose and rebuild.

The bottom line

The best lead generation strategy for solar companies isn't a single tactic — it's a stack. Meta for volume, YouTube for trust, Google LSA for intent, and database reactivation for the free money you're already sitting on. Built correctly with fast follow-up and clean attribution, this consistently produces qualified leads under $80 and installed customers under $1,200 in most U.S. markets. The operators winning in solar right now aren't the ones with the biggest canvassing teams. They're the ones who built a paid acquisition machine, own their database, and treat speed-to-lead like a religion. If you're still running the 2019 playbook, you're not just leaving money on the table — you're funding your competitors' scale.

faq.question: How much should a solar company spend on ads per month to see results?
faq.answer: Minimum $15K/month to get statistically meaningful data across Meta, YouTube, and Google LSA. Under that, you're guessing. Companies serious about scaling typically run $30K-$100K/month and see CPLs drop as the pixel matures and creative library expands.

faq.question: How long until a paid solar lead gen program hits sub-$80 CPL?
faq.answer: Expect 30-60 days of learning. Weeks 1-3 you'll see $120-$180 CPLs as Meta's algorithm learns. By week 6-8 with 8-12 creative variations tested and audiences optimized, sub-$80 is realistic in most markets. Slower in ultra-competitive metros like Los Angeles or Phoenix.

faq.question: Is door-knocking completely dead for solar?
faq.answer: No, but it should be a supplement, not the core strategy. Door-knocking still works for finishing deals on homes near an active install or in targeted HOAs. As a primary lead source, the unit economics no longer pencil out for most markets.

faq.question: Should I use a solar-specific lead vendor or run my own ads?
faq.answer: Run your own ads. Shared lead vendors sell the same lead 3-5 times and your close rate collapses. Exclusive lead vendors charge $200-$400 per lead with no control over volume or quality. Owned paid channels give you control, better economics at scale, and a compounding database asset.

faq.question: What's a realistic close rate on Meta solar leads?
faq.answer: 8-15% lead-to-installed-customer for well-run operations. Broken down: 30% lead-to-appointment-set, 60% appointment-show, 25% show-to-close. If you're under 5% overall, the problem is almost always speed-to-lead, qualification questions, or sales process — not the ads.

articles.title: Google Local Services Ads vs Google Ads for Contractors: CPBJ Breakdown
articles.description: LSAs vs Google Search Ads for contractors: real cost-per-booked-job math, when each wins, and the stacked setup that prints jobs.
articles.keyword: google local services ads vs google ads for contractors
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most contractors running paid media are lighting money on fire in one of two ways: they're all-in on Google Ads with a $180 cost-per-lead and a 22% booking rate, or they're relying solely on Local Services Ads (LSAs) and capping growth the moment Google throttles their impressions. Both are wrong. The right answer depends on your service, your ticket size, and your close rate — and once you know the math, running both stacked is almost always the winner. This is for HVAC, roofing, plumbing, electrical, remodeling, and home services operators doing $500K–$20M who want to stop guessing which channel deserves the next $10K. We're going to break down cost-per-booked-job (CPBJ) on both channels using real ranges, show you the exact scenarios where LSAs crush Search and vice versa, and give you a stacking playbook that pushes blended CPBJ down 30–50%. By the end, you'll know which channel to fund first, what to expect per dollar, and how to structure both accounts so they feed each other instead of bidding against themselves.

The only metric that matters: cost-per-booked-job

Forget CPC. Forget CPL. If you're a contractor, the metric that pays your payroll is cost-per-booked-job (CPBJ) — total ad spend divided by jobs that actually got on the schedule and paid. Here's why lead-level metrics lie: LSAs and Google Search Ads have wildly different lead qualities. An LSA lead is a phone call from someone who tapped your Google profile after seeing reviews and a green checkmark. A Search Ad lead is often a form fill from someone comparing five contractors. Book rates diverge by 2-3x. Quick math to run on your own data: - Google Ads CPBJ: Spend ÷ (Leads × Book Rate). Example: $6,000 spend, 40 leads, 25% book rate = 10 jobs = $600 CPBJ.

  • LSAs CPBJ: Spend ÷ Booked Jobs (dispute unqualified leads to lower spend). Example: $6,000 spend, 35 valid leads, 55% book rate = 19 jobs = $316 CPBJ. Before you compare channels, tag every lead source in your CRM (ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro, Jobber, or GoHighLevel) and calculate CPBJ monthly. If you can't do this, you're not ready to scale either channel — fix tracking first.

How Google Local Services Ads actually work

LSAs sit at the very top of the search results, above traditional Google Ads. You pay per lead (call or message), not per click. To run them, you must pass Google's screening: license verification, insurance, and background checks for owners and field techs. That gate is why LSAs convert — searchers trust the Google Guaranteed badge. Key mechanics contractors miss: - Lead price varies by trade and market: HVAC leads run $25–$75, roofing $35–$120, plumbing $20–$60, remodeling $50–$200. Your bid strategy (max per lead vs max spend) affects volume more than most realize.

  • Reviews drive ranking harder than bid: An account with 80+ 5-star Google reviews at 4.9 stars will out-rank a higher bidder with 20 reviews. Job one is a review engine (NiceJob, Podium, or a GoHighLevel automation firing 30 min post-close).
  • You can dispute bad leads: Wrong service area, spam, wrong service — Google refunds them, often 8–15% of leads. Contractors who don't dispute are overpaying by that same margin.
  • Response time matters: Google measures pickup rate. Miss calls, your ranking tanks. Route to a live answering service (Nexa, Ruby) if you can't hit 90%+. LSAs are pay-per-lead, but the lead is warmer, the intent is higher, and the trust signal is already built in before your phone rings.

How Google Search Ads work for contractors (and where they leak money)

Traditional Google Search Ads (the sponsored results below LSAs) are pay-per-click. You bid on keywords, write ad copy, drive to a landing page, and hope the form fills or call comes in. On paper, more control. In practice, more leaks. Where contractors bleed money on Search: 1. Broad match with no negatives: Bidding on "AC repair" without excluding "DIY," "parts," "how to," "jobs" burns 20–40% of spend on non-buyers. 2. Sending traffic to the homepage: Homepages convert at 2–4%. A dedicated service-page landing (built in Unbounce, Instapage, or a GoHighLevel funnel) with call button above the fold, reviews, and a single offer converts at 8–15%. 3. No call tracking: If you're not using CallRail or CallTrackingMetrics with dynamic number insertion, you can't tell which keyword produced the booked job. You're optimizing blind. 4. Ignoring device split: 70%+ of contractor searches are mobile. Desktop-heavy landing pages tank conversion. Benchmarks I see across HVAC, roofing, and plumbing accounts: CPC $8–$28, conversion rate 8–14% on a proper landing page, book rate 20–35% from Search leads (lower than LSAs because the searcher hasn't seen your reviews yet). Blended, that's a CPBJ of $450–$900 for a well-run account, $1,200+ for a sloppy one.

Side-by-side CPBJ breakdown: LSAs vs Google Ads

Here's what the math actually looks like for a mid-sized HVAC contractor spending $10K/month on each channel in a Tier 2 metro: Local Services Ads

  • Spend: $10,000
  • Leads at $45 avg: 222
  • Disputed/refunded (12%): -27 leads
  • Valid leads: 195
  • Book rate: 50%
  • Booked jobs: 97
  • CPBJ: $103 Google Search Ads
  • Spend: $10,000
  • Clicks at $14 avg CPC: 714
  • Conversion rate (calls + forms): 11%
  • Leads: 78
  • Book rate: 28%
  • Booked jobs: 22
  • CPBJ: $455 At first glance, LSAs demolish Search — 4.4x more efficient. But this is where operators make the wrong call. LSAs will cap out in your market. Google only shows 3 LSA slots and rotates a limited pool. Once you've captured your available share (usually $8K–$25K/month depending on metro and trade), incremental spend does nothing. Search Ads, by contrast, scale further. And Search wins on specific job types: high-ticket remodels, commercial work, and niche services where the searcher wants to read a page before calling. LSAs dominate emergency and same-day trades (burst pipe, no heat, roof leak). Search wins on considered purchases (kitchen remodel, roof replacement, panel upgrade). The rule of thumb: LSAs first, Search second, always both eventually.

When LSAs win outright

Fund LSAs before touching Search if you match any of these: - Emergency/same-day service dominant: Plumbing leaks, HVAC no-cool/no-heat, garage door won't open, locksmith. Intent is 10/10 and searchers call the first credible option. LSAs are that option.

  • Average ticket under $2,000: Service calls, tune-ups, small repairs. Search CPBJ eats the margin. LSAs at $80–$150 CPBJ leave room.
  • Strong review profile: 50+ Google reviews at 4.7+. You'll dominate the LSA carousel and pull leads below the market average cost.
  • Small team, limited landing page infrastructure: LSAs don't need a website funnel. Your Google Business Profile IS the landing page.
  • New to paid media: LSAs are lower-skill to run well. You dispute bad leads, keep response time high, ask for reviews. Search Ads punish beginners. I've onboarded roofing and plumbing clients where we pushed LSA spend to $18K/month before touching Google Ads and hit CPBJ under $150. If your market has room and your reviews are strong, exhaust LSAs first. It's the cheapest booked job you'll ever buy.

When Google Search Ads win outright

There are real scenarios where Search beats LSAs on booked-job economics: - High-ticket, considered purchases: Full roof replacements ($15K–$40K), kitchen remodels ($40K–$150K), whole-home HVAC installs ($10K–$25K). Searchers compare, read, and want detail. A well-built landing page with financing, before/after gallery, and free estimate form converts better than a phone call from LSAs.

  • Commercial work: LSAs are largely residential. B2B searches for "commercial HVAC contractor" or "industrial roofing" belong on Search.
  • Niche services LSAs don't categorize well: Foundation repair, EV charger installation, spray foam insulation, custom pool builds. LSAs force you into broad buckets that misroute leads.
  • Geographic edge markets: If your service area has weak LSA competition data or you serve a wide radius, Search gives you targeting control LSAs can't match.
  • You have a real content and landing page operation: If you have a marketing team running CRO, using Hotjar, iterating headlines monthly — Search rewards that skill. If your average job is $10K+ and you sell on consultation rather than dispatch, Search Ads plus a proper funnel (landing page → phone call or booked estimate via Calendly) will outperform LSAs on revenue per ad dollar even at higher CPBJ.

The stacked playbook: running LSAs and Google Ads together

This is where most contractors leave 30–50% CPBJ reduction on the table. Running both channels correctly stacked creates compounding effects. Here's the setup: 1. Max out LSAs first. Bid to max leads, dispute aggressively, drive review velocity. Establish your CPBJ floor. 2. Add Search Ads targeting only what LSAs can't cover: high-ticket keywords ("roof replacement quote," "new HVAC system cost"), commercial terms, and specific service lines LSAs miscategorize. 3. Use Search Ads for brand defense: Bid on your own brand name. Cheap clicks, blocks competitors, and captures searchers who saw you in LSAs and Googled you to verify. 4. Layer remarketing on Search Ads: Anyone who visited your site but didn't call gets served display and YouTube ads for 30 days. Cheap way to close the loop on LSA callers who didn't book. 5. Feed the CRM back into both: Push offline conversions from ServiceTitan or GoHighLevel back into Google Ads so Smart Bidding optimizes for booked jobs, not form fills. 6. Split budget by CPBJ, not gut: If LSA CPBJ is $120 and Search CPBJ is $480, don't split 50/50. Fund LSAs to saturation, then Search. A stacked account I manage in the roofing space runs 60% LSA / 40% Search and delivers a blended CPBJ of $210 on $40K/month spend. Neither channel could hit that alone.

How to decide this week: a simple decision tree

Stop debating in theory. Run this checklist against your business: Start with LSAs only if:

  • You have 25+ Google reviews at 4.5 stars or better
  • Your average ticket is under $5,000
  • You can answer 90%+ of calls in business hours
  • Your service is dispatch/emergency-oriented Start with Google Search Ads only if:
  • Your average ticket is $10K+ and sells on consultation
  • You have a dedicated landing page (not your homepage)
  • You have call tracking installed (CallRail minimum)
  • You have someone competent running the account (in-house or agency) Run both stacked once:
  • LSA spend has plateaued (adding budget doesn't add leads)
  • You're booking 15+ jobs/month from LSAs
  • You have a CRM tracking source-to-revenue
  • Your close/booking process is documented and consistent If you can't check the boxes for either channel, the answer isn't more ad spend — it's fixing tracking, reviews, and response speed first. Ads amplify what already exists. If the underlying operation leaks, ads leak faster.

The bottom line

LSAs and Google Search Ads aren't competing products — they're different tools for different jobs. LSAs win on efficiency and simplicity, especially for emergency, low-to-mid ticket residential work with a strong review base. Search wins on scale, control, and high-ticket considered purchases. Run LSAs first if you qualify, layer Search on top once LSAs plateau, and measure everything at the cost-per-booked-job level — not the click or lead level. The contractors printing money on Google in 2026 aren't picking a side. They're stacking both channels, feeding CRM data back into the algorithms, and killing waste weekly. Pull your last 90 days of ad spend, calculate CPBJ by channel, and if you can't — that's the first fix before another dollar goes into either account.

faq.question: Can I run LSAs and Google Ads at the same time without them bidding against each other?
faq.answer: Yes. LSAs and Google Search Ads occupy separate ad slots and don't compete in the same auction. Running both actually increases your share of the SERP — you can occupy the LSA carousel AND a top Search Ad position simultaneously, which lifts total click share.

faq.question: How much should a contractor spend on LSAs to know if they work?
faq.answer: Give it 30 days at a minimum of $2,000–$3,000 in spend, assuming you're actively disputing bad leads and requesting reviews. Anything shorter or cheaper doesn't give Google's algorithm enough signal to rank you consistently.

faq.question: Why is my LSA cost-per-lead so much higher than the estimates I see online?
faq.answer: Three usual culprits: weak review profile (under 30 reviews or below 4.5 stars), slow call response tanking your ranking, and not disputing invalid leads. Fix those three and your effective cost-per-lead usually drops 20–40% within 60 days.

faq.question: Should I hire an agency for LSAs or run them in-house?
faq.answer: LSAs are simple enough to run in-house if you have someone dedicated to disputing leads weekly, monitoring response times, and driving review velocity. Google Search Ads are where an experienced agency earns their fee — the technical bar is much higher.

faq.question: Do LSAs work for commercial contractors?
faq.answer: Generally no. LSAs are built around residential service categories and consumer searchers. Commercial contractors get better results from Google Search Ads targeting B2B keywords, paired with LinkedIn Ads for larger accounts.

articles.title: How to Get Clients for a Marketing Agency Without Buying Leads
articles.description: The outbound, authority, and referral system that fills a marketing agency pipeline with qualified clients — no bought leads, no cold spam, no gimmicks.
articles.keyword: how to get clients for a marketing agency
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most agency owners have the same broken pipeline: a referral trickle, a dead LinkedIn, and a Google Ads account that hemorrhages cash trying to compete with HubSpot for "marketing agency near me." Then they buy a $2,000 lead list, blast it, get flagged, and blame the market. Here's the reality: the agencies pulling in $50K-$300K/month in new MRR aren't buying leads. They're running a three-lane system — targeted outbound, compounding authority content, and an engineered referral loop — that produces booked calls on demand. No paid lists. No SDR sweatshops. No praying to the algorithm. This is for founders and growth leads at agencies doing $20K-$500K/month who want to stop guessing where next month's clients come from. Below is the exact playbook: the ICP work, the outbound stack, the authority engine, and the referral mechanics that fill a pipeline in 60-90 days.

Why buying leads is the slowest path to a full pipeline

Purchased lead lists convert at 0.1-0.5% on cold email, and that's before you account for domain damage, spam complaints, and the fact that everyone else on that list is being pitched the same week. You're paying to fight in a red ocean. The math doesn't work. A $2,000 list of 5,000 contacts generating 5 booked calls at a 20% close rate on $3K/month retainers means you spent $2,000 plus 40 hours of SDR time to land $9K in ARR. Meanwhile your sender reputation is now cooked and your next campaign performs worse. What actually works is narrow. Pick a vertical (med spas, commercial roofers, SaaS Series A, personal injury law — pick one), build a list of 200-500 companies that match a tight ICP, and run multi-channel outreach where every touch references something specific about their business. This is the opposite of scale-first. It's precision-first, then scale what converts. Agencies that win in 2026 treat lead generation like media buying: tight targeting, controlled variables, ruthless attribution. If you can't tell me the CAC and LTV of a client acquired via cold LinkedIn versus a podcast guest spot, you're not running a pipeline — you're running a lottery.

Nail the ICP before you send a single message

The number one reason agencies can't get clients is that their ICP is "businesses that need marketing." That's not a market, it's a demographic. You need a wedge sharp enough to make prospects say "they clearly work with people like me." Build your ICP using five filters: 1. Vertical — one industry, not three. Med spas doing $1M-$5M/year, not "healthcare." 2. Revenue band — companies too small can't pay; too big have in-house teams. Sweet spot is usually $1M-$20M. 3. Trigger event — new funding round, new marketing hire, recent expansion, Meta ad launch. Use Apollo, Crunchbase, LinkedIn Sales Navigator, or Ocoya to detect these. 4. Tech stack signal — running Klaviyo but no SMS? Using Shopify but no post-purchase flow? These are wedges. 5. Geography — local proof beats global promises. "We work with 12 med spas in Texas" outperforms "we work with businesses nationwide." Run this filter through Apollo or Clay and you'll get a list of 300-800 companies where your pitch is unavoidable. When your ICP is this tight, your case studies, ad creative, LinkedIn posts, and cold emails all reinforce each other. That compounding relevance is what breaks through in a saturated market.

Build the outbound engine: cold email, LinkedIn, and video

Outbound is the fastest lane to booked calls when done right. Cheap and lazy outbound is what killed the channel's reputation — smart outbound still converts at 3-8% reply rates and 1-2% booked call rates on well-targeted lists. Stack we recommend: - Instantly.ai or Smartlead for cold email infrastructure (multiple sending domains, warmup, deliverability monitoring)

  • Clay for enrichment and personalization at scale
  • Apollo or LinkedIn Sales Navigator for list building
  • Loom or Vidyard for personalized video touches
  • HeyReach or Expandi for LinkedIn automation (use sparingly) Run a four-touch sequence over 12-14 days: personalized email referencing a specific observation about their business, LinkedIn connection with a one-line note, a Loom teardown of their current funnel or ad account, then a break-up email. Never pitch in touch one. Lead with a specific insight — "your Meta ads are running to a homepage, not a landing page" — and let curiosity do the selling. Budget 8-15 sending domains, 30-50 mailboxes, and send no more than 20-30 emails per mailbox per day. Warm every domain for 3 weeks before use. Monitor bounces obsessively — anything above 3% and you pause. This isn't optional infrastructure; this is the difference between $0 pipeline and $80K/month booked.

Turn authority content into an inbound flywheel

Outbound gets you calls this month. Authority content gets you calls forever. The agencies with the best inbound aren't posting motivational quotes on LinkedIn — they're publishing specific, opinionated teardowns that make ICP prospects self-identify. The three-format authority stack: 1. LinkedIn posts, 4-5x per week. Founder account, not company page. Post specific numbers, client wins, opinionated takes on industry norms. Aim for 500-1,500 impressions minimum per post; anything under 200 means your positioning is off. 2. Long-form teardowns. Publish 1-2 detailed audits per month on your blog and YouTube — pick a real company in your ICP, tear down their funnel, publish it. This is the highest-leverage content in agency growth. Prospects who watch a 15-minute teardown of a competitor come in pre-sold. 3. Podcast guest spots. Book 2-4 podcast appearances per month on shows your ICP actually listens to. Use Podmatch or a manual outreach VA. One good guest spot on a 5K-download show outperforms three months of your own content. Repurpose everything with tools like Opus Clip and Descript. One 45-minute podcast becomes 12 LinkedIn posts, 6 shorts, a blog post, and an email newsletter. The goal is that when your outbound hits an ICP prospect's inbox, they Google you and find 40 pieces of relevant content within 60 seconds.

Engineer referrals instead of hoping for them

Every agency owner says "most of our business comes from referrals." Almost none of them have a referral system — they have referral luck. The fix is making referrals a designed process, not an accident. Four mechanics to install: - The 90-day check-in. At month three of every client relationship, run a formal review call. If NPS is 8+, ask directly: "Who are two other business owners in your network who should be running these plays?" Give them a Loom-recorded intro they can forward.

  • The partner tier. Identify 10-20 non-competing service providers your clients also work with — web developers, fractional CFOs, CRM consultants, PR firms. Set up quarterly co-marketing (joint webinars, guest content, warm intros) with a formal 10-15% referral fee.
  • The client case study loop. Every closed client win becomes a case study asset within 60 days. Publish it, tag the client, and they'll share it — that share reaches other founders in their vertical.
  • The alumni network. Former clients are your best pipeline. Stay in touch quarterly with genuine value (industry benchmarks, intros, event invites), not "just checking in." Track referrals like any other channel in HubSpot or GoHighLevel. If you can't tell me your referral CAC and volume by month, you don't have a referral engine — you have anecdotes.

Systematize sales so booked calls actually close

You can generate 40 booked calls a month and still starve if your close rate is 8%. Most agencies over-invest in demand generation and under-invest in the sales system that converts it.
