They either stack 14 interests, two custom audiences, and a lookalike into one ad set (suffocating delivery), or they go fully broad with no signals and let Meta burn budget on toddlers and retirees. The 2024–2026 reality: Meta's targeting works best when you give it room to learn. Broad targeting (age + gender + country, no interests) often beats narrow stacks for cold acquisition — but only if your creative does the targeting work for you. Diagnostic steps: 1. Check audience size. For lead gen in the US, you want 1M–10M for interest-based and 5M+ for broad. 2. Look at the Audience breakdown by age and gender. If 60% of spend is going to 18–24 year olds and you sell to homeowners, your creative is attracting the wrong avatar. 3. Are you excluding existing leads and customers? Upload your CRM list (HubSpot, GoHighLevel, etc.) as a Custom Audience and exclude it from cold campaigns. The fix: Run a broad audience with sharper creative that calls out your buyer in the first 3 seconds ("Roofing contractors in Texas — read this"). Let the creative filter, not the targeting.

Culprit 3: Your creative is the actual problem (it usually is)

Creative drives 60–70% of paid social performance. If your CTR is below 1% and your CPM is above $40, your creative is the bottleneck — not your targeting, not your bidding. Go into Ads Manager and pull these columns: CTR (link click-through rate), Hook rate (3-sec video views ÷ impressions), Hold rate (ThruPlays ÷ 3-sec views), and Cost per lead. Here's what good looks like for service businesses: - CTR: 1.5%+

  • Hook rate: 25%+
  • Hold rate: 15%+
  • Frequency: under 2.5 in the first 14 days If your hook rate is under 20%, your first 3 seconds are dead. If your CTR is under 1%, your offer or message isn't landing. If hold rate is fine but CTR is low, you've got an offer/CTA problem. What's working in 2026: - Founder-shot UGC with text overlays (not polished brand video)
  • Direct, problem-aware hooks: "If your ads aren't getting leads, it's one of these 7 things"
  • Static images with bold, scroll-stopping copy beat fancy motion graphics for lead gen
  • 4–6 creative variants per ad set, refreshed every 2–3 weeks If you're running the same two ads you launched 60 days ago, that's also why.

Culprit 4: Your offer is forgettable

"Schedule a free consultation" is not an offer. It's a chore. If your CTA asks the prospect to give up 30 minutes of their life for vague value, expect a 0.5% conversion rate. A strong offer makes the next step feel like the prospect is getting away with something. Compare these: - Weak: "Book a free strategy call"

  • Strong: "Get the 14-point Facebook ad audit we use on $50k/mo accounts — free PDF, no call required" - Weak: "Apply for funding"
  • Strong: "See how much you pre-qualify for in 60 seconds. Soft pull, no impact to credit." Offer audit questions: 1. Is the value crystal clear in under 5 seconds?
  1. Is the friction (time, info required, perceived risk) low?
  2. Is there a reason to act now, not later?
  3. Does it match the awareness level of cold traffic? Cold Facebook traffic is problem-aware at best. They aren't ready to talk to sales. Lead magnets, calculators, audits, and quizzes consistently outperform "book a call" CTAs by 3–5x in cost per lead for cold campaigns. Save the call CTA for retargeting.

Culprit 5: Your landing page is leaking leads

You can have a perfect ad and still get zero leads if the landing page is broken. The benchmark for a paid-traffic lead gen landing page is a 15–30% conversion rate. Under 10% and you have a page problem. Plug your URL into PageSpeed Insights first. If mobile load time is over 3 seconds, you're losing 40%+ of clicks before they even see the form. Meta traffic is 90%+ mobile. Common landing page killers: - Form has 7+ fields (cut to name, email, phone, one qualifier)

  • Headline doesn't match the ad's promise (scent break)
  • Video autoplay with sound on
  • Cookie banners and chat widgets blocking the CTA on mobile
  • No social proof above the fold
  • Generic stock photos instead of real outcomes Check your funnel in Google Analytics 4 or GoHighLevel. If 200 people clicked the ad, 180 landed on the page, and only 4 submitted the form, the page is the leak — not the ads. Fast fixes: Match the H1 to the ad headline word-for-word. Cut the form fields in half. Add three customer quotes with photos. Remove every link in the nav. A landing page should have one job and one exit: submit or leave.

Culprit 6: Your follow-up is so slow the leads die

Here's a stat that should hurt: leads contacted within 5 minutes are 100x more likely to convert than leads contacted after 30 minutes (InsideSales / Harvard Business Review). Most service businesses respond in 24–48 hours, if at all. If you're "not getting leads from Facebook ads," check first whether you're getting leads and just losing them. Pull your CRM. Count submissions from the last 30 days. Cross-reference with how many were actually called or emailed within 10 minutes. Build this stack: 1. Instant lead capture — Meta Lead Ads → Zapier or native CRM integration → GoHighLevel/HubSpot. Don't rely on the CSV download from Ads Manager. People forget. Leads rot. 2. Speed-to-lead automation — SMS within 60 seconds ("Hey [Name], saw you requested the [offer]. Got 2 minutes?"), email within 5, call within 10. 3. 5–7 touch cadence over 14 days — most conversions happen on touches 3–5, not touch 1. 4. Calendly or GoHighLevel calendar embedded in the first SMS so they can self-book. If your follow-up game is weak, doubling ad spend just creates more wasted leads. Fix the back end before scaling the front.

Culprit 7: Ad fatigue is silently killing your account

Even great campaigns die. Frequency creeps up, CTR drops, CPL doubles, and suddenly the ads that worked in month one are bleeding money in month three. Watch these signals in Ads Manager: - Frequency above 3.0 in a 7-day window — your audience is seeing the same ad too often

  • CTR declining 20%+ week over week while CPM stays flat
  • CPL rising while conversion rate on the landing page stays steady — that means the ads are attracting worse leads, not the page failing
  • Negative feedback score trending toward "Below Average" in the Account Quality dashboard The cure is structural, not tactical: 1. Plan to refresh creative every 2–3 weeks for evergreen campaigns. Build a content engine, not one-off ads.
  1. Run a 3-3-3 testing structure: 3 new hooks, 3 new angles, 3 new formats per month.
  2. Separate cold prospecting from retargeting campaigns. Different creative, different frequency caps.
  3. Use Advantage+ Creative sparingly — it can mask which variants are actually winning. Fatigue isn't a sign Facebook ads stopped working. It's a sign your creative pipeline isn't keeping up with the platform's appetite.

How to diagnose which culprit is yours in 20 minutes

Don't guess. Work the funnel top to bottom: 1. Objective check (1 min): Is it Leads or Sales? If not, that's your answer. 2. Audience check (3 min): Look at age/gender/placement breakdowns. Does delivery match your buyer? 3. Creative check (5 min): Pull CTR, hook rate, hold rate. Anything red? That's your answer. 4. Offer check (2 min): Read your ad as a stranger. Would you click? 5. Landing page check (5 min): Run PageSpeed Insights, count form fields, check the headline match. 6. Follow-up check (3 min): Pull last 20 leads. Were they contacted in under 10 minutes? 7. Fatigue check (1 min): Frequency over 3? CTR trending down? Refresh creative. Nine times out of ten, you'll find the issue in the first three steps. The other one out of ten is a stack of two or three smaller leaks compounding.

The bottom line

"Facebook ads don't work" is almost never true. "Facebook ads don't work the way I'm running them" is true constantly. The seven culprits — objective, audience, creative, offer, landing page, follow-up, fatigue — cover roughly 95% of underperforming accounts we audit. Pick one. Diagnose with real numbers from Ads Manager, GA4, and your CRM. Fix it. Give the campaign 5–7 days to re-stabilize. Then move to the next leak. Most accounts can double lead volume in 30 days without spending an extra dollar — they just need to stop bleeding at the seams.

faq.question: How long should I run a Facebook ad campaign before deciding it's not working?
faq.answer: Give a new campaign at least 5–7 days and 50+ conversions to exit the learning phase before judging it. Killing ads after 48 hours based on a $30 spend is the fastest way to never find a winner. If you can't afford to spend $500–$1,500 on a real test, your budget is too small for Meta to optimize against.

faq.question: What's a realistic cost per lead on Facebook ads in 2026?
faq.answer: It depends entirely on industry and offer. Local service businesses typically see $8–$30 per lead, B2B SaaS $40–$120, lenders and financial services $15–$60, and high-ticket coaching $25–$80. If your CPL is 2–3x the industry benchmark, you have a fixable problem — not a platform problem.

faq.question: Should I use Meta Instant Forms or send traffic to a landing page?
faq.answer: Instant Forms produce 2–4x more leads at lower CPL, but lead quality is usually lower because of the friction-free submission. Landing pages produce fewer, higher-intent leads. For high-volume top-of-funnel, use Instant Forms with qualifying questions. For higher-ticket offers or sales calls, send to a landing page.

faq.question: Why did my Facebook ads stop working after they were doing great?
faq.answer: Almost always ad fatigue. Frequency climbs above 3, the same audience has seen your creative too many times, and performance decays. Refresh creative every 2–3 weeks, expand or rotate audiences, and separate cold from retargeting campaigns. The account isn't broken — the creative pipeline stalled.

faq.question: Can I run Facebook ads without a landing page?
faq.answer: Yes — use Meta Instant Forms (Lead Ads) and pipe submissions directly into your CRM via native integration or Zapier. This works well for top-of-funnel lead capture. For anything requiring more education or higher commitment, a dedicated landing page will outperform forms on lead quality.

articles.title: Best Lead Generation Companies for Contractors: Worth It?
articles.description: We break down the top pay-per-lead platforms for contractors, what they really cost over 24 months, and when building your own funnel wins.
articles.keyword: best lead generation companies for contractors
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Angi, HomeAdvisor, Thumbtack, Networx, CraftJack, Houzz Pro. If you've spent more than six months running a contracting business, you've cut a check to at least one of them. And if you're being honest, you've also stared at a $7,400 monthly invoice and wondered why your pipeline still feels thin. Here's the contrarian take most lead gen reviews won't give you: the best lead generation companies for contractors are excellent at one thing — getting you started. They are terrible at building enterprise value. After 24 months of renting leads, most contractors have spent $80K–$250K and own exactly zero of the customer relationships, search rankings, or brand equity that money produced. This article is for general contractors, roofers, HVAC operators, remodelers, and specialty trades doing $500K–$10M in revenue who are evaluating where to put their next marketing dollar. We'll rank the major pay-per-lead marketplaces, show the real math on long-term cost, and lay out when owning your funnel beats renting every time.

The pay-per-lead landscape in 2026

The marketplace model is simple: a platform aggregates homeowner demand through SEO, paid ads, and TV, then sells each inquiry to 3-5 contractors simultaneously. You pay $15-$150 per lead depending on trade and geography. Here are the players that actually matter for contractors: - Angi Leads (formerly HomeAdvisor): Largest inventory, lowest lead quality on average. Expect $20-$85 per shared lead. Close rates typically 4-8%.

  • Thumbtack: Better UX, mobile-first homeowner base. Leads run $15-$60. Skews smaller jobs ($500-$5K tickets).
  • Networx: Mid-tier volume, primarily roofing, HVAC, and plumbing. $25-$100 per lead.
  • CraftJack (Home Depot owned): Phone-verified leads, slightly higher quality. $30-$120 range.
  • Houzz Pro: Premium positioning, design-build and high-end remodel. Lower volume, higher ticket.
  • Modernize: Strong in solar, windows, roofing. Exclusive lead tier available for 2-3x the price. The newer entrants — Hatch, Service Direct, and 99 Calls — sell exclusive (not shared) leads at $80-$300 each. Quality is materially better, but you're now paying agency-level CPAs without the brand asset that comes with running your own ads.

What you're actually buying when you rent leads

Let's be precise about the product. A shared marketplace lead is a homeowner who filled out a form on someone else's website, and is being called by you and 3-4 competitors within 90 seconds. The economics work like this. Assume $45 per lead at a 6% close rate. That's $750 per acquired customer before you've paid a salesperson, a CSR, or done any follow-up. On a $12,000 roof, that's a 6.25% CAC — workable. On a $1,800 deck repair, it's 42% — catastrophic. Three things you are not buying: 1. The customer relationship. When that homeowner needs another service in 18 months, they go back to Angi. Not you. 2. The data. Angi keeps the search behavior, the email, the demographic profile. You get a name and phone number. 3. The brand impression. The homeowner thinks they hired "someone from Angi," not your company. Compare this to a Google Ads click that lands on your site, gets cookied, enters your email sequence in GoHighLevel or HubSpot, and is now a long-term asset on your balance sheet. Same dollar spent, completely different outcome.

The 24-month true cost of renting vs owning

I ran this model with a roofing client last quarter. Two-year horizon, $15K/month marketing budget. Here's how the numbers shake out. Scenario A — Pure marketplace spend:

  • $360K total spent across Angi + Networx + CraftJack
  • ~8,000 leads acquired at $45 blended
  • 6% close rate = 480 jobs
  • Zero owned audience at month 24
  • Cost per job: $750
  • Asset value created: $0 Scenario B — Owned funnel (Google Ads + Local Service Ads + SEO + retargeting):
  • $360K total spent (same budget)
  • Months 1-6: Higher CAC ($1,100/job) while SEO ramps
  • Months 7-24: CAC drops to $380/job as organic and repeat customers kick in
  • ~620 jobs over 24 months
  • Email list of ~4,200 past inquiries
  • Domain authority and ranking #1-3 for 15-25 local terms
  • Estimated asset value: $180K-$400K if you ever sell the business The owned-funnel scenario produces 29% more jobs at the same spend AND creates a sellable asset. The catch: it requires patience for 4-6 months and operational discipline most contractors don't have on day one. That's why marketplaces exist — they sell the shortcut, and the shortcut is real. It's just expensive.

When pay-per-lead marketplaces are the right call

I'm not anti-marketplace. They have a place. Use them when: - You're under 12 months old and have no domain authority, no Google reviews, no historical ad data. Marketplaces give you cash flow to survive while you build assets.

  • You're entering a new geo or service line and need to test demand before investing in localized SEO and ads.
  • You have idle crew capacity that you need to fill this week. Marketplace leads convert to revenue in 7-21 days. SEO converts in 90-180.
  • Your average ticket is above $8,000. The math forgives a $750 CAC when the gross margin is $4,000+. Don't use marketplaces when your ticket is under $3K, when your close rate on shared leads is below 5%, or when you've been on the platform for 18+ months and your CAC hasn't dropped. The platform isn't going to reward your tenure. It's an auction, and new bidders show up every quarter. The smart play: treat marketplaces as a tactical lever, not a strategy. Cap them at 30-40% of your lead volume. Anything higher and you're building someone else's business.

The owned-funnel stack that actually works for contractors

If you're going to build instead of rent, here's the stack I'd deploy for a $2M-$8M contractor today. It's not theoretical — this is what's working in 2026. Traffic layer:

  • Google Local Service Ads (LSAs): Pay-per-lead but you own the Google review profile. Run these first.
  • Google Search Ads on commercial-intent terms ("roof replacement [city]," "kitchen remodel near me")
  • Meta Ads for retargeting + lookalikes off your customer list. Not cold prospecting unless you have a strong creative team.
  • Local SEO through a Google Business Profile optimized weekly, plus 2-4 long-form service pages per month Conversion layer:
  • Landing pages built in Unbounce or Webflow, NOT your main site. One page per service per city.
  • Calendly or a GoHighLevel booking widget. Speed-to-lead under 5 minutes or you lose 50% of the value.
  • A two-way SMS sequence triggered the moment a form fills. Nurture layer:
  • GoHighLevel or HubSpot CRM with a 12-touch email sequence over 90 days for unconverted leads
  • Quarterly newsletter to past customers — 20-30% of next-year revenue should come from this list
  • Review request automation immediately post-job completion Budget split for a $15K/month spend: $4K LSAs, $5K Google Search, $2K Meta retargeting, $2K SEO content, $2K tools and management.

How to evaluate any lead gen company before signing

If you're going to write checks to a third party — whether a marketplace or an agency — run them through this filter. I've used this with dozens of contractor clients and it kills bad deals fast. 1. Exclusivity. Are leads shared with competitors? If yes, your max acceptable CPL drops by 60%. 2. Attribution. Can they show you call recordings, form submissions, and source data in real-time? If they're hiding behind a dashboard with no raw data, walk. 3. Cancellation terms. Month-to-month or annual? Any contractor lead gen contract over 6 months is a red flag. 4. Lead replacement policy. What counts as a bad lead and what's the credit process? Get this in writing. 5. Geography and service match. Are you their 47th roofer in your zip code or their 3rd? Ask directly. 6. What happens at month 12. Will CPL go up, down, or stay flat? Get historical data from existing clients in similar markets. For agencies running your owned funnel, the questions shift: who owns the ad account, the domain, the CRM data, and the creative assets? Answer should be: you, you, you, and you. If any of those sit inside the agency's account, you're renting again — just with extra steps.

The hybrid model: rent to start, own to scale

The contractors I see win the long game don't pick a side. They run a deliberate 24-month transition. Months 1-6: 70% marketplace spend, 30% owned funnel build-out. Use marketplace cash flow to fund SEO content, ad testing, and CRM setup. Capture every marketplace lead's email and add to your nurture list (yes, this is allowed if you do the work). Months 7-12: 50/50 split. LSAs and Google Search should be matching marketplace volume by now at a lower CPA. If they're not, your landing pages or speed-to-lead are broken — fix those before adding more spend. Months 13-18: 30% marketplace, 70% owned. You should be ranking for 8-15 local terms and getting 40-60 organic inquiries per month. Marketplace becomes overflow capacity, not core volume. Months 19-24: 10-15% marketplace, 85% owned plus referrals. Marketplaces are now a tactical tool for slow weeks or new service launches, not a dependency. The contractors who skip this transition and stay 100% marketplace at year three are the ones who sell their business for 2x EBITDA instead of 5x. The buyer sees no defensible customer acquisition engine, and prices accordingly.

The bottom line

The best lead generation companies for contractors aren't actually the marketplaces — they're the platforms and channels you can own. Angi, Thumbtack, CraftJack, and the rest are useful tools for a specific stage of business, but they extract value that you should be compounding inside your own brand. Every dollar spent on a marketplace at year three is a dollar that didn't build an asset. Run the 24-month math on your own business. Pull your marketplace spend, divide by jobs closed, and compare to what the same money would do in LSAs + Google Search + SEO with a real CRM behind it. If the answer scares you, that's the signal to start the transition. Rent leads to survive, own the funnel to scale.

faq.question: Is Angi Leads worth it for contractors?
faq.answer: Angi can work in your first 12 months or as overflow capacity, but it's a poor long-term strategy. Expect 4-8% close rates on shared leads and CPAs around $600-$900 per closed job. Beyond 18 months on the platform, most contractors see flat or rising costs with no compounding return.

faq.question: How much should a contractor spend on lead generation?
faq.answer: A healthy benchmark is 6-12% of revenue for contractors under $5M, dropping to 4-7% as you scale and referrals/repeat business grow. Within that, no single channel — including marketplaces — should exceed 40% of total lead volume.

faq.question: What's the difference between shared and exclusive leads?
faq.answer: Shared leads are sold to 3-5 contractors simultaneously, so you're racing to call first. Exclusive leads come only to you, typically cost 2-4x more, and close at 15-25% versus 4-8% for shared. The math usually favors exclusive once your average ticket is above $5,000.

faq.question: Can I run Google Local Service Ads instead of using marketplaces?
faq.answer: Yes, and you probably should. LSAs are still pay-per-lead but you own the Google review profile, you appear at the top of search above marketplaces, and Google verifies the homeowner intent. CPLs typically run $25-$80 with materially better quality than shared marketplace leads.

faq.question: How long does it take to replace marketplace leads with my own funnel?
faq.answer: Plan for 6-9 months to match marketplace volume from owned channels, and 12-18 months to fully replace it at a lower blended CPA. The first 90 days are the hardest because SEO hasn't kicked in and you're paying to learn what ad creative and landing pages convert.

articles.title: Best CRM for Service Businesses: Honest 2026 Comparison
articles.description: We break down the best CRM for service businesses by speed-to-lead, pipeline, and automation. Real comparisons, real numbers, no vendor fluff.
articles.keyword: best CRM for service businesses
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most service businesses don't have a CRM problem. They have a speed-to-lead problem disguised as a CRM problem. The data is brutal: a Lead Connect study found that 78% of customers buy from the first company that responds, and contacting a lead within 5 minutes makes you 100x more likely to qualify them than waiting 30 minutes. Yet the median service business takes 47 hours to respond to a web inquiry. If you run an HVAC company, a law firm, a med spa, a roofing crew, an MSP, or any agency selling expertise — your CRM isn't a Rolodex. It's a revenue engine. The wrong pick costs you booked jobs, attribution clarity, and 10-20 hours a week in manual follow-up. This is a no-fluff breakdown of what a service business actually needs from a CRM and how the leading options (GoHighLevel, HubSpot, Pipedrive, Close, Jobber, ServiceTitan, Salesforce) stack up on the things that move money.

What a service business actually needs from a CRM

Forget the 400-feature spec sheets. A service business CRM has to do five things well, and almost nothing else matters until these are bulletproof: 1. Speed-to-lead under 5 minutes — ideally under 60 seconds. That means inbound triggers from web forms, Facebook Lead Ads, Google LSAs, and call tracking firing automations instantly. 2. A pipeline you'll actually update — drag-and-drop, mobile-friendly, with stages that match how jobs really close (Lead → Contacted → Quoted → Scheduled → Won). 3. Two-way SMS and email in one inbox — your team should never log into three apps to follow up. 4. Calendar booking baked in — Calendly is great, but native booking with round-robin assignment and reminders cuts no-shows by 25-40%. 5. Automation without a Zapier tax — if you need 14 Zaps to send a quote follow-up, you picked wrong. Notice what's missing: AI deal scoring, custom object modeling, NPS surveys. Those are nice. They don't book the appointment. If a vendor demo opens with anything other than "here's how fast a new lead gets a text back," you're being sold to.

The speed-to-lead test: where most CRMs lose money

Here's the benchmark to hold every CRM against: a lead fills out your form at 9:47 PM on a Tuesday. What happens in the next 60 seconds? The right answer is: an SMS goes out from a local number, an email confirms next steps, the lead is added to a nurture sequence, a booking link is offered, and your on-call rep gets a push notification with the lead's details and source. How the leaders perform out of the box: - GoHighLevel: All of the above, native, no add-ons. ~$297/mo agency tier.

  • HubSpot: Possible, but you'll need Marketing Hub Professional ($800+/mo) plus SMS via Twilio integration.
  • Pipedrive: Email yes, SMS requires LeadBooster + third-party. Weak on multi-channel automation.
  • Close: Excellent on calling and SMS, strong sequences, weaker on landing pages and forms.
  • Salesforce: Capable of anything if you have a $40K implementation budget and an admin on staff. The gap between vendors isn't features — it's time to first text. Test this in a demo. Have them submit a form live and watch the clock. If you don't see a text on your phone in under 90 seconds, walk.

GoHighLevel: the default pick for most service businesses

GoHighLevel (GHL) has eaten the service business CRM market for a reason. It bundles CRM, pipeline, SMS, email, funnels, calendars, reputation management, and call tracking into one stack at $97-$497/month depending on tier. Where it wins:

  • Native two-way SMS, calling, voicemail drops, and email — no integration tax.
  • Workflow builder that handles speed-to-lead, missed-call-text-back, review requests, and rebooking out of the box.
  • White-label option for agencies servicing multiple clients.
  • Phone numbers and A2P 10DLC registration in-platform. Where it hurts:
  • The UI looks like it was designed by ten different contractors. Steep learning curve weeks 1-3.
  • Support is community-driven; expect to live in Facebook groups and YouTube.
  • Reporting is functional but not pretty — exporting to Looker Studio is common. Best for: home services, med spas, agencies, coaches, lenders, local service businesses under 50 employees. If you're booking appointments and following up via SMS, this is the answer 80% of the time. Most operators recover the cost in the first week from missed-call-text-back alone.

HubSpot: when you're scaling past $5M and need polish

HubSpot is the right answer when you've outgrown the duct-tape phase and need a CRM that looks good in board decks, integrates with everything, and supports a full marketing-sales-service org. Where it wins:

  • Best-in-class reporting and attribution. Closed-loop tracking from ad click to revenue.
  • Cleanest UI in the category. Your team will actually use it.
  • Massive integration library (1,500+ apps) and a strong API.
  • Service Hub adds ticketing, knowledge base, and customer portal — useful for MSPs and B2B service. Where it hurts:
  • Pricing scales aggressively. Starter is fine at $50/mo, but real automation requires Marketing Hub Professional ($890/mo) and Sales Hub Professional ($100/seat/mo). Easy to hit $2-3K/mo.
  • SMS is bolt-on via Twilio, Salesmsg, or Kixie. Not native.
  • Contact-tier pricing punishes list growth. Best for: service businesses $5M+ revenue, B2B agencies, professional services (law, accounting, consulting), and anyone where the buyer journey is long and the deal size justifies the platform tax. If you're spending $20K+/month on paid media, HubSpot's attribution alone pays for itself.

The specialists: Jobber, ServiceTitan, Close, Pipedrive

Sometimes the right CRM isn't a general-purpose CRM at all. Jobber ($69-$349/mo) — Built for home service trades under $2M. Combines CRM, scheduling, dispatching, invoicing, and payments. If you're running 1-15 field techs (cleaning, landscaping, plumbing), Jobber beats GHL on operations. It's weaker on marketing automation. ServiceTitan ($300+/seat/mo, custom pricing) — The enterprise pick for $5M+ home service businesses. HVAC, plumbing, electrical. Brutal pricing and a 60-90 day implementation, but the dispatching, call-by-call coaching, and reporting are unmatched. Close ($49-$139/seat/mo) — A sales rep's dream. Built for outbound-heavy teams that live on the phone. Power dialer, predictive dialer, native SMS, sequences. Best for B2B service businesses doing high-volume outbound (agencies, SaaS, lenders, recruiters). Pipedrive ($14-$99/seat/mo) — The cheapest "real" CRM that doesn't suck. Clean pipeline UI, decent automation, weak on multi-channel. Good for small B2B service teams of 2-10 reps who mostly sell over email and Zoom. The rule: if your business has a vertical-specific workflow (dispatching, job costing, technician routing), buy the specialist. If your differentiation is marketing and sales speed, buy a horizontal platform like GHL or HubSpot.

Automation that pays for itself in week one

Regardless of which CRM you pick, these are the automations that print money. If your CRM can't do these, it's the wrong CRM. 1. Missed-call text-back — Caller doesn't connect? Auto-text within 30 seconds: "Hey, sorry we missed you — this is [Name] at [Company]. What can we help with?" Recovers 20-35% of missed calls. ROI: typically 10-50x in month one. 2. Speed-to-lead SMS + email — Form fill triggers SMS in <60 sec, email at +2 min, second SMS at +5 min if no reply. Booking link in every touch. 3. Quote follow-up sequence — 5-touch sequence over 14 days. Day 1, 3, 7, 10, 14. Mix of SMS and email. Most service businesses send one follow-up and quit. The 4th and 5th touches close 18% of quotes. 4. Review request automation — Triggered when job marked complete. SMS with Google review link. Service businesses that automate this average 4-8x more reviews per month. 5. Rebooking / reactivation — Past customer hasn't booked in 90/180/365 days? Auto-trigger an offer. Cheapest revenue you'll ever generate. If you're running paid traffic and not doing all five, you're lighting ad spend on fire upstream of a leaky bucket.

How to actually pick (a 7-day evaluation framework)

Stop reading G2 reviews. Run this seven-day process instead: Day 1-2: Define your non-negotiables. Write down your top 3 lead sources, average deal size, sales cycle length, and team size. If you can't fit this on a sticky note, you're not ready to pick a CRM. Day 3: Shortlist 3 vendors max. Based on this article: pick GHL if you're a local service business, HubSpot if you're scaling B2B, a specialist if you have vertical-specific ops needs. Day 4-5: Demo with one rule. Every demo opens with: "Submit a test lead on my website. Show me what happens in the next 5 minutes." Time it. Most demos collapse here. Day 6: Pricing math. Add up: platform cost + per-seat cost + SMS/email costs + integration costs + implementation. Annualize it. Divide by expected new revenue. If the ratio isn't under 5%, push back on the vendor. Day 7: Pick and commit for 90 days. The worst CRM decision is changing CRMs every 6 months. Pick, implement the five automations above, and don't touch it for a quarter. Most service businesses spend three months evaluating and zero months implementing. Flip that ratio.

The bottom line

The best CRM for service businesses isn't the one with the most features — it's the one your team will actually use, that texts leads in under 60 seconds, and that runs the five automations that recover lost revenue. For most local service businesses, that's GoHighLevel. For scaling B2B, it's HubSpot. For vertical-heavy ops, it's Jobber, ServiceTitan, or Close. The pick matters less than the implementation. A mediocre CRM with missed-call-text-back, speed-to-lead, and a 5-touch follow-up sequence will outperform a Ferrari CRM running on default settings every single time. Audit your speed-to-lead this week, pick the platform that fits your model, and ship the automations before you ship anything else.

faq.question: Is GoHighLevel really better than HubSpot for service businesses?
faq.answer: For local service businesses under $5M in revenue, yes — GHL bundles SMS, calling, calendars, and automation natively at a fraction of HubSpot's cost. HubSpot wins once you need real attribution reporting, complex sales processes, or have a marketing team that needs polish and integrations.

faq.question: How much should a service business spend on a CRM?
faq.answer: Budget 1-3% of revenue on your CRM stack, all-in (platform + SMS + email + implementation). A $1M HVAC company should be in the $200-$500/month range. A $10M agency can justify $2-5K/month if attribution and reporting are tight.

faq.question: What's the fastest way to improve speed-to-lead without changing CRMs?
faq.answer: Add a missed-call-text-back automation and an instant SMS on form fill. You can do this in any CRM with Twilio or a tool like Salesmsg in under a day. These two automations alone typically lift booked appointments by 15-30%.

faq.question: Do I need a separate CRM if I already use QuickBooks or Jobber?
faq.answer: Jobber has CRM features that work for trades under $2M doing mostly inbound — you probably don't need a second tool. QuickBooks is not a CRM and shouldn't be used as one; pair it with a real CRM and sync customers via integration.

faq.question: How long does CRM implementation actually take?
faq.answer: For GHL or Pipedrive, expect 2-4 weeks to get the core pipeline and top 5 automations live. HubSpot Professional is typically 6-12 weeks with proper data migration. Salesforce and ServiceTitan are 60-120 day projects and usually require outside help.

articles.title: How Much Does a Marketing Agency Cost for a Small Business?
articles.description: Real pricing ranges for retainers, performance deals, and project work — plus when each model actually makes sense for small service businesses.
articles.keyword: how much does a marketing agency cost for a small business
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most small business owners asking what a marketing agency costs get one of two useless answers: "it depends" or a wildly inflated quote from someone who senses desperation. Neither helps you decide if hiring out is worth it. Here's the honest version: a competent agency for a small service business runs anywhere from $1,500/month for a narrow scope to $15,000+/month for full-funnel media buying and content. Performance deals can look cheaper on paper and burn you on the back end. Project work sounds safe and often delivers nothing repeatable. This article breaks down what you actually pay under each pricing model, what's included at each tier, and how to decide which one fits a service business doing $500K to $10M in revenue.

The three pricing models you'll be quoted

Almost every agency proposal you'll see falls into one of three buckets. Knowing the mechanics matters because each one shifts risk between you and the agency in very different ways. - Monthly retainer: A fixed fee for a defined scope. Predictable for both sides. Most common for ongoing services like paid media management, SEO, and content.

  • Performance / rev-share: You pay a smaller base (or nothing) plus a fee per lead, per appointment, per closed deal, or a percentage of ad-attributed revenue. Agency carries more risk and prices it accordingly.
  • Project / one-time: Flat fee for a defined deliverable — a website, a launch funnel, a brand refresh, a 90-day sprint. A fourth hybrid is creeping in: retainer + performance bonus, where a base fee covers the labor and a kicker rewards hitting CPL or ROAS targets. For service businesses with clean attribution (lenders, home services, med spas, law firms), this is often the cleanest structure. The wrong model will cost you more than the wrong agency. A $3K/month retainer with a team that doesn't understand your offer beats a "pay per lead" deal that floods your CRM with tire kickers every time.

Retainer pricing: what you actually pay per month

Retainers are priced on scope, channels, and team seniority. Here are the honest ranges for U.S.-based agencies working with small service businesses: - $1,500–$3,000/month: Single channel, junior execution. Usually one platform (Meta Ads or Google Ads), basic reporting, limited creative. Fine for a local business with a tight geo and a simple offer.

  • $3,000–$6,000/month: Two channels, a strategist on the account, monthly creative refresh, CRM/funnel hygiene. This is the sweet spot for most service businesses doing $1M–$3M.
  • $6,000–$10,000/month: Full-funnel — paid media, landing pages, email/SMS nurture in HubSpot or GoHighLevel, weekly reporting, dedicated account manager.
  • $10,000–$20,000+/month: Multi-channel media, in-house creative team, conversion rate optimization, sales enablement support. Justified when ad spend is $30K+/month. A rule of thumb that holds up: agency fee should be roughly 15–25% of your monthly ad spend at the low end, dropping to 10–15% as spend scales past $20K/month. If an agency wants $5K/month to manage $4K in ad spend, you're paying for their overhead, not your growth.

Performance pricing: cost-per-lead and rev-share reality

Performance deals sound founder-friendly until you read the contract. Typical structures: - Cost per lead (CPL): $25–$150 for low-ticket local services (cleaning, lawn care), $150–$500 for mid-ticket (HVAC, roofing, med spa), $300–$1,500+ for high-ticket (mortgage, solar, legal, B2B).

  • Cost per appointment: 2–4x the CPL number. The agency screens before handoff.
  • Cost per closed deal: 10–25% of deal value, typically with a minimum monthly commitment.
  • Rev-share: 8–15% of attributed revenue, almost always with a base retainer of $2K–$5K to cover labor. The catch: performance shops optimize for what they get paid on. A pure CPL deal incentivizes volume, not quality. Expect a higher percentage of unqualified leads unless qualification criteria are written into the contract — specific zip codes, minimum loan amounts, project size, whatever defines a real prospect for your business. Also watch the "lead" definition. Is it a form fill? A phone call over 60 seconds? A booked appointment on Calendly? Get it in writing. The cheapest CPL with a loose definition almost always costs more per closed deal than a slightly higher CPL with strict criteria.

Project pricing: when one-time work makes sense

Project work is the right call when you need a specific asset built and have the internal capacity (or another vendor) to run it after. Honest ranges: - Landing page or funnel build: $1,500–$8,000 depending on complexity, copy, design, and integrations.

  • Website (small business, 5–15 pages): $5,000–$25,000. Anything under $3K is a template job — fine if you know that going in.
  • Brand identity (logo, guidelines, basic collateral): $3,000–$15,000.
  • 90-day launch sprint (offer, funnel, ad creative, initial campaigns): $8,000–$25,000.
  • CRM build-out in GoHighLevel or HubSpot: $2,500–$10,000 for setup, pipelines, automations, and reporting dashboards. Projects fail when there's no plan for what happens after delivery. A $15K funnel that nobody drives traffic to is $15K wasted. Before signing a project contract, answer two questions: who's running this once it's live, and what's the monthly budget to feed it? If you can't answer both, a retainer is the better call.

What's actually included at each tier

Pricing without scope is meaningless. Here's what you should expect deliverable-wise at each retainer level: $1,500–$3,000/month:

  • 1 ad platform managed
  • 2–4 ad creative variations per month
  • Monthly reporting (usually a Looker Studio or Google Analytics dashboard)
  • Email check-ins, no dedicated strategist $3,000–$6,000/month:
  • 2 channels (e.g., Meta + Google)
  • Weekly creative iteration
  • Landing page updates
  • Bi-weekly strategy call
  • Conversion tracking audit and pixel hygiene $6,000–$10,000/month:
  • Full-funnel: ads, landing pages, email/SMS nurture
  • Dedicated account manager + media buyer
  • Weekly reporting and optimization
  • CRM integration (GoHighLevel, HubSpot, Salesforce)
  • Creative team producing 8–15 assets/month $10,000+/month:
  • Multi-channel media (Meta, Google, YouTube, LinkedIn, TikTok where it fits)
  • In-house video and design
  • CRO program with structured testing
  • Sales enablement: call recording review, script iteration, lead scoring
  • Weekly executive-level reporting If an agency quotes $5K/month and the deliverables list looks like the $2K tier, they're charging for their brand, not their work. Ask for a sample reporting dashboard and a redacted client deliverable before signing.

When hiring an agency actually pays off

Agencies aren't always the right move. Here's a clean decision framework based on revenue, margin, and internal capacity: 1. Under $500K revenue, no marketing hire: Use a freelancer or a junior in-house generalist. Agency overhead doesn't fit the math. 2. $500K–$2M, owner-led marketing: A specialist agency on a $2K–$4K retainer for one channel can free up 15–20 hours/week of owner time. Usually worth it. 3. $2M–$10M, one marketing hire: An agency partnering with your internal lead is the highest-leverage setup. Internal owns brand and strategy, agency owns execution and media buying. 4. $10M+: Build in-house for core channels, use agencies for specialized work (creative production, technical SEO, paid social scaling). The other math that matters: your customer lifetime value. If your average client is worth $5,000+ and your close rate on qualified leads is 20%+, a $5K/month agency only needs to generate 5 closed deals to pay for itself. For a lender, contractor, or B2B service business, that's usually achievable in month two or three. If your LTV is $500 and your close rate is 5%, the math is brutal — fix the offer before you hire an agency.

Red flags that will cost you money

After enough rodeos, the warning signs are obvious. Walk if you see any of these: - No clear reporting cadence or dashboard. If they can't show you a sample report in the sales call, they don't have one.

  • Vague KPIs. "We'll grow your brand" is not a KPI. CPL, CAC, ROAS, booked appointments — pick two and put them in the contract.
  • 12-month contracts with no out clause. A 90-day initial commitment is fair (most channels need that to optimize). A 12-month lockup with no performance triggers is a trap.
  • They won't name the team working on your account. Bait-and-switch from the senior who pitched you to a junior who runs it is the oldest play in the book.
  • Setup fees over $2,500 with no clear deliverable. Some setup is real (CRM build, pixel install, creative kickoff). "Onboarding fees" of $5K+ with vague scope are margin padding.
  • They don't ask about your sales process. If they don't want to see how leads get handled after they're delivered, they don't care about your outcomes. The best agencies will turn down clients they can't help. If everyone you talk to says yes immediately, you're shopping in the wrong pool.

The bottom line

There's no universal answer to what a marketing agency should cost your small business — but there are honest ranges, and now you have them. Retainers run $1,500–$20,000+/month based on scope. Performance deals trade predictability for shared risk. Project work makes sense when you have a specific asset to build and a plan to feed it. The real question isn't "how much does it cost" — it's "what return do I need to justify this spend, and does the agency's model align with that outcome?" Pick the pricing structure that puts the agency on the same side of the table as you, write the KPIs into the contract, and start with a 90-day commitment before you sign anything longer. If the work is good, the renewal takes care of itself.

faq.question: Can I get a real marketing agency for under $1,000 a month?
faq.answer: Generally no — at least not in the U.S. for managed media or full-service work. Under $1,000/month you're looking at offshore execution, software-only solutions like GoHighLevel with DIY setup, or a freelancer doing a few hours a week. For a small service business, $1,500–$2,500/month is the realistic floor for managed ad work with a U.S. team.

faq.question: Should I pay an agency a percentage of ad spend or a flat retainer?
faq.answer: Flat retainer is almost always better for the client when ad spend is under $20K/month, because percentage-of-spend creates an incentive to spend more rather than spend efficiently. Above $20K/month, a percentage model (typically 10–15%) can be fair and scales with the work involved.

faq.question: How long before a marketing agency starts producing results?
faq.answer: Paid media should show meaningful data within 30 days and optimized performance by day 60–90. SEO and content take 4–9 months for compounding results. If an agency promises results in week one on a cold account, they're either lying or rebranding existing leads as new.

faq.question: Is a performance-based agency cheaper than a retainer?
faq.answer: On paper, sometimes. In practice, you usually pay a premium per lead or per deal because the agency is pricing in their risk. The total cost over 6–12 months is often higher with performance deals, but the cash flow is more forgiving because you only pay when leads come in.

faq.question: What's a fair contract length to sign with a new agency?
faq.answer: 90 days is the standard initial commitment and it's reasonable — most channels need that long to optimize. Avoid 12-month lockups unless there are performance-based out clauses. After the initial period, month-to-month or quarterly renewals keep both sides honest.

articles.title: How Much Do Google Ads Cost for a Small Business in 2026
articles.description: Real 2026 Google Ads CPC and cost-per-lead benchmarks by industry, healthy starting budgets, and the 5 places small budgets get torched.
articles.keyword: how much do Google Ads cost for a small business
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Here's the uncomfortable truth: most small businesses spending under $3,000/month on Google Ads are funding Google's earnings call, not their own pipeline. The platform isn't broken — the budgets are too thin to survive the learning phase, and the targeting is too loose to compete with operators who actually know what they're doing. This article is for founders, fractional CMOs, and agency owners running paid search for service businesses, lenders, local trades, and B2B. No fluff about "it depends." You'll get 2026 CPC ranges by industry, real cost-per-lead benchmarks, what a defensible starting budget actually looks like, and the five line items where small budgets bleed out before the first conversion hits. If you're trying to decide whether Google Ads is worth it at $1,500/month or $15,000/month, this is the math.

The short answer: what small businesses actually spend in 2026

Most small businesses we audit spend between $1,500 and $10,000 per month on Google Ads, with the median sitting around $3,500. That's media spend only — not management fees, not landing page builds, not call tracking. Break that down by channel mix and you get a clearer picture: - Search campaigns: $2–$4 per click on the low end (local services like cleaning, handyman), $15–$50+ on the high end (legal, insurance, SaaS, lending).

  • Performance Max: Cheaper CPCs ($0.80–$3) but wildly variable lead quality. Burns budget fast without exclusions.
  • Display/YouTube: $0.10–$2 CPC, but for most small service businesses this is brand spend dressed up as performance. The number that actually matters is cost per qualified lead (CPQL), not CPC. A $40 click that closes a $6,000 contract is cheap. A $3 click that fills your inbox with tire-kickers is expensive. We'll get to industry-specific CPQL ranges in a minute. The other variable nobody talks about: geography. Running plumbing ads in Manhattan vs. Tulsa is a 4–6x cost difference for the same intent keyword. If you're benchmarking against a competitor in another market, you're benchmarking against fiction.

2026 CPC and cost-per-lead benchmarks by industry

These ranges are pulled from active Google Ads accounts we manage and audit across North America. Use them as guardrails, not gospel — your market, Quality Score, and offer all move the number. Home services (HVAC, plumbing, roofing, electrical)

  • CPC: $8–$25
  • Cost per lead: $45–$180
  • Cost per booked job: $120–$400 Legal (personal injury, family, criminal)
  • CPC: $40–$300+ (PI is the worst)
  • Cost per lead: $150–$900
  • Cost per signed case: $600–$5,000+ Financial services / lending (SBA, MCA, mortgage)
  • CPC: $15–$60
  • Cost per lead: $80–$350
  • Cost per funded deal: $600–$3,500 Healthcare (dental, med spa, cosmetic)
  • CPC: $4–$18
  • Cost per lead: $40–$160
  • Cost per booked consult: $90–$300 B2B SaaS / agency services
  • CPC: $10–$45
  • Cost per lead (demo request): $150–$600
  • Cost per SQL: $400–$1,500 Local retail / e-commerce
  • CPC: $0.80–$3.50
  • Cost per purchase: $25–$120 (depends on AOV) If your numbers are 30%+ worse than these ranges and you've been running for 90+ days, the problem is account structure or offer — not the platform. If you're 30%+ better, audit your conversion tracking. We see false positives in Google Ads tracking more often than legitimate outperformance.

What a healthy starting budget actually looks like

Google's learning algorithm needs 30–50 conversions per campaign per month to optimize properly. Work backwards from that. If your cost per lead is $100, you need ~$3,000–$5,000/month per campaign just to feed the algorithm. Run two campaigns (say, brand + non-brand, or two service lines) and you're at $6,000–$10,000/month minimum to give the account a real shot. Here's the budget framework I give clients: 1. Floor budget (test phase, 60–90 days): 20x your target CPL. If CPL target is $150, budget $3,000/month minimum. 2. Scale budget (post-validation): 50–100x target CPL across the account. 3. Management overhead: Add 15–25% for proper management. A $5,000 ad budget with a $500 freelancer is going to underperform a $4,000 budget with a $1,000 operator running it. Where small budgets actually work:

  • Single-location service businesses targeting one metro
  • Tight keyword lists (10–30 high-intent terms)
  • Strong landing pages with call tracking (CallRail, WhatConverts) and CRM integration (GoHighLevel, HubSpot)
  • Offer-led ads, not brand-led Where small budgets die:
  • Trying to run search + PMax + Display simultaneously
  • National targeting on a sub-$5K budget
  • Broad match without negative keyword discipline
  • B2B with 6-month sales cycles and no nurture sequence behind the form fill

The 5 places small Google Ads budgets get wasted

After auditing hundreds of accounts under $10K/month, the leaks are predictable. 1. Broad match without negatives. Google's AI will spend your budget on "free," "jobs," "DIY," and competitor brand terms unless you actively block them. Build a negative keyword list of 200+ terms before launch. Refresh it weekly for the first 60 days. 2. Performance Max with no asset group discipline. PMax is a black box that will cannibalize your branded search traffic and report it as "new" conversions. If you run PMax, exclude brand terms via account-level negatives (you'll need to request this from Google support for some account types). 3. Sending all traffic to the homepage. Homepage conversion rates average 1–2%. A dedicated landing page with one offer, one CTA, and social proof converts at 6–12%. That's a 5x improvement on the same ad spend. 4. No call tracking. 40–60% of service business leads come via phone. If you're not tracking calls with CallRail or WhatConverts and feeding them back as conversions, Google is optimizing toward form fills only — which are often the lower-quality lead source. 5. Pausing campaigns too early. Google needs 2–3 weeks of learning phase per campaign change. Operators who tinker daily reset the algorithm constantly. Set a 14-day no-touch rule after launch and after any major change.

Total cost of ownership: it's not just media spend

When a founder asks "how much do Google Ads cost," they're usually only thinking about the click charges. Real TCO for a small business looks like this: - Media spend: $3,000–$10,000/month

  • Management (agency or in-house operator): $800–$3,500/month
  • Landing page builds: $500–$3,000 one-time, or built in Unbounce/Instapage ($99–$300/month)
  • Call tracking (CallRail, WhatConverts): $50–$300/month
  • CRM + automation (GoHighLevel, HubSpot): $97–$800/month
  • Conversion tracking setup (GA4, GTM, server-side): $500–$2,500 one-time For a small service business doing this properly, all-in cost is $5,000–$15,000/month, with media being 60–70% of that. The mistake I see weekly: a founder spends $4,000/month on ads, $0 on infrastructure, then blames Google when the leads don't close. The infrastructure is where conversion rate doubles. A 2x conversion rate cuts your effective CPL in half without changing your ad budget. If you can't fund both ads and infrastructure, fix the infrastructure first and run a smaller ad budget. A $2,000/month spend on a tight funnel beats $5,000/month into a leaky one every time.

How to know if your Google Ads spend is actually working

Forget impressions, CTR, and Quality Score for a second. Three numbers tell you if the account is healthy: 1. Cost per qualified lead (CPQL), not raw CPL. A qualified lead is one your sales team would actually call back. If raw CPL is $80 but only 30% are qualified, your real CPQL is $267. Track this monthly in a simple spreadsheet — pull leads from GoHighLevel or HubSpot and tag them qualified/unqualified. 2. Customer acquisition cost (CAC) vs. LTV. Healthy ratio is 3:1 LTV-to-CAC minimum. Below 3:1 and you're either acquiring poorly or your offer is too cheap. Above 5:1 and you should be spending more. 3. Payback period. How many months until a new customer pays back their CAC? Under 6 months is excellent for service businesses. Over 12 months means you need either bigger upfront tickets or stronger retention before you scale spend. If those three numbers are in range, double the budget. Most small businesses stop scaling exactly when they should be pressing harder. If those numbers are out of range, more budget makes the problem bigger, not smaller. Fix the funnel, the offer, or the targeting before adding spend. Monthly reporting should fit on one page. If your agency sends 14-page decks, they're hiding something.

When Google Ads is the wrong channel for a small business

Not every small business should run Google Ads. Here's when to spend that budget elsewhere: Skip Google Ads if:

  • Your average customer value is under $100 and you have no repeat purchase mechanic
  • You're in a category with near-zero search volume (new product categories, very niche B2B)
  • Your sales cycle is 9+ months and you have no email nurture or retargeting in place
  • You can't commit to 90 days of testing minimum
  • Your website converts under 1% and you have no budget to fix it Better channels for those scenarios:
  • Meta Ads: Better for demand generation, lower-ticket offers, and visual products. CPCs are $0.50–$3 for most small businesses.
  • LinkedIn Ads: Expensive ($8–$15 CPC) but the only place for true B2B targeting by job title and company size.
  • Local SEO + GBP optimization: For service businesses in a defined geography, this beats paid in 12–18 months at a fraction of the recurring cost.
  • Outbound (cold email, cold calling): For B2B with contracts over $10K, outbound still has the best CAC if executed well. Google Ads wins when someone is actively searching for what you sell. If demand doesn't exist yet, you're paying to create it — and that's a different (more expensive) game.

The bottom line

Google Ads costs for a small business in 2026 land between $1,500 and $15,000/month all-in, with media spend representing 60–70% of that. The CPC matters less than the cost per qualified lead, and the CPL matters less than the LTV-to-CAC ratio. Operators who track those three numbers and fund the infrastructure around the ads — landing pages, call tracking, CRM — get 2–3x the results of operators throwing more money at media alone. If you're starting fresh: build the funnel first, commit to a 90-day test at 20x your target CPL, and pick one campaign type (search) before adding PMax or Display. If you're already running and underwater, audit the five waste areas above before adding a dollar of budget. Most accounts have a 30–50% efficiency gain hiding in plain sight.

faq.question: Can I run Google Ads with a $500/month budget?
faq.answer: Realistically, no — unless you're hyper-local (one zip code, one service) with a CPL under $25. Below $1,500/month you won't generate enough conversions for Google's algorithm to optimize, and you'll spend most of the budget in the learning phase without ever stabilizing performance.

faq.question: Why is my CPC so much higher than industry averages I see online?
faq.answer: Three usual suspects: low Quality Score from weak ad-to-landing-page relevance, broad match keywords without negative lists, and competitive geography. Most published "average CPC" data is national, but your auction is hyper-local. A $12 average CPC in your trade can easily be $40 in a major metro.

faq.question: Is it better to hire an agency or run Google Ads in-house?
faq.answer: Under $5,000/month media spend, a competent freelancer or agency at $800–$1,500/month usually beats in-house because you get pattern recognition from other accounts. Over $15,000/month, in-house starts making sense if you can hire someone who's managed accounts at that level — not a generalist marketer learning on your dime.

faq.question: How long before Google Ads becomes profitable?
faq.answer: Plan for 60–90 days to reach stable performance, and 4–6 months to know if the channel is profitable at your CAC and LTV. Anyone promising profitability in 30 days is either lucky, lying, or running brand search and calling it new acquisition.

faq.question: Should I run Google Ads or Meta Ads first?
faq.answer: If people are actively searching for what you sell (services, B2B software, local trades), start with Google. If you're creating demand for a product people don't know they need, start with Meta. Most small service businesses get faster ROI from Google because they're capturing existing intent.

articles.title: Meta Ads for Med Spas: The Booked-Appointment Funnel Playbook
articles.description: How to run Meta ads for med spas that book real appointments — offers, compliance traps, creative that converts, and the funnel stack that ties it together.
articles.keyword: Meta ads for med spas
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most med spas running Meta ads are buying leads, not appointments. There's a $4,000 difference between those two outcomes every month, and it shows up in your chair utilization, not your CRM dashboard. The operators winning right now treat Meta as a booked-appointment channel — with a specific offer architecture, a compliance-aware creative process, and a follow-up stack that closes the gap between form-fill and butt-in-chair. The ones losing are still boosting before-and-after photos and wondering why their cost per lead looks great but the front desk is quiet. This playbook covers the offers that actually convert cold traffic, the compliance pitfalls that get accounts restricted, the creative formats producing sub-$25 booked appointments in 2026, and the funnel stack — Meta Ads Manager, GoHighLevel, and a real booking tool — that ties it all together.

Why most med spa Meta ads fail before the click

The default med spa ad — a carousel of before-and-afters with "Book your free consultation today!" — fails for three reasons, and none of them are creative quality. First, the offer is wrong. A "free consultation" sounds like a sales appointment, because it is one. Cold traffic on Meta is in discovery mode, not buying mode. You're asking for a 60-minute commitment from someone who was watching a Reel about their friend's wedding 12 seconds ago. Second, the targeting is lazy. Most spas still run broad with a "women 25-65, interested in beauty" stack. Meta's algorithm in 2026 doesn't need your interest layering — it needs a clean conversion event and 50+ weekly optimization signals. If you're optimizing for Lead instead of Schedule or Purchase, you're training the algorithm to find form-fillers, not bookers. Third, the funnel ends at a contact form. The lead lands in a spreadsheet, your front desk calls them three hours later, gets voicemail, and the lead dies. Industry data puts med spa lead-to-appointment conversion around 18-28% when there's no automation, versus 45-60% with sub-5-minute speed-to-lead. Fix the offer, fix the optimization event, fix the speed-to-lead — in that order. Creative is the last 20%.

The offer architecture that converts cold traffic

Stop selling consultations. Sell a specific, priced, time-bound treatment that gets a credit card on file. That's the only offer structure that consistently produces sub-$50 booked appointments on Meta. Here's the offer hierarchy I use across med spa accounts: 1. Tripwire offer — a high-perceived-value service at a loss-leader price. Examples: $99 HydraFacial (regularly $199), $149 first Botox area ($12-14/unit cap), $199 first laser hair removal session. The price has to be a real decision, not a trial. 2. Package upsell — at booking confirmation, offer the 3-pack or membership at 15-20% off. Expect 25-35% take rate if the offer is built into the confirmation flow. 3. No-show insurance — require a $50 deposit applied to the service. This single change typically cuts no-shows from 30%+ down to 8-12%. The psychology: a paid offer pre-qualifies. Anyone willing to put $50 down on a $99 HydroFacial is a real customer, not a deal-hunter who'll ghost. Your show rate goes up, your lifetime value goes up, and your front desk stops chasing tire-kickers. Avoid "free" anything in the primary offer. Free consults attract people researching, not buying. Save the free consultation for retargeting traffic that's already engaged with your brand.

Compliance pitfalls that get your account restricted

Meta's health and personal attributes policy is the single biggest reason med spa accounts get throttled or banned, and most operators don't know they're violating it until reach drops 70% overnight. The non-negotiables: - No before-and-after photos in feed ads. Meta classifies these as implying negative self-perception. You can use them on your landing page, but not in the ad creative. This is the #1 rejection trigger.

  • No "you" language about body parts or conditions. "Tired of your double chin?" or "Hate your wrinkles?" — both will get flagged. Reframe to outcome language: "The treatment everyone's booking for jawline definition."
  • No medical claims without substantiation. "FDA-approved" requires the exact device clearance. "Permanent results" on most aesthetic treatments is a claim violation.
  • Botox and injectable brand names are restricted. Use "neurotoxin treatment" or "wrinkle relaxer" in copy. Saying "Botox $9/unit" in an ad will get rejected and can trigger an account-level review. The workaround that works: lifestyle creative showing the experience (clean treatment rooms, confident clients walking out, the product packaging) plus outcome-focused copy that talks about how people feel and what they're doing, not what their face looked like before. Run every ad through Meta's policy preview before publishing, and keep a second ad account warm in case your primary gets restricted.

Creative formats producing sub-$25 booked appointments

The creative winning in med spa accounts right now isn't polished brand video. It's three specific formats, in order of CPA performance: 1. Founder/provider talking-head Reels (15-30 seconds). Your injector or aesthetician, phone camera, talking directly about one treatment. Hook in the first 2 seconds: "This is the treatment that booked out our schedule for the next 6 weeks." Then 10 seconds of why it works, 5 seconds of the offer, end card with the price. These consistently produce the lowest CPA because they build trust and pre-frame the consultation. 2. Client testimonial UGC. Real clients (with signed releases) talking about the experience — not the results. "I was nervous because I'd never done this, but the consultation was actually informative and not pushy." This handles objections inside the ad. 3. Treatment room walkthrough. 15-second pan of your space, voiceover about the offer. Low production cost, high relevance score, and it makes a cold lead feel like they've already been there. What doesn't work in 2026: stock footage, slide-deck-style carousels with text overlays, before/after comparisons (also a compliance issue), and any ad that opens with the logo. Production cadence: shoot 8-12 new creatives per month. Meta's algorithm fatigues creative in 7-14 days at meaningful spend. If you're running the same three ads for six weeks, your CPA inflation isn't an algorithm problem — it's a creative refresh problem.

The funnel stack: from ad click to butt in chair

The ad is 30% of the system. The funnel stack does the other 70%. Here's the configuration that consistently produces 45-60% lead-to-appointment rates: Step 1 — Landing page, not a form. Send traffic to a dedicated landing page (Unbounce, Instapage, or a GoHighLevel funnel). Above the fold: offer, price, one CTA. Below: 2-3 testimonials, the provider's credentials, FAQ. Total page weight under 1.5MB or mobile bounce kills you. Step 2 — Direct booking, not lead form. Embed Calendly, Vagaro, or GoHighLevel's calendar with the deposit collection built in. Skipping the "submit form, get called back" step typically doubles booked-appointment conversion. Step 3 — Speed-to-lead automation for incomplete bookings. If someone fills the form but doesn't book, fire a SMS within 90 seconds: "Hey [name], saw you were checking out our HydraFacial offer — want me to grab a Saturday spot for you?" GoHighLevel handles this natively. Step 4 — Confirmation and reminder sequence. Booking confirmation email + SMS, 48-hour reminder, 2-hour reminder, post-appointment review request. This sequence alone reduces no-shows by 40-50%. Step 5 — Server-side conversion tracking. Install the Meta Conversions API (not just the pixel) so iOS 17+ and ad blockers don't black-hole your data. Without CAPI, you're optimizing on 60-70% of actual conversion signal.

Budget, bidding, and the metrics that actually matter

For a single-location med spa, the minimum viable test budget on Meta is $75-100/day for 21 days. Below that, you don't generate enough conversion signal for the algorithm to optimize, and you'll quit before the account stabilizes. Campaign structure (kept deliberately simple): - 1 campaign, Sales objective, optimizing for Purchase (deposit) or Schedule event

  • 2 ad sets: one broad (no targeting except location radius — 15 miles urban, 25 miles suburban), one 1% lookalike of past customers
  • 4-6 ads per ad set, mix of the three creative formats above Bidding: start on Highest Volume (lowest cost). Switch to Cost Cap only after you have 30+ purchases and know your true CPA. Manual bidding before that is guessing. The metrics that matter, in order: 1. Cost per booked appointment (not cost per lead)
  1. Show rate (target 80%+)
  2. First-visit revenue (should be 1.5-2x your CPA at minimum)
  3. 60-day customer LTV (the real number that justifies scaling spend) Ignore CTR, CPM, and frequency until the unit economics work. A 0.8% CTR ad producing $30 booked appointments beats a 3.5% CTR ad producing $80 leads that never show. Operators who optimize Meta dashboards instead of P&L outcomes stay small.

Scaling without breaking your account

Once you're producing booked appointments at a CPA that works (typically $35-75 depending on offer and market), scaling Meta is mechanical — but most operators break their account by scaling wrong. The two scaling rules: Rule 1: Scale budget by 20-30% every 3-4 days, not 100% overnight. Meta's algorithm re-enters the learning phase any time you change spend by more than ~30% on an ad set. Doubling budget overnight kicks the campaign back to learning and your CPA spikes for 5-7 days. Slow, incremental increases keep performance stable. Rule 2: Duplicate winners, don't just raise budgets. When an ad set hits 50+ conversions and stable CPA, duplicate it at a higher starting budget rather than scaling the original. This gives you parallel learning and protects you if one ad set fatigues. For multi-location spas, run separate campaigns per location with geo-radius targeting — not one campaign with multiple locations. Meta's geographic optimization is weaker than operators assume, and consolidated campaigns over-serve the location with the cheapest impressions. When CPA starts climbing (it will, around month 3-4), the fix is almost always one of three things: creative fatigue (refresh assets), offer fatigue (introduce a new tripwire), or audience saturation (expand geo or test a new lookalike). Diagnose in that order — creative first, because it's the cheapest to fix.

The bottom line

Meta ads for med spas work when you treat the platform as a booked-appointment channel, not a lead-generation channel. That means a paid tripwire offer instead of a free consult, compliance-aware creative that doesn't trigger Meta's health policy, a funnel stack that converts clicks to deposits without a phone tag round, and patience to let the algorithm stabilize before scaling spend. If you're currently buying leads at $15 and wondering why your treatment rooms are empty, the problem isn't your CPL — it's that you optimized for the wrong outcome. Rebuild the offer, install Conversions API and a real booking flow, refresh creative every 10-14 days, and measure cost per butt-in-chair. The accounts that do this consistently book out their schedule 4-6 weeks deep.

faq.question: What's a realistic cost per booked appointment for a med spa on Meta?
faq.answer: In most US markets, $35-75 per booked appointment is achievable with a paid tripwire offer (like $99 HydraFacial with a $50 deposit) and proper funnel automation. Premium injectable offers can run $75-150 per booking but typically produce higher first-visit revenue.

faq.question: Can I run Botox ads on Meta?
faq.answer: You can advertise injectable services, but you can't use brand names like Botox, Dysport, or Juvederm in ad copy, and you can't show before-and-afters in feed ads. Use category language like "wrinkle relaxer" or "neurotoxin treatment" and lifestyle creative instead of clinical imagery.

faq.question: Should I use Meta lead forms or send traffic to a landing page?
faq.answer: Landing pages with direct booking and deposit collection consistently outperform lead forms for med spas. Lead forms generate cheaper leads but much lower show rates — usually a worse cost per actual appointment unless you have aggressive speed-to-lead automation in place.

faq.question: How long before Meta ads start producing booked appointments?
faq.answer: Expect 10-14 days of learning phase before CPA stabilizes, assuming $75-100/day minimum spend and at least 4-6 creative variations. Most accounts hit their optimal CPA in weeks 3-4. Pulling budget before day 21 is the most common reason med spa Meta accounts fail.

faq.question: Do I need the Meta Conversions API or is the pixel enough?
faq.answer: You need both. The browser pixel alone misses 30-40% of conversion signal due to iOS privacy, ad blockers, and cookie restrictions. Server-side Conversions API (CAPI) captures what the pixel misses and is now essential for the algorithm to optimize properly toward booked appointments.

articles.title: Google Ads for Law Firms Cost Per Lead: What You'll Actually Pay
articles.description: Real CPL benchmarks for PI, family, and criminal law on Google Ads — plus the bidding, tracking, and intake fixes that protect ROI.
articles.keyword: Google Ads for law firms cost per lead
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Legal is the most expensive vertical in Google Ads. Not "one of" — the most expensive. "Personal injury lawyer" routinely clears $300+ per click in Houston, Atlanta, and Los Angeles, and I've seen $500 CPCs on mass tort terms when a national plaintiff firm decides to flex its budget. That math has a downstream effect: cost per lead in legal Google Ads ranges from roughly $80 for criminal defense in a mid-size market to $1,500+ for a signed PI case lead in a Tier 1 metro. If you're a managing partner, marketing director, or agency running paid search for attorneys, this is the spread you're playing inside. This article breaks down what you should actually expect to pay per lead by practice area, why legal CPCs are structurally broken, and the specific bidding, tracking, and intake levers that keep your ROI from getting buried.

Why legal clicks are the most expensive in Google Ads

Three things stack to make legal CPCs brutal: case value, auction concentration, and aggregator bidding. A single signed PI case can be worth $50K–$500K in attorney fees. When the lifetime value of one client is six figures, firms can rationally bid $200+ per click. That alone resets the auction floor for everyone. Then layer in lead aggregators — Lawinfo, FindLaw, Avvo, Nolo, LegalMatch — bidding on the same keywords to resell the lead 4–8 times. They're not trying to win a case; they're trying to capture a form fill. Their bid logic is decoupled from yours. Finally, Google's broad match and Performance Max push your spend into adjacent queries you didn't intend to buy. "Lawyer near me" in Miami pulls in immigration, divorce, DUI, and accident searchers — half of whom you can't monetize. The takeaway: you're not competing with the firm down the street. You're competing with national PI brands, aggregators, and Google's own automation. Plan your budget and match types accordingly. If you don't have at least $15K–$25K/month to test legal search in a competitive metro, you'll burn through learning data before the algorithm stabilizes.

Personal injury CPL benchmarks: $400 to $1,500+

Personal injury is the apex predator of legal paid search. Here's the realistic spread I see across accounts: - Tier 1 metros (LA, NYC, Houston, Miami, Atlanta): $900–$1,500 CPL for a qualified case lead. CPCs $250–$450.

  • Tier 2 metros (Phoenix, Charlotte, Denver, Tampa): $500–$900 CPL. CPCs $120–$250.
  • Tier 3 / secondary markets: $250–$500 CPL. CPCs $60–$120. Those are raw lead numbers — form fills and calls. Signed case acquisition cost typically runs 3–6x the CPL depending on intake quality. A $700 CPL with a 20% sign rate = $3,500 cost per signed case. For a firm averaging $40K in fees per case, that's still a 10x+ return. The firms losing money in PI search usually share one of three problems: they're bidding on "car accident" with broad match (truck driver job searches included), they're not running call tracking with conversation analytics, or their intake team takes 4+ hours to call back a form fill. Fix those three and your effective CPL drops 30–50% without touching the bids. Use CallRail or CallTrackingMetrics for call data, route every lead through a CRM like Lawmatics or Clio Grow, and enforce a 5-minute callback SLA.

Family law CPL: $90 to $350

Family law sits in the middle of the legal CPL curve. Divorce, custody, and child support keywords run $20–$80 CPCs in most metros. Expect: - Divorce / custody (Tier 1 metros): $200–$350 CPL

  • Divorce / custody (Tier 2–3): $90–$200 CPL
  • High-net-worth divorce: $400–$800 CPL but case values justify it The nuance with family law is intent quality varies wildly by keyword. "Cheap divorce lawyer" and "uncontested divorce online" pull in DIY shoppers who'll never retain a $5K+ flat fee. "Divorce attorney consultation" and "custody lawyer [city]" pull in serious buyers. Segment campaigns by intent tier and bid accordingly. I'd rather pay $300 CPL on consultation-intent keywords than $90 CPL on price-shopper keywords with a 3% retention rate. Also: family law has the highest emotional volatility of any legal vertical. Leads call at 11pm after a fight, then ghost the next morning. Your intake needs immediate response (use CallRail's call flows plus an SMS auto-responder via your CRM) and a follow-up sequence that runs 10–14 days. Firms that only follow up twice are leaving 25–40% of signable cases on the table at any CPL.

Criminal defense CPL: $80 to $400

Criminal defense has the most variance because the urgency curve is steep. A DUI arrest at 2am converts within 24 hours or never. A white-collar federal indictment takes 2–6 weeks of shopping. Realistic CPL ranges: - DUI / misdemeanor (most metros): $80–$200 CPL

  • Felony / drug charges: $150–$300 CPL
  • Federal / white collar: $300–$600 CPL but case values are $25K–$250K+ What kills criminal defense ROI isn't CPC — it's after-hours lead loss. 40%+ of arrest-related searches happen between 8pm and 6am. If your intake is 9-to-5, you're paying $150 a click to send leads to voicemail. Fix this with three layers: a 24/7 answering service (Smith.ai or Ruby Receptionists work well for legal), an SMS auto-reply that gives the caller a real human contact path, and a Calendly-style booking link for non-emergency consults. I've seen firms cut effective CPL by 35% just by adding after-hours call handling. Also run dayparting reports monthly. If your conversion rate at 11pm–6am is half of daytime, either fix the intake or pull bids during those hours. Don't subsidize your weaknesses.

The hidden cost: spam, bot traffic, and unqualified leads

Reported CPL in Google Ads is a lie if you're not filtering. Legal lead forms attract three categories of garbage: 1. Existing clients of other firms asking second-opinion questions 2. Opposing parties fishing for info (especially in family/criminal) 3. Bot submissions and competitor sabotage — yes, it happens A "$200 CPL" account often has a true qualified CPL of $350–$500 once you strip out unusable leads. You need to measure both numbers. Build this stack: - reCAPTCHA v3 on every form, scored

  • Honeypot fields to catch lazy bots
  • CallRail conversation intelligence or Marchex to auto-score calls for qualified intent
  • A lead scoring field in your CRM (Lawmatics, Clio Grow, or HubSpot) that intake fills in within 24 hours
  • A weekly report comparing raw CPL vs qualified CPL vs signed-case CPA Without this, you'll optimize toward the wrong leads. Google's algorithm will happily find you 10x more bottom-funnel form fills from people who'll never retain — because to the algorithm, a conversion is a conversion. Send qualified-only conversions back to Google via offline conversion import.
